d912d011742a4b58.topic: Used to / Be used to / Get used to:Diferencia clara con ejemplos cotidianos.

lesson.title: Used to, Be Used To, and Get Used To: A Clear Everyday Guide
lesson.prompt: Used to / Be used to / Get used to:Diferencia clara con ejemplos cotidianos.
lesson.script:
Hello! Today we’re going to clarify three very common expressions that often confuse English learners: used to, be used to, and get used to. They look similar, but they have different meanings and different grammar. By the end of this lesson, you’ll be able to use them naturally in everyday conversations.

Let’s start with used to. We use used to to talk about past habits or past situations that are no longer true. The structure is: subject plus used to plus base verb. For example: I used to live in a small town. This means I lived there in the past, but I don’t live there now. Another example: She used to play tennis every weekend. That was her habit before, but probably not now.

Be careful with questions and negatives. We say: Did you use to work here? Not “did you used to.” And the negative is: I didn’t use to drink coffee. Again, use, not used, after didn’t.

Now, let’s look at be used to. This means that something is normal or familiar for you. It is not strange or difficult anymore. The structure is: subject plus be used to plus noun or verb with ing. For example: I am used to waking up early. This means waking up early is normal for me. Another example: They are used to the cold weather. The cold weather is familiar to them.

Notice the grammar: after be used to, we use a noun or an ing verb. We don’t say: I am used to wake up early. We say: I am used to waking up early.

Finally, we have get used to. This means to become familiar with something over time. It describes a process, a change. The structure is: subject plus get used to plus noun or verb with ing. For example: I’m getting used to my new job. At first it was difficult, but now it is becoming more normal. Another example: You will get used to driving on the left. Maybe it feels strange now, but with practice, it will feel normal.

Let’s compare them in one situation. I used to work from home means I worked from home in the past, but not now. I am used to working from home means working from home is normal for me. I am getting used to working from home means I’m still adapting to it.

Here’s another everyday example. I used to eat dinner late means it was a past habit. I am used to eating dinner late means it feels normal now. I’m getting used to eating dinner late means I’m still adjusting.

So remember: used to is for past habits. Be used to is for things that are normal now. Get used to is for the process of adapting. Practice with your own life: What did you use to do? What are you used to? And what are you getting used to right now?

92aea28f811e5de1.topic: Phrasal verbs del día a día (parte 1) Vocab: figure out, run into, come up with, look forward to, get along with

lesson.title: Everyday Phrasal Verbs: Part 1
lesson.prompt: Phrasal verbs del día a día (parte 1) Vocab: figure out, run into, come up with, look forward to, get along with
lesson.script:
Hi everyone! Today we’re going to learn five very common phrasal verbs that native speakers use all the time in daily conversations. These expressions are useful, natural, and perfect for making your English sound more fluent. The five phrasal verbs are: figure out, run into, come up with, look forward to, and get along with.

Let’s start with figure out. To figure out means to understand something or find the solution to a problem. For example: I can’t figure out how to use this app. Or: We need to figure out what time the train leaves. In Spanish, it can be similar to “entender” or “resolver,” depending on the situation.

Next, run into. This means to meet someone by chance, without planning it. For example: I ran into my old teacher at the supermarket. Or: Guess who I ran into yesterday? My cousin! Be careful: run into can also mean to hit something, like a car running into a wall, but in everyday conversation, it often means meeting someone unexpectedly.

Now let’s look at come up with. This means to think of an idea, a plan, or a solution. For example: She came up with a great idea for the project. Or: We need to come up with a new strategy. This is a very useful phrase at work, at school, and in creative situations.

The fourth phrasal verb is look forward to. This means to feel excited about something that will happen in the future. For example: I’m looking forward to the weekend. Or: We’re looking forward to seeing you soon. Important grammar point: after “look forward to,” use a noun or a verb with -ing. So we say: I’m looking forward to meeting you, not “to meet you.”

Finally, get along with. This means to have a good relationship with someone. For example: I get along with my coworkers. Or: Do you get along with your neighbors? If you don’t have a good relationship, you can say: We don’t really get along.

Let’s review quickly. Figure out means understand or solve. Run into means meet someone by chance. Come up with means create or think of an idea. Look forward to means feel excited about the future. And get along with means have a good relationship.

Try using these five phrasal verbs today. For example: I’m looking forward to practicing English, and I hope I can come up with my own examples. Great job, and see you in the next lesson!

32d6c5c10e4c9681.topic: Articles: a / an / the / Ø — cuándo NO usar 'the' Errores típicos de hispanohablantes.

lesson.title: When NOT to Use “The” in English
lesson.prompt: Articles: a / an / the / Ø — cuándo NO usar 'the' Errores típicos de hispanohablantes.
lesson.script:
Hi everyone! Today we’re going to talk about a small word that causes big problems for Spanish speakers: “the.” In Spanish, we often say “el,” “la,” “los,” or “las” in many situations where English uses no article at all. In English, this “no article” option is sometimes called the zero article, or Ø. Let’s look at when NOT to use “the,” with common mistakes and natural examples.

First, do not use “the” when you talk about things in general using plural nouns. In Spanish you might say “Los perros son leales,” but in English we say “Dogs are loyal,” not “The dogs are loyal.” If you say “the dogs,” you mean specific dogs, maybe the dogs in your house or the dogs we talked about before. So: “I love books,” “Children need attention,” and “Cars are expensive.” No “the” when you mean all books, children, or cars in general.

Second, do not use “the” with uncountable nouns when speaking generally. For example: “I like music,” not “I like the music,” if you mean music in general. Say “Water is important,” “Money doesn’t buy happiness,” and “English is useful.” But use “the” when the noun is specific: “The music at the party was great,” or “The water in this bottle is cold.”

Third, don’t use “the” with most languages, school subjects, sports, or meals in general. Say “I’m learning English,” not “the English.” Say “She studies biology,” “He plays football,” and “We had lunch at two.” However, if you describe a specific meal, you can use “the”: “The lunch we had yesterday was delicious.”

Fourth, do not use “the” with most countries, cities, streets, and continents. Say “I live in Spain,” “She’s from Mexico,” “They visited Paris,” and “Africa is huge.” But remember some exceptions: “the United States,” “the United Kingdom,” “the Netherlands,” and countries with words like “republic,” “kingdom,” or plural names.

Finally, use “a” or “an” for one non-specific singular countable noun. Say “I need a pen,” not “I need pen.” Use “an” before a vowel sound: “an apple,” “an hour.” Use “the” only when the listener knows exactly which one: “I need the pen on your desk.”

So, the key question is: am I talking generally, or about something specific? General plural or uncountable nouns usually take no “the”: “People need love,” “Life is complicated,” “Coffee is popular.” Specific nouns often take “the”: “The coffee in this café is amazing.” Keep noticing this difference, and your English will sound much more natural.

ee4ca41931907177.topic: Preposiciones que confunden: in / on / at (tiempo y lugar)

lesson.title: In, On, At: Time and Place Made Clear
lesson.prompt: Preposiciones que confunden: in / on / at (tiempo y lugar)
lesson.script:
Hello! Today we’re going to clear up one of the most common problems for Spanish-speaking learners of English: the prepositions in, on, and at. These three little words can be confusing because Spanish often uses one preposition, like en, where English uses different ones. But don’t worry. There are useful patterns.

Let’s start with time.

Use in for longer periods of time. For example: in the morning, in June, in 2025, in the summer, in the 1990s. Think of in as something inside a large time space. You can say, I was born in 1998, or We usually travel in August.

Use on for specific days and dates. For example: on Monday, on my birthday, on Christmas Day, on July 4th. You can say, I have a meeting on Friday, or The course starts on September 10th.

Use at for exact times and specific moments. For example: at 8 o’clock, at noon, at midnight, at the weekend in British English, or on the weekend in American English. You can say, Let’s meet at 6:30, or I usually go to bed at midnight.

Now let’s look at place.

Use in when something is inside a space, area, city, country, or room. For example: in the kitchen, in Madrid, in Spain, in a box, in the office. You can say, She lives in Mexico, or My keys are in my bag.

Use on when something is on a surface, a line, or a street. For example: on the table, on the wall, on the floor, on the first page, on Oxford Street. You can say, The picture is on the wall, or There’s a stain on your shirt.

Use at for a specific point or location. For example: at the door, at the bus stop, at the airport, at home, at work, at school. You can say, I’ll wait for you at the entrance, or He’s at the office right now.

Here’s a helpful comparison: I’m in the building means inside the building. I’m on the roof means on the surface at the top. I’m at the building means at that location, maybe outside or near it.

To finish, remember this simple idea: in is for larger spaces or periods, on is for surfaces and specific days, and at is for exact points in time or place. Practice with real sentences, and soon these prepositions will feel much more natural.

0ab47c6c89c5f95c.topic: Make vs. Do — colocaciones que debes memorizar. Vocab: make a decision, do the dishes, make sense, do your best

lesson.title: Make vs. Do: Collocations You Need to Memorize
lesson.prompt: Make vs. Do — colocaciones que debes memorizar. Vocab: make a decision, do the dishes, make sense, do your best
lesson.script:
Have you ever said “do a decision” or “make the dishes” and felt that something sounded wrong? Don’t worry, this is one of the most common problems for English learners, especially Spanish speakers. In Spanish, we often use one verb, like “hacer,” for many situations. But in English, we usually choose between two verbs: make and do. And the tricky part is that many expressions are fixed collocations. That means native speakers always say them in a certain way.

Today, we’ll focus on four very useful expressions: make a decision, do the dishes, make sense, and do your best. These are not just grammar rules; they are phrases you need to memorize and practice until they sound natural.

Let’s start with make a decision. We use make when we talk about creating, producing, or choosing something. A decision is something you create in your mind after thinking about different options. So we say, make a decision.

For example: “I need to make a decision about my job.” Another example: “She made a difficult decision yesterday.” Notice that in the past, we say made a decision, not maked. Make becomes made.

A common mistake is saying “do a decision.” That sounds unnatural in English. The correct phrase is always make a decision. You can also say make an important decision, make a quick decision, or make the right decision.

Now let’s look at do the dishes. We use do for tasks, chores, work, and activities, especially when we are not creating a physical object. When you wash plates, glasses, and cutlery after eating, the natural phrase is do the dishes.

For example: “Can you do the dishes after dinner?” Or: “I did the dishes this morning.” Again, be careful with the past tense. Do becomes did.

Many learners say “make the dishes,” but in English, that sounds like you are creating the plates, maybe in a factory! If you are cleaning them, you do the dishes.

Next: make sense. This expression means that something is logical, clear, or easy to understand. We use make because the idea produces meaning in your mind.

For example: “Your explanation makes sense.” That means your explanation is logical. Another example: “This sentence doesn’t make sense.” That means the sentence is confusing or incorrect.

You can ask: “Does that make sense?” This is a very common question in conversations, meetings, and classes. It means: “Do you understand?” or “Is that clear?”

Be careful: we don’t say “do sense.” The correct collocation is make sense. And in the past, we say made sense. For example: “At first I was confused, but after he explained it, everything made sense.”

Finally, let’s talk about do your best. This means to try as hard as you can, to make your maximum effort. We use do because we are talking about effort and action, not creating something.

For example: “Don’t worry about being perfect. Just do your best.” Another example: “She did her best on the exam.” This is a very useful phrase because it sounds encouraging and natural.

A common mistake is saying “make your best.” But in English, the correct expression is do your best. You can also change the possessive adjective: I’ll do my best, you do your best, he does his best, they did their best.

Now, how can you remember when to use make and when to use do? Here is a simple guide. Use make when the idea is about creating, producing, choosing, or causing something. For example: make a decision, make a cake, make a plan, make a mistake, make sense. Use do when the idea is about tasks, chores, work, study, exercise, or effort. For example: do the dishes, do homework, do exercise, do a job, do your best.

But remember, this is not always enough. English has many fixed phrases, so the best strategy is to learn collocations as complete chunks. Don’t memorize only “decision.” Memorize “make a decision.” Don’t memorize only “dishes.” Memorize “do the dishes.”

Let’s practice with a few quick sentences. Repeat them mentally or out loud.

“I need to make a decision.”

“Can you do the dishes?”

“That doesn’t make sense.”

“I’ll do my best.”

Now let’s make them a little more natural.

“I need to make a decision before Friday.”

“I usually do the dishes after dinner.”

“Your idea makes sense, but we need more time.”

“I’m nervous, but I’ll do my best.”

Great. Here’s your quick recap. In English, we say make a decision, not do a decision. We say do the dishes, not make the dishes. We say make sense, not do sense. And we say do your best, not make your best.

Your challenge today is simple: write four sentences using these expressions. One with make a decision, one with do the dishes, one with make sense, and one with do your best. Practice them as complete phrases, and they’ll start to sound natural very quickly.

7be18917480a7c84.topic: Say vs. Tell vs. Speak vs. Talk

lesson.title: Say, Tell, Speak, and Talk: How to Use Them Naturally
lesson.prompt: Say vs. Tell vs. Speak vs. Talk
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “She told me that,” but then wondered, wait… should it be said, told, spoke, or talked? These four verbs are very common in English, and they all connect to communication. But they are not the same. Today, you’ll learn the difference between say, tell, speak, and talk, with simple patterns and natural examples.

Let’s start with say.

We use say when we focus on the words someone uses. The important thing is the message, not necessarily the listener. For example: “She said she was tired.” “He said, ‘I’ll call you later.’” “What did you say?”

Notice the pattern: say something. You can say a word, a sentence, an opinion, or a message. If you want to mention the listener, use say to. For example: “She said hello to me.” “He said something strange to his boss.” But be careful: we do not normally say “She said me.” That is a common mistake. Say to me, not say me.

Now, let’s look at tell.

We use tell when we focus on giving information to a person. With tell, we usually need a person after the verb. For example: “She told me she was tired.” “He told his parents the truth.” “Can you tell me your name?”

The basic pattern is: tell someone something. Tell me the truth. Tell her the story. Tell us what happened.

So, compare these two sentences: “She said she was tired.” “She told me she was tired.” Both are correct, but the grammar is different. Say focuses on the words or message. Tell focuses on the person receiving the information.

Tell is also common with certain expressions: tell a story, tell the truth, tell a lie, tell a joke, tell the difference, tell someone what to do. For example: “My grandfather tells great stories.” “Please tell the truth.” “I can’t tell the difference between these two words.”

Now, let’s move to speak.

Speak is often used in more formal situations, or when we talk about languages and the ability to use language. For example: “Do you speak English?” “She speaks three languages.” “I need to speak to the manager.” “The president spoke about the economy.”

Speak can sound a little more serious or official than talk. If you say, “I need to speak to you,” it may sound important, serious, or formal. If you say, “I need to talk to you,” it sounds more neutral or conversational.

We also use speak for one-way communication in public situations. For example: “He spoke at a conference.” “She spoke to the audience for an hour.” Here, one person is giving a speech or presentation.

Now, let’s talk about talk.

Talk is usually more informal and conversational. It suggests a conversation between people. For example: “We talked for hours.” “I talked to my friend last night.” “They were talking about their vacation.”

The common patterns are: talk to someone, talk with someone, and talk about something. For example: “I talked to Ana.” “We talked with the teacher.” “They talked about the problem.”

In American English, “talk with” often emphasizes conversation between two people. “Talk to” can also mean conversation, but sometimes it feels more one-directional. For example, “I talked to my son about his grades” could mean I gave him advice or explained something. But in everyday English, both are common.

Let’s compare speak and talk.

“Can I speak to you?” sounds a bit more formal or serious. “Can I talk to you?” sounds more natural in casual conversation. “She speaks English” means she has the ability to use the language. “She talks English” is not correct for language ability. Use speak for languages: speak Spanish, speak French, speak English.

Now let’s put all four verbs together in a mini story.

Yesterday, my teacher said, “You need more practice.” She told me that my pronunciation was improving, but I needed to speak more English in class. Later, I talked to my classmates about the lesson.

Did you notice the difference? The teacher said specific words. She told me information. I needed to speak English, because English is a language. Then I talked to my classmates, because we had a conversation.

Here are some common mistakes Spanish speakers make.

Mistake number one: “She said me the answer.” The correct sentence is: “She told me the answer,” or “She said the answer to me.” But the most natural option is “She told me the answer.”

Mistake number two: “I told that I was busy.” The correct sentence is: “I said that I was busy,” or “I told him that I was busy.” Remember, tell usually needs a person.

Mistake number three: “I talk English.” The correct sentence is: “I speak English.” Use speak for languages.

Mistake number four: “We spoke about movies all night.” This is correct, but in casual conversation, “We talked about movies all night” sounds more natural.

Let’s finish with a simple rule you can remember.

Use say for words or messages: “She said hello.” Use tell for information plus a person: “She told me a secret.” Use speak for languages or formal situations: “He speaks German,” or “She spoke at the meeting.” Use talk for conversations: “We talked about work.”

Quick recap: say something, tell someone something, speak a language or speak formally, and talk to someone about something. Try making four sentences today, one with each verb. The more you use them in real examples, the more natural they will feel.

fcc96e95cb149036.topic: Conectores básicos para sonar más fluido. Vocab: however, although, therefore, besides, in fact, actually

lesson.title: Sound More Fluent with Basic Connectors
lesson.prompt: Conectores básicos para sonar más fluido. Vocab: however, although, therefore, besides, in fact, actually
lesson.script:
Do you ever feel that your English sentences are correct, but they sound a little simple or disconnected? For example: “I was tired. I went to class. I learned a lot.” This is clear, but it doesn’t flow very naturally. Today, you’ll learn six useful connectors that can make your English sound more fluent, more organized, and more confident: however, although, therefore, besides, in fact, and actually.

Let’s start with however. We use however to show contrast. It is similar to “but,” but it sounds a little more formal and polished. For example: “I wanted to go out. However, it started to rain.” You could also say, “The course is difficult. However, I’m enjoying it.” Notice that however often comes at the beginning of a new sentence, followed by a comma. In speaking, we make a small pause after it: “However, I’m enjoying it.”

Now let’s look at although. Although also shows contrast, but the grammar is different. Although connects two ideas in the same sentence. For example: “Although I was tired, I went to the meeting.” This means: I was tired, but I went anyway. Another example: “Although English pronunciation can be difficult, it gets easier with practice.” Be careful: don’t say “Although I was tired, but I went.” In English, use although or but, not both together in the same connection.

Next, we have therefore. Therefore means “for that reason” or “as a result.” It is useful when you want to show a logical consequence. For example: “I didn’t study for the test. Therefore, I didn’t get a good grade.” Another example: “The company is growing quickly. Therefore, they need to hire more people.” Therefore sounds more formal than “so,” but it is very useful in presentations, emails, and academic English.

Now, let’s talk about besides. Besides is used to add extra information, often to give another reason. For example: “I don’t want to go to that restaurant. It’s expensive. Besides, the service is terrible.” Here, besides means “also” or “another important point is.” Another example: “You should apply for the job. You have the right experience. Besides, you speak two languages.” It helps you add a strong extra argument.

Next is in fact. We use in fact to emphasize something, or to add surprising or more specific information. For example: “She speaks English very well. In fact, she used to live in London.” Another example: “The film wasn’t boring. In fact, it was one of the best films I’ve seen this year.” In fact is great when you want to correct an expectation or make your point stronger.

Finally, let’s look at actually. Actually is a very common word, but Spanish speakers need to be careful with it. Actually does not usually mean “actualmente.” In English, actually means “in reality,” “to tell the truth,” or “surprisingly.” For example: “I thought the exam would be easy, but actually, it was quite hard.” Another example: “Do you live in Madrid?” “Actually, I live in Valencia.” Here, actually gently corrects the other person’s idea.

Let’s compare in fact and actually, because they can sometimes feel similar. In fact often adds emphasis: “He’s very good at languages. In fact, he speaks five.” Actually often corrects or clarifies: “People think he’s American, but actually, he’s Canadian.” So, in fact strengthens information, while actually often changes or corrects information.

Now let’s put all six connectors into a short natural example. Listen to this: “I wanted to study abroad. However, I didn’t have enough money at first. Although it was difficult, I saved for a year. Therefore, I was able to pay for my course. Besides, my family helped me with some expenses. In fact, they were the reason I didn’t give up. Actually, the experience was even better than I expected.”

Can you hear how the ideas connect more smoothly? The story feels more organized and natural.

Here’s a quick tip: don’t try to use all of these connectors in every conversation. That can sound unnatural. Instead, choose one or two and use them well. For example, when you want contrast, use however or although. When you want a result, use therefore. When you want to add another reason, use besides. When you want to emphasize, use in fact. And when you want to correct or clarify, use actually.

Let’s recap. However means “but” and introduces contrast. Although also shows contrast, but it connects two parts of one sentence. Therefore shows a result. Besides adds another reason. In fact emphasizes or gives stronger information. And actually means “in reality” or “to be honest,” not “actualmente.”

Your challenge today is simple: write five sentences about your life using these connectors. For example: “Although I’m busy, I study English every day.” The more you use connectors, the more fluent and natural your English will sound.

c627ef32cfab375e.topic: Countable vs. Uncountable: much / many / a few / a little

lesson.title: Much, Many, A Few, and A Little: Countable vs. Uncountable Made Easy
lesson.prompt: Countable vs. Uncountable: much / many / a few / a little
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “I have many money,” or “I need a few water”? Don’t worry, you’re not alone. Spanish speakers often make these mistakes because English divides nouns into two important groups: countable and uncountable. And once you understand that difference, words like much, many, a few, and a little become much easier to use.

Let’s start with the basic idea. Countable nouns are things you can count one by one. For example: one apple, two apples, three apples. One book, two books. One chair, five chairs. These nouns can be singular or plural.

Uncountable nouns are things we don’t usually count one by one. They are often materials, liquids, abstract ideas, or general categories. For example: water, rice, money, information, advice, furniture, time, and traffic. In English, we don’t normally say “one water” or “two informations.” Instead, we say “some water,” “a glass of water,” “some information,” or “a piece of advice.”

Now let’s connect this to much and many.

We use many with countable plural nouns. For example: “I have many friends.” “There are many restaurants in this city.” “How many emails did you receive?” Notice that friends, restaurants, and emails are plural countable nouns. You can count them: one friend, two friends, three friends.

We use much with uncountable nouns. For example: “I don’t have much time.” “There isn’t much traffic today.” “How much money do you need?” Time, traffic, and money are uncountable in English. Even though you can count dollars or euros, the word money itself is uncountable.

Here’s a very useful pattern: in questions, we often use “How many” for countable nouns and “How much” for uncountable nouns.

“How many people are coming?” People are countable.
“How many books did you buy?” Books are countable.
“How much coffee do you drink?” Coffee is uncountable.
“How much information do you need?” Information is uncountable.

Now, let’s talk about a few and a little.

We use a few with countable plural nouns. It means “some,” or “a small number.” For example: “I have a few questions.” “She invited a few friends.” “We stayed there for a few days.” Questions, friends, and days are countable, so we use a few.

We use a little with uncountable nouns. It means “some,” or “a small amount.” For example: “I need a little help.” “Add a little sugar.” “We have a little time before the meeting.” Help, sugar, and time are uncountable, so we use a little.

Let’s compare them side by side.

“I have a few coins.” Coins are countable. You can count them: one coin, two coins.
“I have a little money.” Money is uncountable.

“She drank a few cups of coffee.” Cups are countable.
“She drank a little coffee.” Coffee is uncountable.

“We bought a few chairs.” Chairs are countable.
“We bought a little furniture” sounds strange because furniture is uncountable, but it is possible if you mean a small amount. More naturally, we might say, “We bought a few pieces of furniture.” Pieces are countable.

This is a key trick: if an uncountable noun feels difficult, use a container or a unit. For example, you can’t say “three waters” in standard English when you mean the liquid, but you can say “three bottles of water” or “three glasses of water.” You can’t say “two advices,” but you can say “two pieces of advice.” You can’t say “many furnitures,” but you can say “many pieces of furniture.”

Let’s look at common mistakes and correct them.

Incorrect: “I have many homework.”
Correct: “I have a lot of homework,” or “I have much homework.” But in everyday spoken English, “a lot of homework” sounds more natural.

Incorrect: “I need a few information.”
Correct: “I need a little information,” or “I need a few pieces of information.”

Incorrect: “How many money do you have?”
Correct: “How much money do you have?”

Incorrect: “There are much people here.”
Correct: “There are many people here.”

One more important point: much is common in questions and negative sentences, but in positive sentences, native speakers often prefer “a lot of.” For example, “Do you have much work today?” sounds natural. “I don’t have much work today” sounds natural. But “I have much work today” sounds a bit formal or unnatural. It’s more common to say, “I have a lot of work today.”

The same is true with many, although many is more acceptable in positive sentences. “I have many friends” is correct, but “I have a lot of friends” often sounds more natural in conversation.

So, here’s your quick recap. Use many with countable plural nouns: many books, many people, many ideas. Use much with uncountable nouns: much time, much money, much information. Use a few with countable plural nouns: a few friends, a few minutes, a few questions. Use a little with uncountable nouns: a little water, a little help, a little patience.

And remember, when in doubt, ask yourself: Can I count this noun one by one? If yes, use many or a few. If no, use much or a little. Practice today by making four sentences: one with many, one with much, one with a few, and one with a little.

3eefdd11a6951589.topic: Gerundios e infinitivos: ¿'I enjoy to swim' o 'I enjoy swimming'?

lesson.title: Gerunds and Infinitives: Say “I Enjoy Swimming,” Not “I Enjoy to Swim”
lesson.prompt: Gerundios e infinitivos: ¿'I enjoy to swim' o 'I enjoy swimming'?
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “I enjoy to swim,” and then wondered why it sounded a little strange? You’re not alone. Gerunds and infinitives are one of the most common challenges for Spanish-speaking learners of English, because in Spanish you often use the infinitive: “Me gusta nadar.” But in English, after some verbs, we need the gerund: “I enjoy swimming.”

Today, let’s make this clearer and more natural.

First, what is a gerund? A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used like a noun. For example: swimming, reading, dancing, studying. You can say, “Swimming is fun,” or “I love reading.”

And what is an infinitive? The infinitive is “to” plus the base verb: to swim, to read, to dance, to study. For example: “I want to swim,” or “She needs to study.”

Now, here is the important part: some verbs are followed by a gerund, and some verbs are followed by an infinitive. There is not always a perfect rule, so the best strategy is to learn common verb patterns.

Let’s start with verbs followed by a gerund. After these verbs, use the -ing form: enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, mind, suggest, and consider.

So we say: “I enjoy swimming,” not “I enjoy to swim.”

More examples: “She avoids eating too much sugar.” “We finished watching the movie.” “He keeps talking during the class.” “Do you mind opening the window?” “They suggested going to a new restaurant.” “I’m considering changing jobs.”

Notice that these verbs are followed by actions, but the action uses -ing.

Now let’s look at verbs followed by an infinitive. After these verbs, use “to” plus the base verb: want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, offer, and promise.

For example: “I want to travel.” “She needs to study.” “We decided to stay home.” “He hopes to find a better job.” “They plan to visit London.” “I’m learning to drive.” “She offered to help me.” “He promised to call.”

For Spanish speakers, this often feels more familiar because it is similar to Spanish: “Quiero viajar,” “Necesito estudiar,” “Decidimos quedarnos.” In English, these verbs usually take the infinitive.

But be careful: not every English verb works like Spanish. For example, in Spanish you say, “Disfruto nadar” or “Me gusta nadar.” In English, with “enjoy,” we say “I enjoy swimming.”

What about “like,” “love,” and “hate”? Good news: these verbs can often be followed by either a gerund or an infinitive, with little difference in meaning.

You can say: “I like swimming” or “I like to swim.” “She loves dancing” or “She loves to dance.” “They hate waiting” or “They hate to wait.”

In everyday English, both are common. Sometimes the gerund sounds more like a general preference: “I like swimming,” meaning swimming as an activity. The infinitive can sound a little more specific or intentional: “I like to swim in the morning.” But in many cases, both are correct.

Now, let’s talk about a few verbs where the meaning changes depending on whether you use a gerund or an infinitive.

The first one is “stop.” “I stopped smoking” means I quit smoking. I don’t smoke anymore. But “I stopped to smoke” means I stopped another activity in order to smoke. For example, “I was driving, and I stopped to smoke.” Very different meaning.

Another one is “remember.” “I remember locking the door” means I have a memory of doing it. But “I remembered to lock the door” means I didn’t forget; I did the action.

And “try” can also change. “Try doing yoga” means experiment with yoga to see if it helps. “Try to do yoga” means make an effort to do it, maybe even if it’s difficult.

So, how can you remember all this? Don’t try to memorize a huge list in one day. Start with the most common verbs. Repeat them in short phrases.

Say these out loud: “I enjoy working.” “I avoid eating late.” “I finished studying.” “I want to improve.” “I need to practice.” “I decided to learn English.”

Also, when you learn a new verb, don’t learn it alone. Learn the pattern. Don’t just write “enjoy.” Write “enjoy doing something.” Don’t just write “want.” Write “want to do something.” This will help your brain remember the correct structure.

Let’s do a quick practice. Which one sounds correct: “I enjoy to cook” or “I enjoy cooking”? Correct: “I enjoy cooking.”

What about: “She decided studying” or “She decided to study”? Correct: “She decided to study.”

And: “Do you mind to wait?” or “Do you mind waiting?” Correct: “Do you mind waiting?”

Great. So, quick recap: a gerund is the -ing form, like “swimming.” An infinitive is “to” plus a verb, like “to swim.” After “enjoy,” use a gerund: “I enjoy swimming.” After verbs like “want,” “need,” and “decide,” use the infinitive: “I want to swim.” And with verbs like “like,” “love,” and “hate,” both forms are often possible.

Your challenge today is to write five sentences about your life using gerunds and infinitives. For example: “I enjoy learning English,” and “I want to speak more confidently.” The more you practice the patterns, the more natural they will sound.

lesson.title: The 4 Conditionals in English: A Complete Guide
lesson.prompt: Los 4 condicionales — guía completa
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “If I will have time, I will call you”? If yes, don’t worry. This is one of the most common mistakes Spanish speakers make in English. Today, you’ll learn the four main conditionals in English: zero, first, second, and third. By the end, you’ll know when to use each one and how to build them correctly.

Let’s start with the big idea. Conditionals are sentences with “if.” They talk about a condition and a result. For example: “If it rains, I stay home.” The condition is “if it rains.” The result is “I stay home.”

Now, let’s look at the four types.

First, the zero conditional. We use the zero conditional for facts, general truths, habits, and things that are always or normally true. The structure is: if plus present simple, present simple.

For example: “If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.” This is a scientific fact. Another example: “If I drink coffee at night, I don’t sleep well.” This is a personal truth or habit.

You can also change the order: “Water boils if you heat it to 100 degrees.” When “if” is in the middle, you don’t need a comma.

Important: In the zero conditional, both parts usually use the present simple. Don’t say, “If you heat water, it will boil” if you are talking about a general fact. That sounds more like a future possibility. For facts, use: “If you heat water, it boils.”

Second, the first conditional. We use the first conditional for real possibilities in the future. These are situations that can really happen. The structure is: if plus present simple, will plus verb.

For example: “If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.” Rain tomorrow is possible. Staying home is the future result. Another example: “If I finish work early, I’ll call you.”

Here is the key point for Spanish speakers: after “if,” we do not normally use “will.” In Spanish, you might think “si tendré tiempo,” or you may translate from “si tengo tiempo.” In English, say: “If I have time, I will help you.” Not: “If I will have time.”

More examples: “If she studies, she will pass the exam.” “If they invite us, we’ll go to the party.” “If you don’t hurry, you’ll miss the train.”

You can also use “may,” “might,” “can,” or imperatives instead of “will.” For example: “If you’re tired, you can take a break.” “If I have time, I might join you.” “If you see Ana, tell her I called.”

Third, the second conditional. We use the second conditional for imaginary, unlikely, or hypothetical situations in the present or future. The structure is: if plus past simple, would plus verb.

For example: “If I won the lottery, I would travel around the world.” Is this possible? Yes, but not very likely. Another example: “If I had more free time, I would learn Italian.” This describes an imaginary situation now: I don’t have much free time, but I’m imagining it.

With the verb “be,” many grammar books recommend “were” for all subjects: “If I were you, I would talk to him.” This is very common and considered correct, especially in formal English. In informal conversation, you may also hear “If I was you,” but “If I were you” is the safer choice.

More examples: “If she lived closer, we would see her more often.” “If I spoke perfect English, I would feel more confident.” “If you didn’t spend so much money, you could save more.”

Notice the meaning: in the second conditional, we are not talking about a real plan. We are imagining. Compare these two sentences: “If I have time, I’ll call you.” That’s first conditional, a real future possibility. “If I had time, I would call you.” That’s second conditional, meaning I probably don’t have time.

Fourth, the third conditional. We use the third conditional to talk about imaginary situations in the past. It describes something that did not happen, and the imagined result. The structure is: if plus past perfect, would have plus past participle.

For example: “If I had studied more, I would have passed the exam.” This means I didn’t study enough, and I didn’t pass. Another example: “If we had left earlier, we wouldn’t have missed the train.” We left late, and we missed the train.

More examples: “If she had told me, I would have helped her.” “If I hadn’t eaten so much, I wouldn’t have felt sick.” “If they had invited us, we would have gone.”

This conditional is very useful for regrets, criticism, and imagining different past results. In Spanish, you might think of phrases like “si hubiera…” In English, remember: “If I had known, I would have…” For example: “If I had known you were coming, I would have cooked dinner.”

Let’s do a quick comparison.

Zero conditional: general truth. “If you mix red and blue, you get purple.”

First conditional: real future possibility. “If it rains, I’ll take an umbrella.”

Second conditional: imaginary present or future. “If I had a car, I would drive to work.”

Third conditional: imaginary past. “If I had had a car, I would have driven to work.”

Let’s also remember the common mistake: don’t use “will” after “if” in the first conditional. Say: “If I see him, I’ll tell him.” Not: “If I will see him.”

So, here’s your recap: zero conditional is for facts and habits, first conditional is for real future possibilities, second conditional is for imaginary present or future situations, and third conditional is for imaginary past situations and regrets.

Now, practice with your own examples. Try making one sentence for each conditional using your real life: your habits, your plans, your dreams, and one past regret. The more personal your examples are, the faster you’ll remember the structures.

8fa8bded1fe80c4b.topic: Mixed conditionals (el que casi nadie domina)

lesson.title: Mixed Conditionals: The Conditional Most Learners Don’t Master
lesson.prompt: Mixed conditionals (el que casi nadie domina)
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “If I had studied more, I would have a better job now”? If yes, congratulations: you were using one of the most powerful structures in English, the mixed conditional. And if that sentence sounds confusing, don’t worry. Today we’re going to make it clear, natural, and useful.

Most learners know the basic conditionals. The second conditional talks about imaginary situations in the present or future: “If I had more time, I would travel more.” The third conditional talks about imaginary situations in the past: “If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam.”

But real life is not always only present or only past. Sometimes a past situation affects the present. And sometimes a present situation would have changed the past. That is where mixed conditionals come in.

Let’s start with the most common type: past condition, present result.

The structure is: If plus past perfect, then would plus base verb.

For example: “If I had learned English earlier, I would speak more confidently now.”

The first part is about the past: “If I had learned English earlier.” But the result is about now: “I would speak more confidently now.”

Here are more examples: “If she had saved more money, she wouldn’t be so stressed now.” “If we hadn’t missed the train, we would be at the meeting now.” “If I had accepted that job, I would live in London today.”

Notice the time words: now, today, at the moment. They often help show that the result is in the present.

This type is very useful when you want to talk about regrets or past decisions that affect your current life. For Spanish speakers, it can feel similar to sentences like “Si hubiera estudiado más, ahora tendría un mejor trabajo.” But remember: in English, we say “If I had studied more, I would have a better job now.” Not “would had.” Not “would have had” if the result is present. The result is “would have,” meaning “tendría,” not “would have had,” meaning “habría tenido.”

Now let’s look at the second common type: present condition, past result.

The structure is: If plus past simple, then would have plus past participle.

For example: “If I were more organized, I would have finished the project yesterday.”

The condition is about my general situation now: “If I were more organized.” But the result is about the past: “I would have finished the project yesterday.”

More examples: “If he knew her number, he would have called her last night.” “If they were more careful, they wouldn’t have made that mistake.” “If I didn’t have so much fear of flying, I would have visited you last year.”

This type is less common, but it is very expressive. It connects a present characteristic or situation with a past result.

Let’s compare the two types clearly.

Past to present: “If I had gone to bed earlier, I wouldn’t be so tired now.” The past action affects the present state.

Present to past: “If I weren’t such a night owl, I wouldn’t have gone to bed so late.” A present characteristic explains a past action.

Let’s practice with a realistic situation. Imagine you didn’t study English when you were younger, and now you feel nervous in meetings. You can say: “If I had studied English when I was younger, I would feel more confident in meetings now.”

Now imagine you are a very shy person, and because of that, you didn’t speak at an important meeting yesterday. You can say: “If I weren’t so shy, I would have spoken in the meeting yesterday.”

A very common mistake is mixing the verb forms incorrectly. Don’t say: “If I would have studied, I would speak better now.” In English, after “if,” we usually don’t use “would” in these conditional structures. Say: “If I had studied, I would speak better now.”

Another mistake is using the third conditional when you need a present result. For example, “If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor.” This means the result is also in the past. Maybe you were a doctor before, but not now. If you mean now, say: “If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.”

Let’s try a few more natural examples.

“If I had taken that course, I would know how to use this software.”

“If we had left earlier, we wouldn’t be stuck in traffic now.”

“If you had told me the truth, I wouldn’t be angry now.”

“If I spoke better German, I would have applied for that job.”

“If she were more patient, she wouldn’t have reacted like that.”

“If he didn’t care about you, he wouldn’t have helped you yesterday.”

So, here’s the key idea: mixed conditionals connect two different times. Past condition, present result. Or present condition, past result.

Before we finish, repeat these two model sentences in your mind: “If I had practiced more, I would be better now.” And: “If I were more confident, I would have said yes.”

That’s the heart of mixed conditionals. They may look difficult at first, but once you understand the time connection, they become logical. Try creating two sentences today: one about a past decision that affects your present, and one about a present characteristic that affected a past event. The more personal your examples are, the faster you’ll master them.

lesson.title: Reported Speech: Backshift and the Exceptions You Need to Know
lesson.prompt: Reported Speech — backshift y excepciones
lesson.script:
Have you ever tried to tell a story in English and got stuck with sentences like, “He said he is tired” or “He said he was tired”? If yes, you are not alone. Reported speech can feel tricky, especially because English often changes the verb tense when we report what someone said. This change is called backshift.

Let’s start with the basic idea. Direct speech is the exact words someone said. For example: Maria said, “I am busy.” Reported speech tells the same idea, but not with the exact words. Maria said that she was busy.

Notice the change: “am” becomes “was.” That is backshift. In reported speech, when the reporting verb is in the past, like “said,” “told,” “explained,” or “asked,” we often move the original verb one step back in time.

Here are the most common changes. Present simple becomes past simple. “I work from home” becomes: She said that she worked from home. Present continuous becomes past continuous. “I am studying” becomes: He said that he was studying. Present perfect becomes past perfect. “I have finished” becomes: She said that she had finished. Past simple often becomes past perfect. “I lost my keys” becomes: He said that he had lost his keys. And “will” usually becomes “would.” “I will call you” becomes: She said that she would call me.

We also change pronouns, possessives, and time expressions. For example: “I will see you tomorrow” can become: He said that he would see me the next day. “I” changes to “he,” “you” changes to “me,” and “tomorrow” changes to “the next day.” Other common time changes are: today becomes that day, yesterday becomes the day before, next week becomes the following week, and now becomes then.

So far, this seems simple: past reporting verb, move the tense back. But English is not always that strict. There are important exceptions.

Exception number one: if the information is still true, backshift is optional. For example, imagine someone says, “I live in Madrid.” Later, you report it. If she still lives in Madrid, you can say: She said that she lives in Madrid. This sounds natural because the information is still true now. You can also say: She said that she lived in Madrid. This is also correct, but it may sound more distant or simply more like classic reported speech.

Another example: “English is useful.” You can report it as: The teacher said that English is useful. We don’t need to say “was useful” because English is still useful. This exception is very common with facts, general truths, permanent situations, and things that are still relevant.

Exception number two: universal truths usually do not need backshift. If someone said, “Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius,” we normally report: He said that water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. Saying “boiled” is grammatically possible in some contexts, but “boils” is more natural because it is a scientific fact.

Exception number three: if the reporting verb is in the present, there is no backshift. For example: She says, “I’m tired.” Reported speech: She says that she is tired. Not “was tired,” because “says” is present. Another example: He tells me that he doesn’t understand. The reporting verb “tells” is present, so the rest can stay in the present.

Exception number four: modal verbs do not all change in the same way. “Can” usually becomes “could.” “I can help” becomes: She said that she could help. “May” can become “might.” “It may rain” becomes: He said that it might rain. But some modals do not change: should, could, would, might, and must often stay the same. For example: “You should apologize” becomes: She said that I should apologize. “I might be late” becomes: He said that he might be late.

Be careful with “must.” If “must” means obligation, it can stay as “must,” or change to “had to.” For example: “I must leave early” becomes: She said that she must leave early, or She said that she had to leave early. In everyday English, “had to” is very common for past reporting.

Exception number five: when we report very soon after the original statement, we often keep the original tense. Imagine your friend says, “I’m hungry,” and two minutes later you tell someone: He said he’s hungry. That sounds natural because the situation is still happening now. If you say, “He said he was hungry,” it is also correct, but it can sound less immediate.

Let’s compare a few examples so you can feel the difference. Direct speech: “I’m tired.” Reported with backshift: She said she was tired. Reported with no backshift, if it is still true: She said she is tired. Direct speech: “I have a meeting tomorrow.” Reported later: He said he had a meeting the next day. Reported on the same day, and tomorrow is still tomorrow: He said he has a meeting tomorrow.

A useful tip: don’t think of backshift as a mechanical rule that always happens. Think of it as a way to create distance. If the original words feel distant in time, use backshift. If the information is still true, current, or generally true, you can often keep the tense.

Let’s finish with a quick recap. In reported speech, when the reporting verb is in the past, we usually move the tense back: present to past, past to past perfect, and will to would. But we don’t always backshift. We can keep the original tense when the information is still true, when it is a general fact, when the reporting verb is present, or when the situation is still immediate. The key question is: Am I reporting something as distant, or is it still true and relevant now? Practice with real sentences, and reported speech will start to feel much more natural.

2fba27888e7ca610.topic: Passive Voice — cuándo SÍ y cuándo NO usarla

lesson.title: Passive Voice: When to Use It and When to Avoid It
lesson.prompt: Passive Voice — cuándo SÍ y cuándo NO usarla
lesson.script:
Have you ever written a sentence like, “The meeting was organized by the manager,” and wondered, “Is this correct English… or does it sound strange?” Good news: the passive voice is not wrong. In fact, English speakers use it all the time. But the key is knowing when it sounds natural, and when it makes your sentence heavy, vague, or too formal.

Today, we’ll look at when you should use the passive voice, and when it’s better to use the active voice.

First, let’s quickly remember the structure. In the active voice, the subject does the action. For example: “The company launched a new product.” The company is doing the action.

In the passive voice, the subject receives the action. For example: “A new product was launched by the company.” The product receives the action.

The basic structure is: subject plus “be” plus past participle. For example: “The email was sent,” “The documents are checked,” “The house has been sold,” or “The problem will be solved.”

So, when should we use the passive voice?

Use the passive voice when the action is more important than the person who does it. This is very common in news, formal writing, reports, and business English. For example: “Three people were injured in the accident.” Here, the important information is that three people were injured. We may not know who caused the accident, or that may not be the focus.

Another example: “The new law was approved yesterday.” The focus is the law, not the politicians who approved it.

Use the passive voice when you don’t know who did the action. For example: “My phone was stolen.” You don’t know who stole it, so the passive is perfect. In Spanish, you might say something like “Me robaron el teléfono.” In English, “My phone was stolen” sounds very natural.

Use the passive voice when it’s obvious who did the action. For example: “The suspect was arrested.” Who arrested the suspect? The police, obviously. You don’t need to say it. Another example: “The patient was taken to hospital.” We understand that doctors, nurses, or emergency workers took the patient.

Use the passive voice when you want to sound more formal or objective. This is useful in academic and professional contexts. For example: “The results were analyzed carefully.” This sounds more objective than “We analyzed the results carefully.” Both are correct, but the passive version focuses more on the process and less on the people.

You’ll often hear this in reports: “The data was collected in June,” “The participants were interviewed,” or “The proposal has been reviewed.”

Now, when should you avoid the passive voice?

Avoid it when the active voice is clearer, shorter, and more direct. For example, instead of saying, “The report was written by Ana,” it’s usually better to say, “Ana wrote the report.” It’s simpler and more natural.

Compare these two sentences: “A mistake was made by the assistant.” “The assistant made a mistake.” The second sentence is much clearer. The first one sounds a little indirect, maybe even like someone is trying to avoid responsibility.

This is important: passive voice can sometimes hide responsibility. For example: “The budget was reduced.” By whom? The company? The government? The manager? If the person or organization is important, use the active voice: “The government reduced the budget.”

Avoid the passive if you use “by” too much. Many learners think passive voice always needs “by,” but that’s not true. In fact, many passive sentences do not include the agent. We say, “My car was repaired,” not always “My car was repaired by the mechanic.” If you need to say who did the action, ask yourself: would the active voice be better? “The mechanic repaired my car” is probably more natural.

Also, avoid translating directly from Spanish. In Spanish, passive or impersonal structures can be very common, like “Se venden casas” or “Se habla inglés.” In English, we might say, “Houses are sold,” but in many real situations, we prefer a different structure. For example, “They sell houses here,” or “English is spoken here.” It depends on the context.

Let’s look at some natural choices.

If you’re telling a story, active voice is usually better: “Someone broke the window,” “The teacher explained the rule,” “My friend recommended this restaurant.” Stories need movement, and active voice feels more alive.

But if the result is more important than the person, passive voice is better: “The window was broken,” “The rule was explained,” “This restaurant was recommended to me.”

Here’s a practical tip: ask yourself three questions. One: Do I know who did the action? Two: Is that person important? Three: Do I want to focus on the action or the result? If the person is known and important, use active voice. If the person is unknown, obvious, or not important, passive voice is probably a good choice.

Let’s practice with a few examples.

“The police arrested the man.” Active. The police are important and clear.

“The man was arrested.” Passive. This is natural if the important thing is the arrest, not who did it.

“Shakespeare wrote Hamlet.” Active. Don’t say “Hamlet was written by Shakespeare” unless you have a special reason. The writer is important.

“My wallet was stolen.” Passive. Very natural. You don’t know who did it.

“The company will announce the results tomorrow.” Active. Clear and direct.

“The results will be announced tomorrow.” Passive. Also natural, especially if the focus is on the results.

So, quick recap: use the passive voice when the action or result is more important than the person, when you don’t know who did it, when it’s obvious, or when you need a formal and objective tone. Avoid it when the active voice is clearer, shorter, and more direct, especially when the person doing the action is important.

The passive voice is not bad English. It’s a tool. The goal is not to avoid it completely, but to use it with intention. Next time you write a passive sentence, stop for one second and ask: “Do I need the person who did the action, or do I need the result?” That simple question will help you sound much more natural in English.

e6e9e155457afd77.topic: Modal verbs: must / have to / should / ought to

lesson.title: Must, Have To, Should, and Ought To: How to Sound Natural in English
lesson.prompt: Modal verbs: must / have to / should / ought to
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “I must go to work tomorrow,” and wondered if it sounds too dramatic? Or maybe you use “should” for everything because it feels safe? Don’t worry. Today we’ll make the difference between must, have to, should, and ought to clear, simple, and practical.

These four expressions are all connected to obligation, advice, or necessity. But they don’t feel exactly the same. Choosing the right one helps you sound more natural in English.

Let’s start with must.

We use must when the obligation feels strong, personal, or official. It often sounds like the speaker believes something is very important.

For example: “You must wear a seatbelt.” This sounds like a strong rule. Another example: “I must call my mother today.” Here, the obligation feels personal. Maybe I promised, or I feel it is very important.

Must can also be used for logical conclusions. For example: “She’s been studying all day. She must be tired.” This does not mean obligation. It means I am almost sure she is tired. Another example: “You got the job? You must be very happy!”

Now, let’s look at have to.

Have to is also used for obligation, but it often sounds more external. The obligation comes from a rule, a situation, a boss, a school, or reality.

For example: “I have to be at work at eight.” This means my job requires it. “We have to pay taxes.” This is a legal obligation. “She has to take the exam again.” This is because of the situation.

In everyday spoken English, have to is more common than must for obligations. Many native speakers say “I have to go,” not “I must go.” Both can be correct, but “I have to go” sounds more natural in many normal situations.

Be careful with the negative forms, because they are very different.

Must not, or mustn’t, means prohibition. It means something is not allowed.

For example: “You mustn’t smoke in the hospital.” This means it is forbidden. “You must not share your password.” That means don’t do it.

But don’t have to means there is no obligation. It means it is not necessary.

For example: “You don’t have to come to the meeting.” This means you can come if you want, but it is not necessary. “We don’t have to wear formal clothes.” That means casual clothes are okay.

So remember: “mustn’t” means don’t do it. “Don’t have to” means you can, but it’s not necessary.

Now let’s talk about should.

Should is used for advice, recommendations, and opinions about what is a good idea. It is softer than must or have to.

For example: “You should drink more water.” This is advice. “You should see that movie. It’s excellent.” This is a recommendation. “He should apologize.” This means I think apologizing is the right thing to do.

Should is very useful because it is polite and flexible. If a friend says, “I’m always tired,” you can say, “You should try going to bed earlier.” That sounds helpful, not aggressive.

The negative form is shouldn’t. For example: “You shouldn’t eat so much sugar.” “They shouldn’t drive so fast.” It means I think it is a bad idea.

Now, what about ought to?

Ought to is very similar to should. It also expresses advice or moral obligation. For example: “You ought to call your grandmother.” This means it would be the right thing to do. “We ought to leave soon if we don’t want to be late.” This means leaving soon is a good idea.

However, ought to is less common than should in everyday conversation, especially in American English. It can sound a little more formal, traditional, or moral. In many situations, you can use should instead and sound completely natural.

For example, instead of saying, “You ought to study more,” most people would simply say, “You should study more.”

Let’s compare the four with the same situation.

Imagine you have an important exam tomorrow.

“I must study tonight.” This sounds strong and personal. I feel it is very important.

“I have to study tonight.” This sounds like a necessity because of the exam.

“I should study tonight.” This sounds like advice. It is a good idea, but maybe I won’t do it.

“I ought to study tonight.” This also means it is a good idea, maybe with a stronger feeling of responsibility.

Here’s another situation: a museum rule.

“You mustn’t touch the paintings.” This means touching them is prohibited.

“You don’t have to buy tickets online.” This means buying online is optional. You can buy them there if you want.

“You should arrive early.” This is advice.

“You ought to check the opening hours.” This is also advice, though a bit less common.

One more important grammar point: after must, should, and ought to, we use the base form of the verb. We say “You must go,” “You should study,” and “You ought to listen.” With have to, we also use the base verb after “to”: “I have to work,” “She has to leave.” Remember that with he, she, and it, we say has to, not have to: “He has to wake up early.”

So, quick recap. Use must for strong personal or official obligation, and also for logical conclusions, like “She must be tired.” Use have to for obligations that come from rules, circumstances, or external situations. Use mustn’t for prohibition, and don’t have to when something is not necessary. Use should for advice and recommendations. Use ought to in a similar way to should, but remember it is less common and can sound a little more formal or moral.

Now try making four sentences about your own life: one with must, one with have to, one with should, and one with ought to. The more you connect grammar to your real life, the more natural it becomes.

It means I'm almost sure she is tired. Another example, you got the job. You must be very happy. Now, let's look at have to. Have to is also used for obligation, but it often sounds more external. The obligation comes from a rule, a situation, a boss, a school, or reality. For example, I have to be at work at eight. This means my job requires it. We have to pay taxes. This is a legal obligation. She has to take the exam again. This is because of the situation. In everyday spoken English, have to is more common than must for obligations. Many native speakers say I have to go, not I must go. Both can be correct, but I have to go sounds more natural in many normal situations. Be careful with the negative forms, because they are very different. Must not or mustn't means prohibition. It means something is not allowed. For example, you mustn't smoke in the hospital. This means it is forbidden. You must not share your password. That means don't do it. But don't have to means there is no obligation. It means it is not necessary. For example, you don't have to come to the meeting. This means you can come if you want, but it is not necessary. We don't have to wear formal clothes. That means casual clothes are okay. So remember, mustn't means don't do it. Don't have to means you can, but it's not necessary. Now let's talk about should. Should is used for advice, recommendations, and opinions about what is a good idea. It is softer than must or have to. For example, you should drink more water. This is advice. You should see that movie. It's excellent. This is a recommendation. He should apologize. This means I think apologizing is the right thing to do. Should is very useful because it is polite and flexible. If a friend says, I'm always tired, you can say, you should try going to bed earlier. That sounds helpful. Not aggressive. The negative form is shouldn't. For example, you shouldn't eat so much sugar. They shouldn't drive so fast. It means I think it is a bad idea. Now what about ought to? Ought to is very similar to should. It also expresses advice or moral obligation. For example, you ought to call your grandmother. This means it would be the right thing to do. We ought to leave soon if we don't want to be late. This means leaving soon is a good idea. However, ought to is less common than should in everyday conversation, especially in American English. It can sound a little more formal, traditional, or moral. In many situations, you can use should instead and sound completely natural. For example, instead of saying, you ought to study more, most people would simply say, you should study more. Let's compare the four with the same situation. Imagine you have an important exam tomorrow. I must study tonight. This sounds strong and personal. I feel it is very important. I have to study tonight. This sounds like a necessity because of the exam. I should study tonight. This sounds like advice. It is a good idea, but maybe I won't do it. I ought to study tonight. This also means it is a good idea, maybe with a stronger feeling of responsibility. Here's another situation, a museum rule. You mustn't touch the paintings. This means touching them is prohibited. You don't have to buy tickets online. This means buying online is optional. You can buy them there if you want. You should arrive early. This is advice. You ought to check the opening hours. This is also advice, though, a bit less common. One more important grammar point. After must, should, and ought to, we use the base form of the verb. We say you must go. You should study. And you ought to listen. With have to, we also use the base verb after to, I have to work. She has to leave. Remember that with he, she, and it, we say has to, not have to. He has to wake up early. So quick recap, use must for strong personal or official obligation, and also for logical conclusions like she must be tired. Use have to for obligations that come from rules, circumstances, or external situations. Use mustn't for prohibition, and don't have to when something is not necessary. Use should for advice and recommendations. Use ought to in a similar way to should, but remember, it is less common and can sound a little more formal or moral. Now try making four sentences about your own life. One with must, one with have to, one with should, and one with ought to. The more you connect grammar to your real life, the more natural it becomes.

3c66ab9d2f2dbda4.topic: Modales de probabilidad: must be / might be / can't be

lesson.title: Must Be, Might Be, and Can’t Be: Guessing with Confidence
lesson.prompt: Modales de probabilidad: must be / might be / can't be
lesson.script:
Have you ever heard a strange noise at night and thought, “That must be the wind”? Or maybe you saw a friend looking tired and said, “She might be stressed”? In English, we use “must be,” “might be,” and “can’t be” to make guesses about the present. They help us express how sure we are about something, without saying we know it one hundred percent.

Today, you’ll learn how to use these three modal phrases to talk about probability in a natural way.

Let’s start with “must be.” We use “must be” when we are very sure something is true. We don’t have complete proof, but the evidence is strong.

For example: “The lights are off, and nobody is answering the door. They must be out.”

This means: I am almost sure they are not at home.

Another example: “You’ve been working all day. You must be tired.”

Here, I see the situation, and I make a logical guess. Working all day usually makes people tired, so I say, “You must be tired.”

Be careful: in Spanish, you might think of “debe de ser” or “seguramente es.” In English, “must be” is not an obligation here. It is probability. “You must be tired” does not mean “You have to be tired.” It means “I’m almost sure you are tired.”

Now let’s look at “might be.” We use “might be” when something is possible, but we are not very sure. It’s like saying “maybe.”

For example: “She’s not in the office. She might be in a meeting.”

This means: Maybe she is in a meeting. I’m not sure.

Another example: “This restaurant is very popular. The food might be good.”

I don’t know if the food is good, but it’s possible because many people go there.

You can also use “could be” in a similar way. “She could be in a meeting” is very close to “She might be in a meeting.” But today, focus on “might be” for possibility.

Now, what about “can’t be”? We use “can’t be” when we are very sure something is not true. The evidence tells us that it is impossible, or almost impossible.

For example: “That can’t be John. John is in Madrid this week.”

I see someone, but I know John is in Madrid, so I’m sure it is not him.

Another example: “This answer can’t be correct. The total should be 100, but this says 150.”

The information shows me the answer is wrong, so I say, “It can’t be correct.”

So, let’s compare the three forms.

If you are very sure something is true, use “must be.” “He must be the new teacher.”

If you think something is possible, use “might be.” “He might be the new teacher.”

If you are very sure something is not true, use “can’t be.” “He can’t be the new teacher.”

Let’s imagine a situation. You arrive at work, and your colleague Ana is not at her desk.

You see her coat on the chair and her computer is on. You say, “She must be in the building.” You are very sure because her things are there.

But you don’t know exactly where she is. So you say, “She might be in the kitchen.” That is possible, but you are not sure.

Then someone says, “Maybe she is at home.” You answer, “She can’t be at home. Her coat and computer are here.” You are very sure that idea is not true.

Notice the structure. We use modal plus “be” plus a noun, adjective, or place.

For a noun: “He must be a doctor.” “She might be the manager.” “That can’t be your brother.”

For an adjective: “You must be hungry.” “It might be expensive.” “This can’t be real.”

For a place: “They must be at home.” “He might be in class.” “She can’t be here.”

A common mistake is to add “to” after the modal. Don’t say, “He must to be tired.” Say, “He must be tired.” Don’t say, “She might to be busy.” Say, “She might be busy.”

Another important point: these phrases are for guesses about the present. If you want to guess about actions happening now, use “must be” plus verb-ing. For example, “He isn’t answering. He must be driving.” Or, “They might be having lunch.” Or, “She can’t be sleeping; she just sent me a message.”

Let’s practice with a few mini examples.

You hear thunder outside. You say, “It must be raining.”

Your friend doesn’t reply to your message. You say, “He might be busy.”

Someone says your eighty-year-old grandmother is running a marathon right now, but you know she has a broken leg. You say, “That can’t be true.”

Here’s a quick recap. Use “must be” when you are almost sure something is true. Use “might be” when something is possible, but you are not sure. Use “can’t be” when you are almost sure something is not true.

Try this today: look around you and make three guesses in English. One with “must be,” one with “might be,” and one with “can’t be.” For example: “My neighbor’s car is here, so he must be at home. He might be working. He can’t be on vacation.” The more you practice, the more natural these modals will feel.
