67461537d18882ee.topic: Modales en pasado: should have / could have / would have

lesson.title: Past Modals: Should Have, Could Have, Would Have
lesson.prompt: Modales en pasado: should have / could have / would have
lesson.script:
Have you ever looked back at a situation and thought, “I made a mistake,” “I had another option,” or “Things would be different if…”? In English, we use past modals to talk about these ideas. Today, we’re going to learn three very useful structures: should have, could have, and would have.

These phrases are perfect for talking about regrets, missed opportunities, imaginary past situations, and criticism. They may look simple, but they are extremely common in real conversations, movies, interviews, and everyday English.

Let’s start with the form. The structure is: modal plus have plus past participle. For example: should have gone, could have called, would have helped. Be careful: we do not say “should had” or “could went.” The correct form is always have plus the past participle.

First: should have. We use should have to talk about regrets or mistakes in the past. It means that something was a good idea, but it did not happen. For example: “I should have studied more for the exam.” This means I didn’t study enough, and now I regret it. Another example: “You should have told me earlier.” This means you didn’t tell me earlier, and that was a problem.

Should have can also sound like criticism, so use it carefully. If you say, “You should have listened to me,” it can sound a bit strong, like you are blaming the other person. A softer way might be: “Maybe we should have done it differently.”

Now let’s look at the negative form: shouldn’t have. We use it when something happened, but it was a bad idea. For example: “I shouldn’t have eaten so much.” This means I ate too much, and now I feel bad. Or: “She shouldn’t have sent that message.” She sent it, but it was not a good decision.

Second: could have. We use could have to talk about past possibilities or opportunities that did not happen. For example: “I could have gone to the party, but I was too tired.” This means going to the party was possible, but I didn’t go. Another example: “We could have taken a taxi.” Taking a taxi was an option, but we didn’t choose it.

Could have is often connected to missed opportunities. For example: “You could have applied for that job.” This means you had the chance, but you didn’t apply. It can also express surprise or frustration: “You could have told me!” This means, “Why didn’t you tell me?”

We also use couldn’t have when something was impossible in the past. For example: “I couldn’t have finished the project without your help.” This means it was impossible for me to finish it alone. Another example: “She couldn’t have seen us. She was in another city.” So, it was not possible that she saw us.

Third: would have. We use would have to talk about imaginary past situations. It often appears with an if clause. For example: “I would have called you if I had had your number.” This means I didn’t have your number, so I didn’t call you. Another example: “We would have arrived earlier if there hadn’t been so much traffic.” There was traffic, so we didn’t arrive earlier.

Would have is very useful for talking about different results in the past. For example: “If I had known about the meeting, I would have attended.” I didn’t know, so I didn’t attend. “If she had studied medicine, she would have become a doctor.” She didn’t study medicine, so she didn’t become a doctor.

Let’s compare the three with one situation. Imagine you missed an important train.

“I should have left home earlier.” This expresses regret. Leaving earlier was the right thing to do.

“I could have taken a taxi.” This expresses a past possibility. A taxi was an option.

“I would have arrived on time if I had left earlier.” This expresses an imaginary result. I didn’t leave earlier, so I didn’t arrive on time.

Here’s another situation. You forgot your friend’s birthday.

“I should have remembered her birthday.” You regret forgetting it.

“I could have written it in my calendar.” That was a possible solution.

“She would have been happy if I had called her.” That is the imaginary result of a different action.

A common pronunciation note: in spoken English, these forms are often contracted. “Should have” sounds like “should’ve.” “Could have” sounds like “could’ve.” “Would have” sounds like “would’ve.” For example: “I should’ve called you.” “We could’ve gone together.” “They would’ve helped us.”

But be careful with writing. Many learners and even native speakers sometimes write “should of,” “could of,” or “would of.” That is incorrect. The correct written form is should have, could have, and would have, or the contractions should’ve, could’ve, and would’ve.

Let’s finish with a quick recap. Use should have for regrets or past mistakes: “I should have prepared better.” Use could have for past possibilities or missed opportunities: “We could have chosen another restaurant.” Use would have for imaginary past results: “I would have stayed longer if I hadn’t been busy.”

Now think about your own life and make three sentences: one thing you should have done, one thing you could have done, and one thing you would have done in a different situation. This is one of the best ways to make past modals feel natural and useful in real English.

5c8764e066c6a23a.topic: Relative clauses: who / which / that / whose / where. Defining vs. non-defining

lesson.title: Relative Clauses Made Easy: Who, Which, That, Whose, and Where
lesson.prompt: Relative clauses: who / which / that / whose / where. Defining vs. non-defining
lesson.script:
Have you ever tried to describe a person, a thing, or a place in English, but your sentence became too long or confusing? For example: “I met a woman. She speaks five languages.” In English, we can connect these ideas smoothly: “I met a woman who speaks five languages.” That little word “who” helps us sound more natural, more fluent, and more precise.

Today, we’re going to look at relative clauses with who, which, that, whose, and where. We’ll also learn the difference between defining and non-defining relative clauses.

Let’s start with the basic idea. A relative clause gives extra information about a noun. That noun can be a person, a thing, an animal, a place, or even a whole idea. Relative clauses usually begin with words like who, which, that, whose, or where.

Use who for people. For example: “She’s the teacher who helped me improve my pronunciation.” The relative clause is “who helped me improve my pronunciation.” It tells us more about “the teacher.” Another example: “I have a friend who works in Canada.”

Use which for things, animals, and sometimes ideas. For example: “This is the book which changed my life.” Or: “They adopted a dog which had been abandoned.” In everyday English, especially in speaking, many people use “that” instead of “which” in defining clauses, and we’ll talk about that in a moment.

Use that for people, things, and animals, mainly in defining relative clauses. For example: “He’s the guy that fixed my computer.” Or: “This is the phone that I bought last week.” “That” is very common in spoken English because it is flexible and natural.

Use whose to show possession. It means “his,” “her,” “their,” or sometimes “its.” For example: “I know a woman whose son lives in London.” This means: I know a woman, and her son lives in London. Another example: “That’s the company whose products are famous all over the world.” Be careful: “whose” is not only for people. It can also be used for organizations, animals, and things in more formal English.

Use where for places. For example: “This is the restaurant where we had dinner.” Or: “Madrid is the city where I learned Spanish.” “Where” means something like “in which” or “at which,” but it sounds much more natural in everyday conversation.

Now let’s look at the most important distinction: defining and non-defining relative clauses.

A defining relative clause gives essential information. Without it, we don’t know exactly who or what the speaker means. For example: “The woman who lives next door is a doctor.” Which woman? The woman who lives next door. That information is necessary.

Here are more examples: “The movie that we watched last night was amazing.” Which movie? The one we watched last night. “Students who practice every day improve faster.” Which students? The ones who practice every day.

In defining relative clauses, we do not use commas. Also, we can use “that” instead of “who” or “which” in many cases. For example, “The man who called you is my brother” can also be “The man that called you is my brother.” “The car which is parked outside is mine” can also be “The car that is parked outside is mine.”

Now, non-defining relative clauses give extra information. The information is interesting, but not essential. The sentence still makes sense without it. For example: “My sister, who lives in Valencia, is visiting me this weekend.” I have already identified the person: my sister. The clause “who lives in Valencia” just adds extra information.

Notice the commas. In writing, non-defining relative clauses are separated by commas. In speaking, we usually pause a little. Another example: “Barcelona, which is famous for its architecture, attracts millions of tourists.” We already know the place: Barcelona. The relative clause adds extra information.

Very important: in non-defining relative clauses, we do not use “that.” So we can say: “My car, which I bought last year, is already having problems.” But not: “My car, that I bought last year…” That sounds incorrect in standard English. Use “which” for things and “who” for people in non-defining clauses.

Let’s compare defining and non-defining with similar sentences.

“The students who arrived late missed the explanation.” This means only the students who arrived late missed it. The relative clause defines which students.

“The students, who arrived late, missed the explanation.” This suggests all the students arrived late, and they all missed the explanation. The commas change the meaning.

Here’s another pair: “My brother who lives in Mexico is a doctor.” This suggests I have more than one brother, and I’m talking about the one in Mexico. But: “My brother, who lives in Mexico, is a doctor.” This suggests I have one brother, or I’m simply adding extra information about him.

For example: “The book that I’m reading is really good.” We can also say: “The book I’m reading is really good.” “The person who I met yesterday was very kind” can become “The person I met yesterday was very kind.” But if the relative pronoun is the subject, we cannot omit it. “The woman who called me was polite.” Not: “The woman called me was polite,” because that changes the structure.

d3a199446d86ecc2.topic: Future forms: will / going to / present continuous / future perfect

lesson.title: Future Forms in English: Will, Going To, Present Continuous, and Future Perfect
lesson.prompt: Future forms: will / going to / present continuous / future perfect
lesson.script:
Have you ever said, “I will travel tomorrow,” when a native speaker would probably say, “I’m traveling tomorrow”? Don’t worry. Future forms in English can feel confusing because English doesn’t have just one future tense. Instead, we choose different forms depending on the situation, the level of certainty, and whether the plan is already arranged.

In this lesson, we’ll look at four very useful ways to talk about the future: will, going to, the present continuous, and the future perfect. By the end, you’ll know when to use each one more naturally.

Let’s start with will.

We often use will for decisions made at the moment of speaking. For example, imagine your phone rings and you say, “I’ll answer it.” You didn’t plan this before. You decided right now. Or someone says, “I’m cold,” and you reply, “I’ll close the window.” Again, it’s an instant decision.

We also use will for predictions, especially when they are based on opinion, belief, or general thinking. For example, “I think it will rain tomorrow,” or “She’ll love this movie.” In these cases, you are not looking at clear evidence. You are giving your opinion about the future.

Will is also common for promises and offers. “I’ll help you with your homework.” “I won’t tell anyone.” “Don’t worry, I’ll call you later.”

Now let’s move to going to.

We use going to for plans and intentions. These are things you have already decided to do, even if you haven’t organized all the details. For example, “I’m going to study English tonight.” That means you already have the intention. Another example: “They’re going to buy a new car.” They have decided this, but maybe they haven’t chosen the exact car yet.

Going to is also used for predictions based on evidence. This is very important. If you look at the sky and see dark clouds, you say, “It’s going to rain.” You have evidence. If someone is running toward a chair and doesn’t see it, you might say, “He’s going to fall!” Again, you can see the situation now, and it gives you a strong reason to predict what will happen.

So, compare these two sentences: “I think it will rain tomorrow” and “Look at those clouds. It’s going to rain.” The first is an opinion. The second is based on visible evidence.

Next, we have the present continuous for future arrangements.

The present continuous is formed with am, is, or are, plus the verb with ing. For example, “I’m meeting Ana at six,” or “We’re flying to Madrid on Friday.” Even though the form looks like the present, the meaning is future.

We use the present continuous when the future event is arranged. That means there is usually a time, a place, or another person involved. For example, “I’m having dinner with my boss tomorrow.” This sounds like it is already organized. Maybe the restaurant is booked. Maybe the time is confirmed.

Compare these two sentences: “I’m going to see the doctor” and “I’m seeing the doctor at ten tomorrow.” The first sentence tells us your intention. The second tells us you have an appointment. It is more fixed.

Here’s another comparison: “We’re going to visit London next year” means you have the plan or intention. “We’re visiting London next week” sounds more arranged. Maybe you already bought the tickets and booked the hotel.

Now let’s talk about the future perfect.

The future perfect is used to say that something will be completed before a specific time in the future. The structure is will have plus the past participle. For example, “By Friday, I will have finished the report.” This means Friday is the deadline or reference point, and the report will be complete before then.

Another example: “By the end of this year, I will have saved enough money for a new laptop.” Or, “When you arrive, we will have already eaten.” The key idea is completion before a future moment.

Words like by, by the time, before, and when are very common with the future perfect. For example, “By the time she gets home, the children will have gone to bed.” This means the children will go to bed before she gets home.

Let’s put all four forms together with one situation.

Imagine you are organizing a trip. You might say, “I think the trip will be amazing.” That’s a prediction or opinion. Then you say, “We’re going to visit three cities.” That’s your plan or intention. Next, you say, “We’re flying on Saturday morning.” That’s an arrangement, probably with tickets already booked. Finally, you say, “By the time we come back, we will have visited three countries.” That means the visits will be complete before you return.

Let’s do a quick recap.

Use will for instant decisions, offers, promises, and predictions based on opinion. Use going to for plans, intentions, and predictions based on evidence. Use the present continuous for future arrangements that are already organized. And use the future perfect for actions that will be completed before a certain time in the future.

A good way to practice is to choose one real future event in your life and describe it using all four forms. For example: “I think it will be fun. I’m going to prepare carefully. I’m meeting my friend at five. By the end of the day, I will have learned something new.” Try it with your own plans, and your future forms will start to feel much more natural.

92e8c94fb5bf23a5.topic: Inversion básica: 'Never have I seen…', 'Hardly had I…'

lesson.title: Basic Inversion: “Never Have I Seen…” and “Hardly Had I…”
lesson.prompt: Inversion básica: 'Never have I seen…', 'Hardly had I…'
lesson.script:
Have you ever heard someone say, “Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset,” and thought, “Wait… why is the verb before the subject?” Good news: this structure is not a mistake. It’s called inversion, and it can make your English sound more dramatic, elegant, and advanced.

Today we’re going to look at basic inversion after negative or limiting adverbs, especially in sentences like “Never have I seen…” and “Hardly had I…”

Let’s start with the basic idea. In normal English, the subject usually comes before the auxiliary verb. For example: “I have never seen such a beautiful place.” Subject: I. Auxiliary: have. Normal order.

But with inversion, we move the auxiliary before the subject: “Never have I seen such a beautiful place.” Auxiliary: have. Subject: I.

The meaning is basically the same, but the style is different. “Never have I seen…” sounds stronger, more emphatic, and more formal or literary than “I have never seen…”

This kind of inversion often happens when we begin a sentence with a negative or limiting expression. For example: never, rarely, seldom, hardly, scarcely, no sooner, not only, under no circumstances, and at no time.

Let’s look at “never” first.

Normal sentence: “I have never been so surprised.”

With inversion: “Never have I been so surprised.”

Normal sentence: “She had never felt so nervous before.”

With inversion: “Never had she felt so nervous before.”

Notice the structure: negative expression, auxiliary verb, subject, main verb. “Never had she felt…” Not “Never she had felt.” That would be incorrect.

If there is no auxiliary verb in the normal sentence, we usually add “do,” “does,” or “did,” just like in questions.

For example: “I never realized how difficult it was.” With inversion: “Never did I realize how difficult it was.”

Another example: “He rarely makes mistakes.” With inversion: “Rarely does he make mistakes.”

And in the past: “They seldom visited us.” With inversion: “Seldom did they visit us.”

Now let’s talk about “hardly.” This word means “almost not” or “only just.” It is often used with the past perfect to show that one action happened immediately before another.

For example: “I had hardly arrived when it started to rain.”

With inversion: “Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.”

This means: I arrived, and almost immediately, it started to rain.

Here are more examples: “Hardly had we sat down when the phone rang.” “Hardly had she opened the door when the dog ran out.” “Hardly had they started the meeting when the fire alarm went off.”

In Spanish, you might think of this as similar to “apenas había llegado cuando…” But be careful: in English, after “hardly” at the beginning, we invert the auxiliary and the subject. So we say, “Hardly had I arrived,” not “Hardly I had arrived.”

A very similar expression is “scarcely.” For example: “Scarcely had I finished my coffee when my boss called.” This sounds formal, but it is useful in writing and storytelling.

Another common structure is “no sooner… than.”

For example: “No sooner had I left the house than I remembered my keys.”

This means the same idea: I left the house, and immediately after that, I remembered my keys.

Be careful with the connector. With “hardly,” we usually use “when”: “Hardly had I arrived when…” With “no sooner,” we use “than”: “No sooner had I arrived than…”

Now let’s compare normal English and inverted English.

Normal: “I had never heard such an interesting story.” Inverted: “Never had I heard such an interesting story.”

Normal: “We rarely see such clear examples.” Inverted: “Rarely do we see such clear examples.”

Normal: “She had hardly started speaking when everyone began to laugh.” Inverted: “Hardly had she started speaking when everyone began to laugh.”

Normal: “He not only speaks English, but he also speaks French.” Inverted: “Not only does he speak English, but he also speaks French.”

This last example is very common. When “not only” begins the sentence, we use inversion in the first part: “Not only does he speak English…” Then the second part is normal: “but he also speaks French.”

So when should you use inversion? You don’t need it in everyday conversation all the time. If you always speak like this, you might sound too formal or dramatic. But it’s excellent for emphasis, storytelling, presentations, writing, and exams. It helps you sound more sophisticated.

Let’s do a quick practice. Change this sentence: “I have never seen such a big dog.” The inverted version is: “Never have I seen such a big dog.”

Now this one: “She rarely eats fast food.” Because there is no auxiliary, we add “does”: “Rarely does she eat fast food.”

And one more: “I had hardly closed my eyes when the baby started crying.” Inverted: “Hardly had I closed my eyes when the baby started crying.”

Great. Let’s recap. Inversion means putting the auxiliary verb before the subject. We often use it after negative or limiting expressions at the beginning of a sentence, like “never,” “rarely,” “hardly,” and “no sooner.” Say “Never have I seen,” not “Never I have seen.” Say “Hardly had I arrived,” not “Hardly I had arrived.”

Try writing three sentences today: one with “Never have I…,” one with “Rarely do I…,” and one with “Hardly had I… when…” The more you practice, the more natural this advanced structure will feel.

36186b7f2cf21b96.topic: Phrasal verbs (parte 2): trabajo y oficina. Vocab: carry out, deal with, follow up, take over, sort out

lesson.title: Phrasal Verbs for Work and the Office: Carry Out, Deal With, Follow Up, Take Over, Sort Out
lesson.prompt: Phrasal verbs (parte 2): trabajo y oficina. Vocab: carry out, deal with, follow up, take over, sort out
lesson.script:
Have you ever been in a meeting in English and understood every word… except the phrasal verbs? Someone says, “I’ll follow up tomorrow,” or “Can you sort this out?” and suddenly you feel lost. Don’t worry. Today we’re going to learn five very useful phrasal verbs for work and office situations: carry out, deal with, follow up, take over, and sort out.

These expressions are common in emails, meetings, phone calls, and everyday office conversations. If you work with English, or want to sound more natural in professional situations, these five phrasal verbs are essential.

Let’s start with carry out. To carry out means to do or complete a task, a plan, an investigation, or an action. It is a little more formal, so you often see it in reports, emails, and business contexts.

For example: “We need to carry out a customer survey.” This means we need to do the survey. Another example: “The team carried out the project successfully.” That means the team completed the project successfully.

You can also say: “The company is carrying out research into new markets.” In Spanish, you might think of “llevar a cabo.” So remember: carry out a task, carry out a plan, carry out research, carry out an investigation.

Now let’s look at deal with. To deal with means to manage, handle, or take action about a situation, problem, person, or responsibility.

For example: “I have to deal with a difficult client this afternoon.” This means I have to manage the situation with that client. Another example: “Our department deals with customer complaints.” That means the department handles customer complaints.

You can use deal with in many professional situations: “Can you deal with this email?” “She deals with the suppliers.” “We need to deal with the problem before Friday.”

A common mistake is translating too directly from Spanish. In English, we don’t usually say “attend a problem.” We say “deal with a problem.” For people, clients, issues, emails, complaints, and responsibilities, deal with is very useful.

The third phrasal verb is follow up. To follow up means to take an extra action after a first conversation, email, meeting, or request. It is like checking the next step.

Imagine you send an email to a client, but they don’t reply. You can say: “I’ll follow up with the client tomorrow.” This means you will contact the client again to continue the communication.

Another example: “After the meeting, I followed up with a summary email.” This means you sent an email after the meeting to confirm the main points.

In business English, follow up is extremely common. You can follow up with a person, follow up on a topic, or follow up after a meeting. For example: “I’m following up on the proposal we sent last week.” Or: “Thanks for your time today. I’ll follow up next week.”

You can also use follow-up as a noun or adjective with a hyphen. For example: “Let’s schedule a follow-up meeting.” That means a second meeting to continue the topic.

Next, take over. To take over means to assume control or responsibility for something. This can be temporary or permanent.

For example: “Can you take over this project while Ana is on vacation?” This means: Can you become responsible for this project while Ana is away?

Another example: “He took over the team in January.” That means he became the leader of the team in January.

You might hear it in the office when someone is leaving a role: “Maria is leaving the company, so Carlos will take over her responsibilities.” Or during a meeting: “I need to leave early. Can you take over the presentation?”

Be careful: take over can also mean one company buys or gets control of another company. For example: “A larger company took over our main competitor.” But in daily office English, it often means to assume responsibility.

Finally, let’s talk about sort out. To sort out means to organize, solve, or fix something. It is very common in British English, but many international speakers use it too.

For example: “We need to sort out the schedule for next week.” This means we need to organize the schedule. Another example: “There was a problem with the invoice, but I sorted it out.” That means I fixed the problem.

You can sort out a problem, sort out a mistake, sort out a meeting time, or sort out documents. For example: “Can you sort out these files before the meeting?” Or: “I’m trying to sort out an issue with the software.”

In a professional context, sort out can sound practical and natural. It’s not too formal, but it is very useful in everyday work communication.

Now let’s put all five phrasal verbs into one office situation.

Imagine your manager says: “We need to carry out a review of our sales process. Laura will deal with the client feedback, and James will follow up with the sales team after the meeting. While I’m away next week, Marta will take over the project. Please sort out any problems before Friday.”

Let’s break that down. Carry out a review means do the review. Deal with client feedback means manage or handle the feedback. Follow up with the sales team means contact them again after the meeting. Take over the project means assume responsibility for the project. Sort out problems means fix or solve the problems.

Here are a few useful sentences you can practice and adapt to your own work.

“I’ll carry out the analysis and send you the results.”

“Could you deal with this request today?”

“I’ll follow up with the client after lunch.”

“Who will take over the account when she leaves?”

“Let’s sort out the details before we confirm the meeting.”

Before we finish, here is a quick pronunciation tip. In natural English, phrasal verbs often sound connected. We don’t say each word separately like a robot. We say “carry out,” “deal with,” “follow up,” “take over,” and “sort out” smoothly. Try repeating them in short phrases: carry out a task, deal with a client, follow up tomorrow, take over the project, sort out the problem.

Let’s recap. Carry out means to do or complete a task or plan. Deal with means to handle or manage a situation. Follow up means to contact again or continue after a first action. Take over means to assume responsibility or control. Sort out means to organize, solve, or fix something.

Your challenge for today is simple: write five sentences about your own job or studies, using these five phrasal verbs. The more you connect them to real situations, the faster they become part of your natural English.

e8835f3c97f5dc55.topic: Phrasal verbs (parte 3): relaciones y emociones. Vocab: break up, make up, fall out, open up, get over

lesson.title: Phrasal Verbs for Relationships and Emotions
lesson.prompt: Phrasal verbs (parte 3): relaciones y emociones. Vocab: break up, make up, fall out, open up, get over
lesson.script:
Have you ever tried to talk about love, friendship, or a difficult moment in English, but felt that the words were too simple? Maybe you said, “We finished our relationship,” or “I recovered from sadness.” People will understand you, but native speakers usually use phrasal verbs for these situations. Today, we’ll learn five very useful phrasal verbs for relationships and emotions: break up, make up, fall out, open up, and get over.

Let’s start with break up. To break up means to end a romantic relationship. For example: “They broke up last month.” This means they are no longer a couple. You can also say, “She broke up with her boyfriend,” or “He broke up with his girlfriend.” Notice the structure: break up with someone. For example: “I broke up with my partner because we wanted different things.” Be careful: we don’t usually say “I broke with my boyfriend.” The natural expression is “I broke up with my boyfriend.”

Now, the opposite idea in some situations is make up. To make up means to become friendly again after an argument. It can be used for couples, friends, or family members. For example: “We had a big argument, but we made up the next day.” Another example: “After not speaking for a week, they finally made up.” If you want to mention the person, you can say: “I made up with my sister.” This means you had a problem, but now the relationship is okay again.

But be careful, because make up has other meanings too. It can mean invent a story, like “He made up an excuse,” or apply cosmetics, as in “She made herself up for the party.” But in today’s context, make up means to fix a relationship after conflict.

Next, we have fall out. To fall out means to have an argument and stop being friendly with someone. It is especially common in British English, but many English speakers understand it. For example: “They fell out over money.” This means they argued because of money and their relationship became bad. Another example: “I fell out with my best friend last year, but we’re okay now.” The structure is fall out with someone, or fall out over something. “They fell out with their neighbors.” “They fell out over a misunderstanding.”

So, what’s the difference between break up and fall out? Break up is for ending a romantic relationship. Fall out is usually for friends, family, or people who had a disagreement. For example: “Laura broke up with her boyfriend.” Romantic relationship. “Laura fell out with her cousin.” Family conflict.

Now let’s talk about open up. To open up means to start talking honestly about your feelings, problems, or personal experiences. For example: “He doesn’t usually talk about his emotions, but yesterday he opened up to me.” The structure is open up to someone. Another example: “It can be hard to open up when you don’t trust people.” This phrasal verb is very useful because in English, emotional communication is often described with expressions like “open up,” “be honest,” or “share your feelings.”

Imagine this situation: Your friend looks sad, but says, “I’m fine.” Later, after a long conversation, she tells you the truth. You can say, “She finally opened up about what happened.” Notice another structure: open up about something. “He opened up about his childhood.” “She opened up about her anxiety.”

Finally, we have get over. To get over something means to recover emotionally from a difficult experience, especially a breakup, disappointment, or loss. For example: “It took him a long time to get over the breakup.” Another example: “She still hasn’t got over what happened.” In American English, people usually say “hasn’t gotten over.” In British English, “hasn’t got over” is common. Both are understood.

You can also get over a person, meaning you stop feeling romantic pain or emotional attachment. For example: “I’m trying to get over my ex.” Or: “He got over her after a few months.” This doesn’t mean you forget everything. It means you can continue with your life without the same emotional pain.

Let’s put the five phrasal verbs together in a short story. “Marta and Daniel broke up after three years together. At first, Marta was very sad and couldn’t get over him. She didn’t want to talk to anyone, but one day she opened up to her best friend. Later, Daniel and Marta made up as friends, but they didn’t get back together as a couple.”

Did you notice another phrasal verb there? Get back together means to become a couple again. But that’s extra vocabulary for you.

Now let’s compare the main verbs quickly. Break up: end a romantic relationship. “They broke up in June.” Make up: become friendly again after an argument. “We argued, but we made up.” Fall out: argue and stop being friendly. “They fell out with each other.” Open up: talk honestly about feelings. “She opened up to me.” Get over: recover from emotional pain. “He got over the breakup.”

Here are a few common mistakes to avoid. Don’t say “I broke up my boyfriend.” Say: “I broke up with my boyfriend.” Don’t say “We made up us.” Say: “We made up,” or “We made up with each other.” Don’t say “I opened to my friend.” Say: “I opened up to my friend.” And don’t say “I got over from the breakup.” Say: “I got over the breakup.”

Before we finish, try making your own examples. Think of a person you trust. Could you open up to them? Think of a past argument. Did you make up, or did you fall out? Think of a difficult moment. How long did it take you to get over it?

Quick recap: break up is for ending a romantic relationship, make up is for fixing a relationship after an argument, fall out is for having a conflict and becoming distant, open up is for sharing honest feelings, and get over is for recovering emotionally. Practice these in real sentences, because they are very common in natural English conversations about relationships and emotions.

aa93e9716fce0b05.topic: Collocations con 'take', 'have', 'get'. Vocab: take a shower, have a chat, get the hang of

lesson.title: Sound More Natural with Take, Have, and Get
lesson.prompt: Collocations con 'take', 'have', 'get'. Vocab: take a shower, have a chat, get the hang of
lesson.script:
Do you ever say something in English that is grammatically correct, but it still sounds a little strange? For example, maybe you say, “I made a shower,” because in Spanish you say “me duché” or “tomé una ducha” depending on the country. In English, we usually say “take a shower.” This is the magic of collocations: words that naturally go together.

Today, we’re going to look at three very common verbs: take, have, and get. These verbs are simple, but they appear in many expressions. If you learn them in chunks, your English will sound much more natural and fluent.

Let’s start with take.

One very useful expression is take a shower. We don’t usually say “do a shower” or “make a shower.” We say take a shower. For example: “I usually take a shower in the morning.” Or: “I need to take a quick shower before we leave.”

You can also say take a break. For example: “I’ve been studying for two hours. I need to take a break.” This means you stop working or studying for a short time. Another common one is take a photo. For example: “Can you take a photo of us?” In American English, take a shower and take a photo are especially common.

Now let’s move to have.

Have is often used for experiences, conversations, meals, and short activities. A very useful phrase is have a chat. This means to talk with someone in an informal way. For example: “Let’s have a chat after class.” Or: “I had a nice chat with my neighbor this morning.”

Notice that have a chat sounds friendly and relaxed. It’s not usually a serious business meeting. It’s more like a conversation. You can also say have a conversation, which is a little more general or neutral. For example: “We need to have a conversation about the project.” That sounds more serious than “Let’s have a chat.”

Other common expressions with have include have breakfast, have lunch, have dinner, have a coffee, have a good time, and have a problem. For example: “I had breakfast at eight.” “We had a great time at the party.” “I’m having a problem with my computer.”

Be careful: Spanish speakers often want to translate directly. In Spanish, you might say “tomar un café,” and in English you can say “have a coffee.” In some situations, “drink a coffee” is possible, but “have a coffee” sounds more natural when you mean the general experience.

Now, let’s talk about get.

Get is one of the most flexible verbs in English. It can mean receive, become, obtain, arrive, understand, and more. But today we’re focusing on one important expression: get the hang of something.

To get the hang of something means to learn how to do something, especially after practicing for a while. At first, it may feel difficult, but then you start to understand it. For example: “At first, driving on the left was difficult, but I got the hang of it after a few days.”

Another example: “English pronunciation can be tricky, but with practice, you’ll get the hang of it.” This means you will become more comfortable and confident.

You can use it in different tenses. Present: “I’m starting to get the hang of this grammar.” Past: “I got the hang of it after a few lessons.” Future: “Don’t worry, you’ll get the hang of it soon.”

This expression is very natural and encouraging. If a friend is learning to cook, use a new app, or speak English, you can say: “Keep practicing. You’ll get the hang of it.”

Let’s compare these three verbs in context.

Imagine your morning. You wake up, take a shower, have breakfast, and get ready for work. Later, you have a chat with a colleague. Maybe you’re learning a new system at work, and at first it’s confusing, but after a week, you get the hang of it.

Here’s a short mini-story with all three:

“Yesterday was my first day at my new job. I woke up early, took a shower, and had a quick coffee. At the office, I had a chat with my manager, and she explained the new software. At first, I didn’t understand everything, but after a few hours, I started to get the hang of it.”

That sounds natural because the words are working together in common combinations.

So, quick recap. We say take a shower, not “make a shower.” We say have a chat when we mean an informal conversation. And we say get the hang of something when we start to understand how to do it.

Your challenge for today is simple: create three sentences about your real life. One with take a shower, one with have a chat, and one with get the hang of. Say them out loud. The more you practice these chunks, the more natural your English will become.

9633349b0a428a0a.topic: Idioms cotidianos que SÍ se usan. Vocab: piece of cake, hit the nail on the head, under the weather, on the same page

lesson.title: Everyday English Idioms People Actually Use
lesson.prompt: Idioms cotidianos que SÍ se usan. Vocab: piece of cake, hit the nail on the head, under the weather, on the same page
lesson.script:
Have you ever learned an English idiom and then wondered, “Do people really say this?” That is a very good question. Some idioms sound old-fashioned, dramatic, or just strange in real life. But today, we are going to learn four idioms that English speakers really do use in everyday conversations: piece of cake, hit the nail on the head, under the weather, and on the same page.

These expressions are common, useful, and natural. You can use them at work, with friends, in class, or when you are traveling. Let’s start with the first one: piece of cake.

If something is a piece of cake, it means it is very easy. Imagine a friend asks you, “Was the exam difficult?” And you say, “No, it was a piece of cake.” That means the exam was easy for you. Not literally cake, of course. It is just a fun way to say that something was simple.

Here are a few more examples. “Don’t worry about the presentation. It’ll be a piece of cake.” Or, “The first level of the game was a piece of cake.” You can also say, “That recipe looks complicated, but it’s actually a piece of cake.”

Be careful: this idiom is informal, but very normal. You can use it with friends and coworkers. In a very formal business email, maybe choose “It should be straightforward” instead. But in conversation, piece of cake sounds great.

The second idiom is hit the nail on the head. This means to say exactly the right thing, or to describe a situation perfectly. Think about hitting a nail with a hammer. If you hit the nail on the head, you hit it exactly in the right place. In conversation, it means your comment is accurate.

For example, imagine your coworker says, “I think the problem is that our instructions are not clear.” And you answer, “You hit the nail on the head.” That means, “Yes, exactly. That is the real problem.”

More examples: “When she said the team needed better communication, she hit the nail on the head.” Or, “You hit the nail on the head. I’m not angry, I’m just tired.” This idiom is very useful when you want to agree strongly with someone.

The third idiom is under the weather. If you are under the weather, you feel a little sick or not well. It usually does not mean you are seriously ill. It often means you have a cold, a headache, low energy, or you just do not feel one hundred percent.

For example: “I’m feeling a bit under the weather today, so I’m going to stay home.” Or, “She didn’t come to the meeting because she was under the weather.” Another natural example is, “I think I’m coming down with something. I’ve been under the weather all day.”

This expression is softer than saying “I’m sick.” It sounds polite and natural. If you do not want to give many details, you can simply say, “I’m a little under the weather.” People will understand that you are not feeling well.

The fourth idiom is on the same page. This means that people understand and agree about a plan, idea, or situation. It is very common in work conversations, but you can also use it in daily life.

For example, before starting a project, a manager might say, “Let’s make sure we’re all on the same page.” That means, “Let’s make sure everyone understands the plan.” Another example: “Before we book the trip, we need to get on the same page about the budget.” That means everyone needs to agree about how much money to spend.

You can also use it in relationships or friendships. “I thought we were on the same page, but apparently we had different expectations.” Or, “Let’s talk about it so we can be on the same page.” This idiom is excellent for avoiding confusion.

Now, let’s put all four idioms into one natural conversation.

Imagine you are talking to a coworker after a meeting. You say, “I think Ana hit the nail on the head when she said the deadline is too short. We need to get everyone on the same page before we continue. Also, I’m feeling a bit under the weather today, so I hope the next task is a piece of cake.”

That sounds natural, clear, and useful. You are saying: Ana described the problem perfectly, everyone needs to understand the plan, you do not feel very well, and you hope the next task is easy.

Let’s do a quick pronunciation tip. In fast speech, “piece of cake” often sounds like “piece-uhv cake.” “On the same page” connects smoothly: “on the same page.” And with “under the weather,” the “t” in “weather” is soft in American English, almost like “weh-ther.” You do not need to sound perfect, but connecting words will help you sound more natural.

So, quick recap. If something is easy, it is a piece of cake. If someone says exactly the right thing, they hit the nail on the head. If you feel a little sick, you are under the weather. And if everyone understands and agrees, they are on the same page.

Try using one of these idioms today. Write a simple sentence like, “The homework was a piece of cake,” or “I’m feeling under the weather.” The more you use them in real situations, the more natural they will feel.

6c347fcd45e7445c.topic: Expresiones de opinión sofisticadas. Vocab: from my perspective, I'd argue that, it strikes me as, I'm inclined to think

lesson.title: Sound More Sophisticated: Advanced Ways to Give Your Opinion
lesson.prompt: Expresiones de opinión sofisticadas. Vocab: from my perspective, I'd argue that, it strikes me as, I'm inclined to think
lesson.script:
Do you want to stop saying “I think” all the time and sound more natural, fluent, and sophisticated in English? Today, you’ll learn four powerful expressions to give your opinion with more style: “from my perspective,” “I’d argue that,” “it strikes me as,” and “I’m inclined to think.” These expressions are perfect for discussions, exams, meetings, essays, and everyday conversations when you want to sound a bit more advanced.

Let’s start with “from my perspective.” This means “from my point of view” or “in my opinion,” but it sounds a little more thoughtful and mature. We use it when we want to show that our opinion comes from our personal experience, knowledge, or way of seeing the situation.

For example: “From my perspective, learning a language is more about consistency than talent.”

That sounds more elegant than simply saying, “I think learning a language is about consistency.” Another example: “From my perspective, working from home can be very productive if people have clear routines.”

Notice that this expression is useful when there may be different opinions. You are not saying your view is the absolute truth. You are saying, “This is how I see it.”

Now let’s look at “I’d argue that.” This is a very useful phrase when you want to present a strong opinion, especially in debates, essays, or professional conversations. “I’d” is the contraction of “I would,” so the full form is “I would argue that.” It means “I believe strongly, and I can defend this opinion with reasons.”

For example: “I’d argue that social media has changed the way we communicate, but not always for the better.”

This sounds confident and analytical. You are not just giving a casual opinion. You are preparing to support it with arguments. Another example: “I’d argue that companies should invest more in employee well-being because it improves productivity in the long term.”

This phrase is excellent for speaking exams or writing tasks. Instead of repeating “I think,” you can say, “I’d argue that…” and immediately sound more advanced.

Next, we have “it strikes me as.” This expression is a little different. We use it when something gives us a particular impression. In Spanish, it can be similar to “me parece” or “me da la impresión de que,” depending on the context.

For example: “It strikes me as a very practical solution.” This means, “My impression is that the solution is very practical.”

Another example: “His explanation strikes me as honest, but a little incomplete.” Here, you are describing the impression his explanation gives you. You can also use the structure “it strikes me as strange that…” For example: “It strikes me as strange that nobody mentioned the main problem.”

Be careful with the grammar. We usually say “it strikes me as” plus a noun phrase or adjective. For example: “It strikes me as unnecessary,” “It strikes me as a good idea,” or “It strikes me as too expensive.”

Finally, let’s study “I’m inclined to think.” This expression is perfect when your opinion is not one hundred percent fixed, but you are leaning in a certain direction. It means “I tend to think” or “I’m starting to believe.” It sounds diplomatic and nuanced.

For example: “I’m inclined to think that flexible schedules are better for creative work.”

This is softer than “I strongly believe.” It shows that you have an opinion, but you are open to other ideas. Another example: “I’m inclined to think that the problem is not the technology itself, but how we use it.”

This phrase is very useful in professional settings because it sounds balanced. You can use it when you don’t want to sound too direct or too aggressive.

Let’s compare all four expressions with the same idea. Basic version: “I think online learning is useful.” More sophisticated versions: “From my perspective, online learning is useful because it gives students more flexibility.” “I’d argue that online learning is one of the most important educational tools of our time.” “It strikes me as a practical option for people who work full time.” “I’m inclined to think that online learning will continue to grow in the future.”

Do you feel the difference? Each expression has a slightly different tone. “From my perspective” sounds personal and reflective. “I’d argue that” sounds strong and analytical. “It strikes me as” focuses on your impression. And “I’m inclined to think” sounds careful, diplomatic, and open-minded.

Here’s a quick tip: if you are taking an English exam, don’t use all of these expressions in every answer. Choose one or two naturally. For example, in a speaking exam, you might say: “From my perspective, cities need better public transport. I’d argue that this would reduce pollution and improve people’s quality of life.” That already sounds much more advanced than repeating “I think” again and again.

Let’s recap. Instead of always saying “I think,” try these four alternatives: “from my perspective” for a personal viewpoint, “I’d argue that” for a strong opinion, “it strikes me as” for an impression, and “I’m inclined to think” for a softer, more diplomatic opinion.

Now it’s your turn. Choose one topic, like social media, remote work, education, or travel, and create four sentences using these expressions. The more you practice them, the more natural they’ll sound when you speak.

f64cafc61418c413.topic: Linking words avanzados. Vocab: nevertheless, furthermore, moreover, on the contrary, in light of

lesson.title: Advanced Linking Words: Sound More Fluent and Precise
lesson.prompt: Linking words avanzados. Vocab: nevertheless, furthermore, moreover, on the contrary, in light of
lesson.script:
Want to sound more advanced in English almost immediately? One of the fastest ways is to use better linking words. Instead of always saying “but,” “also,” or “because of this,” you can use expressions like “nevertheless,” “furthermore,” “moreover,” “on the contrary,” and “in light of.” These words help you connect ideas in a more elegant, precise, and professional way.

Today, we’ll look at five advanced linking words, what they mean, and how to use them naturally.

Let’s start with “nevertheless.” “Nevertheless” means “however” or “even so.” We use it when we want to show contrast: something is true, but another thing is also true despite that. For example: “The project was difficult. Nevertheless, we finished it on time.” This means the project was difficult, but that didn’t stop us from finishing it.

Here’s another example: “The weather was terrible. Nevertheless, we decided to go hiking.” In Spanish, it’s similar to “sin embargo” or “aun así.” A good tip: “nevertheless” is more formal than “but,” so it works well in essays, presentations, and professional emails.

Now let’s look at “furthermore.” “Furthermore” means “in addition” or “also,” but it sounds more formal and organized. We use it to add extra information that supports the same idea. For example: “Learning English can improve your career opportunities. Furthermore, it allows you to communicate with people from all over the world.”

Notice that the second sentence adds another benefit. It doesn’t contrast with the first idea; it strengthens it. Another example: “This course is practical and easy to follow. Furthermore, it includes real-life examples.” In Spanish, you might think of “además.”

Next, we have “moreover.” “Moreover” is very similar to “furthermore.” It also means “in addition,” and we use it to add information. However, “moreover” often feels a little stronger, as if you are adding an important extra point. For example: “The city is beautiful and full of history. Moreover, it has excellent public transport.”

Another example: “She is highly qualified for the job. Moreover, she has ten years of experience in the industry.” Here, “moreover” introduces an important reason that makes the argument stronger.

So, what’s the difference between “furthermore” and “moreover”? In many cases, they are interchangeable. Both mean “además.” But “moreover” can sound slightly more emphatic, while “furthermore” can sound slightly more neutral and academic. Don’t worry too much about the difference. The most important thing is to use them to add supporting information.

Now let’s talk about “on the contrary.” This one is very useful, but learners often use it incorrectly. “On the contrary” does not simply mean “but.” It means that the opposite is true. Use it when you want to correct an idea or deny something.

For example: “Some people think grammar is boring. On the contrary, it can be very interesting when you understand how it works.” Here, we are saying the opposite of the first idea: grammar is not boring; it is interesting.

Another example: “The new policy did not reduce productivity. On the contrary, it made the team more efficient.” Again, the second idea directly contradicts the first idea.

Be careful. Don’t say: “I like coffee. On the contrary, I like tea.” That sounds strange, because liking tea is not necessarily the opposite of liking coffee. A better sentence would be: “I don’t dislike coffee. On the contrary, I drink it every morning.” That means the opposite of “dislike” is true.

Finally, let’s look at “in light of.” This expression means “considering” or “because of a particular situation or information.” It is often used in formal or professional contexts. For example: “In light of the recent changes, we need to update our plan.” This means that because of the recent changes, or considering the recent changes, we need to update the plan.

Another example: “In light of your experience, we would like to offer you a senior position.” Here, the decision is based on your experience. In Spanish, it is similar to “a la luz de” or “teniendo en cuenta.”

You can also use it at the beginning of a sentence: “In light of the results, the company decided to invest more money.” Or in the middle: “The company decided, in light of the results, to invest more money.” The first version is simpler and more natural for most learners.

Let’s compare all five quickly. Use “nevertheless” to show contrast: “It was expensive. Nevertheless, we bought it.” Use “furthermore” to add information: “It is useful. Furthermore, it is easy to use.” Use “moreover” to add a strong extra point: “He is talented. Moreover, he works extremely hard.” Use “on the contrary” to say the opposite is true: “It wasn’t a failure. On the contrary, it was a great success.” And use “in light of” to mean “considering”: “In light of the evidence, we changed our opinion.”

To sound more fluent, don’t try to use all of these words in every conversation. Choose one or two and practise them until they feel natural. For example, today try writing three sentences with “nevertheless” and three with “in light of.”

Quick recap: “nevertheless” shows contrast, “furthermore” and “moreover” add information, “on the contrary” corrects an idea with the opposite, and “in light of” means “considering.” Master these linking words, and your English will sound clearer, more advanced, and much more confident.

Let's start with nevertheless. Nevertheless means however or even so. We use it when we want to show contrast. Something is true, but another thing is also true despite that. For example, the project was difficult. Nevertheless, we finished it on time. This means the project was difficult, but that didn't stop us from finishing it. Here's another example. The weather was terrible. Nevertheless, we decided to go hiking. In Spanish, it's similar to sin embargo or on a sea. A good tip, nevertheless, is more formal than but. So it works well in essays, presentations, and professional emails. Now let's look at furthermore. Furthermore means in addition or also, but it sounds more formal and organized. We use it to add extra information that supports the same idea. For example, learning English can improve your career opportunities. Furthermore, it allows you to communicate with people from all over the world. Notice that the second sentence adds another benefit. It doesn't contrast with the first idea. It strengthens it. Another example. This course is practical and easy to follow. Furthermore, it includes real-life examples. In Spanish, you might think of además. Next, we have moreover. Moreover is very similar to furthermore. It also means in addition, and we use it to add information. However, moreover often feels a little stronger, as if you're adding an important extra point. For example, the city is beautiful and full of history. Moreover, it has excellent public transport. Another example. She is highly qualified for the job. Moreover, she has 10 years of experience in the industry. Here, moreover introduces an important reason that makes the argument stronger. So what's the difference between furthermore and moreover? In many cases, they are interchangeable. Both mean además. But moreover can sound slightly more emphatic, while furthermore can sound slightly more neutral and academic. Don't worry too much about the difference. The most important thing is to use them to add supporting information. Now let's talk about on the contrary. This one is very useful, but learners often use it incorrectly. On the contrary does not simply mean but. It means that the opposite is true. Use it when you want to correct an idea or deny something. For example, some people think grammar is boring. On the contrary, it can be very interesting when you understand how it works. Here we are saying the opposite of the first idea. Grammar is not boring. It is interesting. Another example. The new policy did not reduce productivity. On the contrary, it made the team more efficient. Again, the second idea directly contradicts the first idea. Be careful. Don't say, I like coffee. On the contrary, I like tea. That sounds strange, because liking tea is not necessarily the opposite of liking coffee. A better sentence would be, I don't dislike coffee. On the contrary, I drink it every morning. That means the opposite of dislike is true. Finally, let's look at in light of. This expression means considering or because of a particular situation or information. It is often used in formal or professional contexts. For example, in light of the recent changes, we need to update our plan. This means that because of the recent changes or considering the recent changes, we need to update the plan. Another example. In light of your experience, we would like to offer you a senior position. Here, the decision is based on your experience. In Spanish, it is similar to a la luz de or teniendo en cuenta. You can also use it at the beginning of a sentence. In light of the results, the company decided to invest more money. Or in the middle, the company decided in light of the results to invest more money. The first version is simpler and more natural for most learners. Let's compare all five quickly. Use nevertheless to show contrast. It was expensive. Nevertheless, we bought it. Use furthermore to add information. It is useful. Furthermore, it is easy to use. Use moreover to add a strong extra point. He is talented. Moreover, he works extremely hard. Use on the contrary to say the opposite is true. It wasn't a failure. On the contrary, it was a great success. And use in light of to mean considering. In light of the evidence, we changed our opinion. To sound more fluent, don't try to use all of these words in every conversation. Choose one or two and practice them until they feel natural. For example, today, try writing three sentences with nevertheless and three with in light of. Quick recap. Nevertheless shows contrast. Furthermore and moreover add information. On the contrary corrects an idea with the opposite. And in light of means considering. Master these linking words and your English will sound clearer, more advanced, and much more confident.

c04f439fef753d39.topic: Sinónimos para 'good', 'bad', 'nice', 'happy'. Vocab: outstanding, dreadful, delightful, thrilled, content, gloomy

lesson.title: Upgrade Your English: Better Words Than Good, Bad, Nice, and Happy
lesson.prompt: Sinónimos para 'good', 'bad', 'nice', 'happy'. Vocab: outstanding, dreadful, delightful, thrilled, content, gloomy
lesson.script:
Do you ever feel that your English sounds a little too simple because you keep using words like good, bad, nice, and happy? Don’t worry. These words are useful, but if you want to sound more natural, expressive, and confident, it’s time to upgrade your vocabulary.

Today, we’ll look at better alternatives, including outstanding, dreadful, delightful, thrilled, content, and gloomy. These words will help you express your ideas with more precision and emotion.

Let’s start with good. Good is one of the most common words in English. We say a good movie, a good student, a good restaurant, or a good idea. But sometimes, good is too basic. If something is extremely good, you can say outstanding.

Outstanding means excellent, impressive, or much better than average. For example: The presentation was outstanding. That means the presentation was not just good. It was excellent. Another example: She is an outstanding teacher. This means she is a very, very good teacher.

Be careful with pronunciation: outstanding. It has three parts: out-standing. You can use it in professional situations, academic contexts, or everyday conversation when you want to sound more advanced.

Now let’s talk about bad. Bad is useful, of course, but it doesn’t always show the level of negativity. If something is very bad, unpleasant, or terrible, you can say dreadful.

Dreadful means extremely bad. For example: The weather was dreadful. This means the weather was really bad, maybe cold, rainy, windy, and horrible. Another example: I had a dreadful headache last night. That means the headache was very strong and unpleasant.

You can also say: The service at the hotel was dreadful. This sounds much stronger than: The service was bad. So remember, dreadful is a strong word. Use it when something is seriously bad.

Next, let’s upgrade the word nice. Nice is very common, but it can be vague. If you say, The hotel was nice, what do you really mean? Beautiful? Comfortable? Friendly? Pleasant? Sometimes, a better word is delightful.

Delightful means very pleasant, charming, or enjoyable. For example: We had a delightful evening. This means the evening was lovely and very enjoyable. Another example: The café has a delightful atmosphere. That means the atmosphere is pleasant, warm, and maybe beautiful.

You can use delightful for experiences, places, people, food, or surprises. For example: What a delightful surprise! Or: Your children are delightful. This means they are charming and pleasant to be around.

Now let’s look at happy. Happy is a basic and important word, but English has many different words for different types of happiness. Two useful alternatives are thrilled and content.

Thrilled means very excited and very happy, especially because something good happened. For example: I was thrilled to get the job. This means I was extremely happy and excited. Another example: She was thrilled with her exam results. That means she was very happy about them.

Use thrilled when the feeling is energetic and strong. Imagine someone smiling, celebrating, and feeling excited. That is thrilled.

Content is different. Content means peacefully happy or satisfied. It is not as energetic as thrilled. It is a calm type of happiness. For example: After a long walk and a good meal, I felt content. This means I felt satisfied and peaceful. Another example: He seems content with his life. That means he is satisfied, comfortable, and not looking for more.

This difference is important. If you win a competition, you are probably thrilled. If you are sitting at home with a cup of tea, feeling calm and satisfied, you are content.

Finally, let’s look at the opposite of happy. Many learners say sad, and that’s perfectly correct. But another useful word is gloomy.

Gloomy means sad, dark, or depressing. It can describe a person, a mood, a place, or even the weather. For example: He felt gloomy after hearing the news. That means he felt sad and low. Another example: It was a gloomy day. This could mean the sky was dark and cloudy, or the general feeling of the day was depressing.

You can also say: The room looked gloomy. That means the room was dark and maybe a little sad or uncomfortable. So gloomy is connected to sadness, darkness, and a low mood.

Let’s compare these words with simple examples.

Instead of saying: The movie was good, you can say: The movie was outstanding.

Instead of saying: The food was bad, you can say: The food was dreadful.

Instead of saying: The garden was nice, you can say: The garden was delightful.

Instead of saying: I’m very happy about the news, you can say: I’m thrilled about the news.

Instead of saying: I’m happy with my life, you can say: I’m content with my life.

Instead of saying: I feel sad today, you can say: I feel gloomy today.

Here’s a quick tip for Spanish speakers: don’t try to translate every word directly. Instead, connect each word with a situation. Outstanding is for something excellent. Dreadful is for something terrible. Delightful is for something pleasant and charming. Thrilled is excited happiness. Content is calm happiness. Gloomy is sadness or darkness.

Now, let’s practice with a mini story.

Yesterday, I went to a new restaurant. The food was outstanding, and the waiter was delightful. I was thrilled because they had my favorite dessert. After dinner, I felt completely content. But when I left the restaurant, the weather was dreadful. It was cold, rainy, and gloomy.

Did you hear all six words? Outstanding, delightful, thrilled, content, dreadful, and gloomy.

To recap: use outstanding instead of very good, dreadful instead of very bad, delightful instead of very nice, thrilled when you feel excited and happy, content when you feel calm and satisfied, and gloomy when something feels sad or dark.

Try using one of these words today in a sentence. The more you use them, the more natural they will feel in conversation.

058104aeffce4e57.topic: Hedging: cómo suavizar opiniones (clave en C1). Vocab: somewhat, rather, tend to, may suggest, it seems that

lesson.title: Hedging in English: How to Soften Opinions Like a C1 Speaker
lesson.prompt: Hedging: cómo suavizar opiniones (clave en C1). Vocab: somewhat, rather, tend to, may suggest, it seems that
lesson.script:
Have you ever said something in English that sounded too direct, even though you didn’t mean to be rude? For example, imagine saying, “This idea is bad,” in a meeting. It is clear, yes, but it may sound harsh. A more advanced speaker might say, “This idea seems somewhat risky,” or “It may suggest a few problems.” That is hedging, and it is a key skill for sounding more natural, polite, and sophisticated in English.

Today, we are going to look at hedging: how to soften opinions, especially in academic, professional, and advanced conversation. This is very important at C1 level because advanced English is not only about using difficult words. It is also about controlling tone.

So, what is hedging? Hedging means making your statement less absolute. Instead of saying something as a hard fact, you show that there is some uncertainty, or that your opinion is open to discussion. This is useful because it makes you sound more diplomatic, especially when you disagree, criticize, or analyze information.

Let’s compare some direct sentences with hedged versions.

Direct: “This solution is wrong.”
Hedged: “This solution seems somewhat problematic.”

Direct: “The results prove that people are unhappy.”
Hedged: “The results may suggest that people are somewhat dissatisfied.”

Direct: “He is arrogant.”
Hedged: “He tends to come across as rather confident, perhaps too confident at times.”

Can you hear the difference? The hedged versions are softer, more careful, and more professional.

Let’s focus on five very useful expressions: somewhat, rather, tend to, may suggest, and it seems that.

First, somewhat. Somewhat means “a little” or “to a certain degree.” It is more formal than “a bit” or “kind of.” For example: “The explanation was somewhat confusing.” This does not mean it was completely confusing. It means there was a degree of confusion. Another example: “The proposal is somewhat unrealistic.” Again, this is softer than saying, “The proposal is unrealistic.”

Second, rather. Rather can also soften adjectives, but be careful. In British English, “rather” is common and can mean “quite” or “a little more than expected.” For example: “The meeting was rather long.” This sounds more elegant than “The meeting was very long.” Another example: “Her response was rather direct.” This suggests that maybe it was too direct, but you are not saying it aggressively.

Now, compare somewhat and rather. “Somewhat disappointing” sounds like “a little disappointing.” “Rather disappointing” can sound stronger, depending on your tone. So, both are hedging words, but they are not always exactly the same.

Third, tend to. This is extremely useful when you want to talk about general patterns without saying “always.” For example, instead of saying, “Spanish speakers use too many long sentences,” you can say, “Spanish speakers tend to use longer sentences in English.” That sounds more respectful and more accurate. Another example: “People tend to be more productive in the morning.” This means it is a common pattern, not a universal rule.

This is especially important because words like always, never, everyone, and nobody can sound too absolute. At advanced levels, we often prefer more careful language: “People tend to,” “It often happens that,” or “There is a tendency to.”

Fourth, may suggest. This is a powerful phrase for analysis. It is common in academic English, presentations, and reports. Instead of saying, “This proves that the strategy failed,” you can say, “This may suggest that the strategy was not fully effective.” Notice two things: “may” adds uncertainty, and “suggest” is softer than “prove.”

For example: “The increase in complaints may suggest that customers are not satisfied with the new system.” This sounds balanced. You are interpreting the data, but you are not claiming that your interpretation is the only possible truth.

Fifth, it seems that. This phrase helps you introduce an opinion or interpretation more gently. For example: “It seems that the team needs more time.” This is softer than “The team needs more time.” Another example: “It seems that there has been a misunderstanding.” This is very useful in delicate situations. Instead of accusing someone by saying, “You misunderstood me,” you can say, “It seems that there has been a misunderstanding.” Much better.

Let’s practice transforming direct opinions into more advanced, hedged opinions.

Direct: “The plan is too expensive.”
Hedged: “The plan seems rather expensive.”

Direct: “The article is biased.”
Hedged: “The article appears to be somewhat biased.”

Direct: “Remote work makes communication difficult.”
Hedged: “Remote work may make communication somewhat more difficult.”

Direct: “Young people don’t read enough.”
Hedged: “Young people tend to read less than previous generations, although this depends on the context.”

Direct: “This decision will cause problems.”
Hedged: “This decision may lead to some problems.”

A very important point: hedging does not mean being weak. Some learners think, “If I hedge, I sound unsure.” Not necessarily. In advanced English, hedging often makes you sound more intelligent because you recognize complexity. Real life is rarely 100 percent clear. Hedging shows that you can express nuance.

This is especially useful in discussions. If you say, “That is wrong,” the other person may become defensive. But if you say, “I’m not sure that’s entirely accurate,” or “That may not be the best way to look at it,” the conversation stays open.

Here is a simple formula you can use: hedging phrase plus adjective or opinion.

“It seems that the process is somewhat slow.”
“This approach may be rather risky.”
“They tend to focus more on short-term results.”
“The data may suggest a change in consumer behavior.”

Now, your challenge: take a strong opinion you have and soften it. For example, instead of “Social media is dangerous,” try: “Social media may have a somewhat negative effect on mental health, especially when it is used excessively.” That sounds much more C1.

So, quick recap. Hedging means softening your opinions to sound more polite, careful, and advanced. Use somewhat to mean “to a certain degree.” Use rather to soften or elegantly intensify adjectives. Use tend to for general patterns. Use may suggest when interpreting information. And use it seems that to introduce opinions gently.

Try using one of these expressions today in a message, a meeting, or a conversation. It may seem like a small change, but it can make your English sound much more natural and sophisticated.
