16f293ffe90ff0a0.topic: Intensificadores que no son 'very'. Vocab: utterly, absolutely, completely, remarkably, incredibly

lesson.title: Stop Saying “Very”: Five Powerful Intensifiers in English
lesson.prompt: Intensificadores que no son 'very'. Vocab: utterly, absolutely, completely, remarkably, incredibly
lesson.script:
Do you use the word “very” all the time? Very good, very interesting, very tired, very difficult… It works, yes. But if you want your English to sound more natural, more expressive, and more advanced, you need more options. Today, we’ll look at five powerful intensifiers that can replace “very” in many situations: utterly, absolutely, completely, remarkably, and incredibly.

Let’s start with a quick reminder. Intensifiers are words that make adjectives or ideas stronger. For example, “It’s cold” becomes “It’s very cold.” But instead of always using “very,” native speakers often choose more specific intensifiers depending on the meaning and feeling they want.

First: absolutely. This is one of the most common and useful intensifiers in English. We use “absolutely” with strong adjectives, especially adjectives that already express an extreme idea. For example: “That movie was absolutely amazing.” Not “very amazing,” but “absolutely amazing.” Other examples: “You’re absolutely right.” “The food was absolutely delicious.” “The view was absolutely stunning.”

A useful expression is “absolutely not.” It sounds strong and clear. For example: “Are you going to apologize?” “Absolutely not.” It means definitely not.

Next: completely. “Completely” means one hundred percent, totally, with nothing missing. It’s often used when something is full, finished, changed, or true in every way. For example: “I completely agree with you.” That means I agree one hundred percent. “The room was completely empty.” No people, no furniture, nothing. “I completely forgot about the meeting.” That means I didn’t remember it at all.

Be careful: “completely” often focuses on totality. So it works very well with words like different, wrong, finished, empty, full, destroyed, lost, and forgotten. For example: “This is a completely different situation.” That sounds natural and precise.

Now let’s look at utterly. “Utterly” is stronger and a little more dramatic. It means totally or completely, but it often adds emotion. You’ll hear it with negative adjectives, but not only negative ones. For example: “I was utterly exhausted after the trip.” Stronger than “very tired.” “The idea was utterly ridiculous.” Stronger than “very silly” or “very ridiculous.” “She felt utterly alone.” That sounds emotional and serious.

You can also say: “That performance was utterly brilliant.” This is positive, but still intense and expressive. “Utterly” is common in more formal, literary, or dramatic speech, so use it when you want a strong effect.

The fourth word is incredibly. This one is very common in everyday English. It means extremely, and it can be used with many adjectives, both positive and negative. For example: “The test was incredibly difficult.” “He’s incredibly talented.” “That was incredibly kind of you.” “The city is incredibly expensive.”

“Incredibly” is flexible and natural. If you’re not sure which intensifier to use, “incredibly” is often a safe choice. It sounds more expressive than “very,” but not too formal. Compare: “She is very smart” and “She is incredibly smart.” The second sentence sounds more enthusiastic.

Finally: remarkably. “Remarkably” means surprisingly or unusually. It doesn’t just make the adjective stronger; it suggests that something is impressive or unexpected. For example: “She speaks English remarkably well.” This means she speaks very well, and it’s impressive. “The hotel was remarkably cheap for the location.” That means it was cheaper than expected. “He stayed remarkably calm during the crisis.” That means his calm reaction was surprising and impressive.

So, remember this difference: “incredibly” means extremely, but “remarkably” often means extremely in a surprising way. For example, “The restaurant was incredibly good” means it was extremely good. “The restaurant was remarkably good” means it was extremely good, maybe better than expected.

Now, let’s compare these intensifiers in real sentences. Instead of saying “I’m very tired,” you can say “I’m absolutely exhausted” or “I’m utterly exhausted.” Instead of “This is very different,” say “This is completely different.” Instead of “She is very intelligent,” say “She is incredibly intelligent.” Instead of “He did very well,” say “He did remarkably well.”

One important tip: not every intensifier works with every adjective. In English, some combinations sound natural because people use them often. We say “absolutely perfect,” “completely wrong,” “utterly ridiculous,” “incredibly beautiful,” and “remarkably calm.” Try to learn these combinations as chunks, not as separate words.

Let’s practice with a few mini examples. Repeat or imagine the sentence in your own life. “I completely agree.” “That’s absolutely true.” “The weather is incredibly hot today.” “Her progress has been remarkably fast.” “I felt utterly confused.” Great. These phrases will help your English sound more natural and more advanced.

Quick recap: use “absolutely” for strong emphasis, especially with extreme adjectives like amazing, perfect, right, or delicious. Use “completely” when you mean one hundred percent or totally. Use “utterly” for strong, emotional, or dramatic emphasis. Use “incredibly” as a natural everyday alternative to “very.” And use “remarkably” when something is impressive or surprising.

Your challenge for today: choose three sentences where you normally use “very,” and rewrite them with absolutely, completely, utterly, incredibly, or remarkably. The more you practice these small changes, the more powerful and natural your English will become.

74212afc5bb469e4.topic: Slang y expresiones modernas (uso real). Vocab: legit, lowkey, no cap, hit different, vibe with

lesson.title: Modern English Slang You’ll Actually Hear: legit, lowkey, no cap, hit different, and vibe with
lesson.prompt: Slang y expresiones modernas (uso real). Vocab: legit, lowkey, no cap, hit different, vibe with
lesson.script:
Have you ever watched a TikTok, a YouTube video, or a Netflix series in English and thought, “Wait… I know all the words, but I still don’t understand the sentence”? That often happens because of slang. Today, we’re going to learn five modern expressions that native speakers really use: legit, lowkey, no cap, hit different, and vibe with.

Before we start, a quick warning: slang is usually informal. You can use these expressions with friends, online, in casual conversations, and sometimes at work if the environment is relaxed. But don’t use them in a formal email, an exam essay, or a job interview unless you’re completely sure it fits the context.

Let’s start with legit.

Legit comes from legitimate, but in everyday English, it means real, true, authentic, or seriously good. For example: “That restaurant is legit.” This means the restaurant is really good, not just okay. You might also hear: “Is this website legit?” That means, “Is this website real and trustworthy?”

Another example: “She’s a legit expert in marketing.” This means she is truly an expert, not someone pretending. So, legit can describe people, places, products, information, and experiences.

Now let’s look at lowkey.

Lowkey means secretly, quietly, or a little bit. It’s used when you want to express something without sounding too intense. For example: “I lowkey love this song.” This means, “I kind of love this song,” or “I love it, but I don’t want to make a big deal about it.”

Another example: “I’m lowkey nervous about the presentation.” You’re nervous, but maybe not extremely nervous, or you don’t want everyone to know. You can also say: “That movie was lowkey amazing.” Meaning: it was surprisingly good.

Be careful: lowkey is very informal. It’s common in social media and casual speech, especially among younger speakers.

Next: no cap.

No cap means “I’m not lying,” “I’m serious,” or “for real.” It is used to emphasize that what you’re saying is true. For example: “That was the best pizza I’ve ever had, no cap.” You’re saying, “I’m serious. I’m not exaggerating.”

Another example: “He’s one of the funniest people I know, no cap.” It means you truly think he is very funny.

You might also hear just “cap,” which means a lie. For example, if someone says, “I can run ten kilometers in twenty minutes,” another person might say, “That’s cap.” Meaning: “That’s not true.” But be careful: this expression is very casual and can sound too slangy in some situations.

Now, let’s talk about hit different.

If something hits different, it feels special, stronger, or more emotional in a certain situation. It doesn’t literally hit you. It means the experience has a different effect on you.

For example: “Coffee hits different on a Monday morning.” This means coffee feels especially good or necessary on a Monday morning. Another example: “This song hits different after a breakup.” The song feels more emotional because of your personal situation.

You can use hit different with food, music, places, memories, weather, or experiences. “A hot shower hits different after a long day.” That means it feels especially amazing after you’re tired.

This expression is great because it communicates emotion in a very natural, modern way.

Finally, let’s learn vibe with.

To vibe with something or someone means to connect with it, like it, enjoy it, or feel comfortable with it. For example: “I really vibe with this song.” This means you really like the song and feel connected to its style or energy.

With people, you can say: “I vibe with her.” That means you get along with her, you feel comfortable, and you like her energy. Another example: “I don’t really vibe with this place.” This means the place doesn’t feel right for you, or you don’t enjoy the atmosphere.

You can also use it as a noun: vibe. For example: “This café has a great vibe.” That means the atmosphere is nice. Or: “I like his vibe.” That means you like his energy, personality, or attitude.

Now let’s put everything together in a natural mini-conversation.

Imagine someone says: “That new café is legit. The music hits different in the evening, and I lowkey love the decoration. The owner is super nice too. I really vibe with that place, no cap.”

This means: “That new café is really good. The music feels special in the evening, and I secretly or kind of love the decoration. The owner is very nice. I really like the atmosphere of that place, seriously.”

Let’s practice a few more examples.

“Her advice was legit helpful.” This means her advice was truly useful.

“I lowkey want to stay home tonight.” This means you kind of want to stay home, maybe secretly.

“This series is amazing, no cap.” This means you are serious; the series is really amazing.

“Rainy days hit different when you don’t have to work.” This means rainy days feel especially nice when you can relax.

“I don’t vibe with that kind of music.” This means you don’t really like or connect with that music.

So, quick recap: legit means real, true, or really good. Lowkey means secretly, quietly, or a little bit. No cap means I’m serious or I’m not lying. Hit different means something feels special or stronger in a certain situation. And vibe with means to like, connect with, or feel comfortable with something or someone.

Try using one of these expressions today in a casual sentence. For example: “This lesson was legit useful, no cap.” See? Now you’re sounding more natural already.

d7c73c6e9e416b2f.topic: Connected speech: por qué los nativos suenan 'rápido'. Linking sounds: 'want to' → wanna, 'going to' → gonna

lesson.title: Why Native Speakers Sound Fast: Connected Speech, Wanna, and Gonna
lesson.prompt: Connected speech: por qué los nativos suenan 'rápido'. Linking sounds: 'want to' → wanna, 'going to' → gonna
lesson.script:
Have you ever listened to a native English speaker and thought, “Wait… did they skip half the words?” Good news: they probably didn’t. What you are hearing is connected speech, and it is one of the biggest reasons English sounds so fast in real life.

In class, we often learn English word by word: I want to go. She is going to call me. What do you want? But in natural conversation, native speakers connect words, reduce sounds, and sometimes change pronunciation. They are not trying to be unclear. They are simply speaking with rhythm and flow.

Let’s start with a very common example: want to. In slow, careful speech, you might hear: I want to leave. But in everyday English, many speakers say: I wanna leave. Want to becomes wanna.

Listen to the difference: I want to go. I wanna go. Do you want to try? Do you wanna try? They want to come with us. They wanna come with us.

Important: wanna is very common in speaking, music, films, and informal messages. But in formal writing, write want to. For example, in an email to your boss, write: I want to discuss the project. Not: I wanna discuss the project.

Now let’s look at going to. When we talk about future plans, going to often becomes gonna. For example: I am going to study tonight becomes I’m gonna study tonight. She is going to call you becomes She’s gonna call you. We are going to be late becomes We’re gonna be late.

Notice something important. Gonna is used when going to means a future plan or prediction. For example: I’m gonna travel next month. It’s gonna rain. They’re gonna love this.

But if going to means movement to a place, we usually do not reduce it to gonna. For example: I’m going to the supermarket. Here, “to the supermarket” is a place, so don’t say: I’m gonna the supermarket. That sounds wrong. You can say: I’m going to the supermarket. Or more naturally: I’m going to the store.

So, quick rule: future plan? Gonna. Movement to a place? Going to.

Let’s practice. Future: I’m going to call you later. Natural: I’m gonna call you later. Movement: I’m going to the office. Natural: I’m going to the office. Not: I’m gonna the office.

Connected speech is not only about wanna and gonna. English has many small reductions. For example, have to often sounds like hafta. I have to work becomes I hafta work. Has to sounds like hasta. She has to leave becomes She hasta leave. Got to often becomes gotta. I’ve got to go becomes I gotta go.

You may also hear kind of become kinda, sort of become sorta, and give me become gimme. For example: It’s kind of difficult becomes It’s kinda difficult. I sort of like it becomes I sorta like it. Give me a minute becomes Gimme a minute.

Now, should you use these reductions? Yes, but carefully. You don’t need to force them. The first goal is to understand them when you hear them. If you watch a movie and hear “Whaddaya wanna do?” you can recognize that it means “What do you want to do?” That is a huge listening victory.

For speaking, start with the most common and natural ones: wanna and gonna. They are very normal in informal spoken English. Try simple sentences: I wanna improve my English. I’m gonna practice every day. Do you wanna join us? It’s gonna be fun.

Also, remember that connected speech depends on speed, context, and formality. In a job interview, a speaker may say, “I want to explain my experience.” With friends, the same person may say, “I wanna tell you something.” Both are correct in the right situation.

Here’s a useful listening tip: don’t try to hear every single word separately. Listen for chunks. Instead of hearing “I / am / going / to / study,” train your ear to hear “I’m gonna study” as one natural unit. English rhythm works in groups, not isolated words.

Let’s do a mini practice. I’ll say the careful version, then the natural version. I want to see it. I wanna see it. We are going to win. We’re gonna win. Do you want to come? Do you wanna come? I have to go now. I hafta go now. Give me a second. Gimme a second.

So, why do native speakers sound fast? Because they connect words, reduce sounds, and speak in chunks. They are not pronouncing English exactly like a textbook. They are using the natural rhythm of the language.

Quick recap: want to often becomes wanna. Going to becomes gonna when it talks about the future, but not when it means movement to a place. And the best way to improve your listening is to learn common chunks, not just individual words.

Today, choose three sentences with wanna or gonna and say them out loud. For example: I wanna learn more. I’m gonna practice today. It’s gonna get easier. Because it really is gonna get easier.

Give me a second. Give me a second. So why do native speakers sound fast? Because they connect words, reduce sounds, and speak in chunks. They are not pronouncing English exactly like a textbook. They are using the natural rhythm of the language. Quick recap. Want to often becomes wanna, going to, becomes gonna when it talks about the future, but not when it means movement to a place. And the best way to improve your listening is to learn common chunks, not just individual words. Today, choose three sentences with wanna or gonna and say them out loud. For example, I wanna learn more. I'm gonna practice today. It's gonna get easier because it really is gonna get easier.

quiz.question: Why can native English speakers sound very fast to learners?
options: Because they usually skip important words completely.
Because they connect words, reduce sounds, and speak in chunks.
Because they speak English exactly as it appears in textbooks.
Because they avoid using common expressions in conversation.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses “gonna” incorrectly?
options: I’m gonna study tonight.
She’s gonna call you later.
It’s gonna rain tomorrow.
I’m gonna the supermarket.

quiz.question: What does the lesson recommend as the first goal with connected speech?
options: To use all reductions in every formal situation.
To write reductions like “wanna” in professional emails.
To understand reductions when you hear them.
To pronounce every word separately and clearly.

quiz.question: What listening strategy does the lesson suggest?
options: Focus only on grammar rules, not pronunciation.
Listen for chunks instead of every single word separately.
Avoid movies because connected speech is too difficult.
Translate every reduced form into Spanish immediately.

c506471e6f31ac50.topic: Schwa (/ə/) — el sonido más importante del inglés

lesson.title: Schwa: The Most Important Sound in English
lesson.prompt: Schwa (/ə/) — el sonido más importante del inglés
lesson.script:
What if I told you that the most common sound in English is not A, E, I, O, or U? It’s a tiny, relaxed sound that many learners don’t notice, but native speakers use it all the time. This sound is called the schwa, and its symbol is /ə/.

If you speak Spanish, this lesson is especially important. In Spanish, vowels are usually clear and strong. The letter A sounds like “a,” E sounds like “e,” and so on. But English is different. In English, many vowels become weak, short, and relaxed when they are not stressed. That weak sound is the schwa.

The schwa sounds like a very relaxed “uh.” Not strong. Not clear. Just “uh.” For example, in the word “about,” the first letter A is not pronounced like the Spanish “a.” We don’t say “A-bout.” We say “uh-BOUT.” The first sound is schwa: /ə/.

Listen to these examples: about, again, banana, support, problem, teacher, family. In many of these words, one vowel is reduced to schwa.

Let’s look at stress, because stress is the key. In English, some syllables are stressed, which means they are longer, louder, and clearer. Other syllables are unstressed, which means they are shorter, softer, and often reduced to schwa.

Take the word “banana.” In Spanish, you might want to pronounce every vowel clearly: ba-na-na. But in English, the stress is on the middle syllable: ba-NA-na. The first and last vowels are weak: /bəˈnænə/. It sounds like “buh-NA-nuh.”

Another example is “photograph” and “photographer.” In “photograph,” the first syllable is stressed: PHO-to-graph. But in “photographer,” the stress moves: pho-TOG-ra-pher. Some vowels change and become weaker. This is one reason English pronunciation can feel unpredictable.

Now, here is something very useful: the schwa can be written with any vowel letter. It is not connected to one spelling. The letter A can be schwa, as in “about.” The letter E can be schwa, as in “problem.” The letter I can be schwa, as in “family,” when pronounced “FAM-uh-lee” or even “FAM-lee.” The letter O can be schwa, as in “support.” And the letter U can be schwa, as in “supply.”

This is why reading English like Spanish often creates an accent. If you pronounce every written vowel clearly, your English may sound too strong or too syllable-by-syllable. Using schwa helps your English sound more natural and fluent.

Schwa is also very common in small grammar words, especially in connected speech. Words like “to,” “of,” “a,” “the,” “can,” and “for” often become weak.

For example, we usually don’t say “I want TO go” with a strong “to.” In natural speech, we say “I want tuh go.” The word “to” becomes /tə/.

We don’t usually say “a cup OF coffee” with a strong “of.” We say “a cup uh coffee.” The word “of” often sounds like /əv/ or just /ə/ in fast speech.

And “can” changes too. If it is not stressed, “can” often sounds like “kun” or “kən.” For example: “I can do it” sounds like “I kən DO it.” But in a short answer, we stress it: “Yes, I CAN.”

This is very important: schwa is not lazy English. It is normal English. Native speakers reduce unstressed sounds because English has a rhythm. English rhythm is like music: strong beats and weak beats. Spanish rhythm is more even, but English rhythm depends a lot on stress.

Let’s practice with a few common words. Repeat them with a relaxed schwa sound.

About: uh-BOUT.
Again: uh-GEN.
Support: suh-PORT.
Today: tuh-DAY.
Teacher: TEE-chur.
Doctor: DOC-tur.
Problem: PROB-lum.
Banana: buh-NA-nuh.

Now let’s try short phrases.

A cup of tea: uh cup uh tea.
I want to go: I want tuh go.
She can do it: She kən do it.
We’re going to leave: We’re going tuh leave.

Notice how the important words stay clear: cup, tea, want, go, do, leave. The small grammar words become softer. This makes the sentence flow naturally.

So, how can you improve your schwa? First, don’t try to pronounce every vowel strongly. Second, learn the stress of new words. When you learn a word, ask: Which syllable is stressed? Third, listen to native speakers and pay attention to the weak sounds, not only the strong ones. Finally, practice reducing common words like “to,” “of,” “a,” and “can.”

Let’s recap. The schwa /ə/ is the most common sound in English. It sounds like a relaxed “uh.” It appears in unstressed syllables and in weak forms of small grammar words. For Spanish speakers, mastering schwa can make your English sound much more natural, smooth, and fluent.

Your challenge today is simple: choose five English words you already know and check where the stress is. Then ask yourself: Is there a vowel that becomes schwa? Once you start hearing it, you will notice it everywhere.

f4c92b5f73724c5c.topic: Word stress — palabras que cambian de significado según el acento. Vocab: PREsent vs. preSENT, REcord vs. reCORD

lesson.title: Word Stress: PREsent or preSENT?
lesson.prompt: Word stress — palabras que cambian de significado según el acento. Vocab: PREsent vs. preSENT, REcord vs. reCORD
lesson.script:
One small change in stress can change the whole meaning of a word. Yes, really. In English, it’s not only what you say, but where you put the emphasis. Today, we’ll look at words that change meaning depending on the stressed syllable, like PREsent and preSENT, or REcord and reCORD.

If your first language is Spanish, this topic is especially important. In Spanish, written accents often show you where the stress goes: teléfono, café, música. In English, we usually don’t write an accent mark. So you have to learn the stress pattern together with the word.

Let’s start with a simple idea. Many two-syllable words in English have one pronunciation when they are nouns or adjectives, and another pronunciation when they are verbs. Very often, the noun or adjective is stressed on the first syllable. The verb is stressed on the second syllable.

Listen to this pattern: PREsent, preSENT. PREsent, preSENT.

When we say PREsent, with stress on the first syllable, it can mean a gift. For example: I bought you a PREsent. It can also mean current or here. For example: The PREsent situation is difficult. Or: Everyone was PREsent in class.

But when we say preSENT, with stress on the second syllable, it is a verb. It means to show, give, or introduce something formally. For example: I will preSENT my project tomorrow. She preSENTed the results in the meeting.

So compare these two sentences. I have a PREsent for you. I will preSENT it after dinner. Same spelling, different stress, different meaning.

Now let’s look at another very common example: REcord and reCORD.

REcord, with stress on the first syllable, is a noun. It means a written or saved piece of information, or sometimes a music album. For example: The doctor checked my medical REcord. Or: That band released a new REcord.

reCORD, with stress on the second syllable, is a verb. It means to save sound, video, or information. For example: I need to reCORD a video for my English class. Or: Can you reCORD the meeting?

Let’s compare: This is an important REcord. Please reCORD the interview.

Notice how the stressed syllable sounds stronger, longer, and clearer. PREsent. The first syllable is strong: PRE. preSENT. The second syllable is strong: SENT. REcord. First syllable strong: RE. reCORD. Second syllable strong: CORD.

This stress pattern appears in many English words. Here are a few more examples.

CONtract and conTRACT. A CONtract is a legal agreement. For example: We signed a CONtract. To conTRACT means to become smaller, or to get an illness. For example: Muscles conTRACT when they move.

OBject and obJECT. An OBject is a thing. For example: There is a strange OBject on the table. To obJECT means to disagree. For example: I obJECT to that decision.

PROject and proJECT. A PROject is a piece of work or a plan. For example: We finished the PROject. To proJECT means to show or send something forward, like an image or a voice. For example: The machine can proJECT the image onto the wall.

EXport and exPORT. An EXport is a product sent to another country. For example: Coffee is an important EXport. To exPORT means to send goods or data out. For example: Colombia exPORTS coffee.

IMport and imPORT. An IMport is a product brought into a country. To imPORT means to bring something in. For example: The company imPORTS cars from Japan.

Now, here’s the important part: don’t try to pronounce both versions the same way. If you say “I will PREsent my project,” people will probably understand you from context, but it will sound unnatural. If you say “Can you REcord this video?” it may sound confusing or less fluent.

A good strategy is to learn these words in pairs and in short sentences. Don’t just memorize “present.” Memorize: a PREsent, to preSENT. Don’t just memorize “record.” Memorize: a REcord, to reCORD.

Let’s practice a few together. Listen and repeat in your mind, or out loud if you can.

I bought a PREsent. I will preSENT my idea.

This is a medical REcord. Please reCORD the audio.

We signed a CONtract. Muscles conTRACT.

That is an OBject. I obJECT.

We finished the PROject. They will proJECT the image.

Great. One final pronunciation tip: the unstressed syllable often becomes weaker. In preSENT, the first syllable is softer: pre. In reCORD, the first syllable is softer: re. English rhythm depends a lot on this contrast between strong and weak syllables.

So, quick recap. In many two-syllable English words, nouns and adjectives often have stress on the first syllable: PREsent, REcord, CONtract. Verbs often have stress on the second syllable: preSENT, reCORD, conTRACT. Stress can change the meaning, so learn the word together with its pronunciation and an example sentence.

Your challenge today: choose three word pairs from this lesson and make two sentences with each one, one as a noun or adjective, and one as a verb. Say them out loud, exaggerate the stress, and your English will sound clearer, more natural, and more confident.

506c3089752f96b3.topic: Sentence stress y ritmo del inglés

lesson.title: Sentence Stress and the Rhythm of English
lesson.prompt: Sentence stress y ritmo del inglés
lesson.script:
Have you ever understood every word in an English sentence, but still felt that the speaker’s rhythm was strange or difficult to follow? That’s because English is not only about words and grammar. It also has music. And one of the most important parts of that music is sentence stress.

Today, we’re going to talk about sentence stress and the rhythm of English, especially for Spanish-speaking learners. This topic can make your English sound much more natural, and it can also help you understand native speakers more easily.

Let’s start with a key idea: English is a stress-timed language. Spanish is more syllable-timed. What does that mean?

In Spanish, syllables usually have a more regular rhythm. Each syllable tends to receive a similar amount of time. For example, in a Spanish sentence, you often pronounce most syllables clearly and evenly.

But English works differently. In English, some words are strong, and other words are weak. The strong words carry the main meaning. The weak words are often shorter, faster, and less clear. This creates the rhythm of English: strong, weak, weak, strong, weak, strong.

Let’s look at an example.

I want to go to the store.

If we pronounce every word with the same stress, it sounds unnatural: I WANT TO GO TO THE STORE. That sounds a bit robotic.

In natural English, we usually stress the important words: WANT, GO, STORE.

So it sounds more like: I WANT to GO to the STORE.

Notice that “I,” “to,” “the,” and sometimes even “to” again are weaker. They are not as important for the main message.

In English, we usually stress content words. Content words are words that carry meaning: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and negative words.

For example: coffee, study, beautiful, quickly, never.

We usually do not stress function words. Function words help with grammar: articles, prepositions, pronouns, auxiliary verbs, and conjunctions.

For example: the, to, of, he, she, can, do, and, but.

Let’s practice with a sentence.

She can speak English very well.

Which words are important? Speak, English, well. Maybe very, too, because it adds emphasis.

So the rhythm is: She can SPEAK ENGLISH very WELL.

The word “can” is usually weak in positive sentences. It may sound like “kn.” She can speak. Not SHE CAN SPEAK, but She can SPEAK.

However, if we want to emphasize ability, we can stress “can.” For example: You think she can’t speak English? She CAN speak English.

So stress can change depending on meaning. That’s very important.

Let’s compare two sentences.

I didn’t say he stole the money.

This sentence can have different meanings depending on which word we stress.

I didn’t say he stole the money. Someone else said it, not me.

I didn’t say he stole the money. I did not say it.

I didn’t say he stole the money. Maybe I suggested it, but I didn’t say it directly.

I didn’t say he stole the money. Maybe someone else stole it.

I didn’t say he stole the money. Maybe he borrowed it or found it.

I didn’t say he stole the money. Maybe he stole something else.

This is why sentence stress is powerful. It doesn’t just make your pronunciation better. It changes the message.

Now, let’s talk about rhythm. In English, the time between stressed words tends to be more regular. This means weak words often get compressed, or reduced, to fit the rhythm.

For example: What are you going to do?

In careful pronunciation, you can hear every word clearly. But in natural speech, it often sounds like: What are you gonna DO?

The most important word is “do,” because it asks about the action. “Going to” often becomes “gonna” in casual speech.

Another example: I have to leave at five.

The stressed words are HAVE, LEAVE, FIVE. In natural speech, “have to” may sound like “hafta.”

I HAFTA LEAVE at FIVE.

For Spanish speakers, one common challenge is giving too much stress to every word. This can make English sound flat or too syllable-by-syllable. To sound more natural, try to make the important words longer, louder, and clearer. Make the small grammar words shorter and softer.

Let’s practice with a few sentences. Listen to the stressed words.

I’m meeting my FRIENDS after WORK.

We need to FINISH the PROJECT by FRIDAY.

She doesn’t LIKE spicy FOOD.

Can you HELP me with this EMAIL?

In each sentence, the stressed words carry the main information. If you only heard those words, you could understand the basic message: friends, work. Finish, project, Friday. Like, spicy food. Help, email.

Here’s a simple exercise you can do. Take any English sentence and underline the words that carry the main meaning. Then read only those words. After that, add the small words back in, but say them quickly and softly.

For example: I need a cup of coffee before class.

Main words: need, cup, coffee, class.

Now say the full sentence: I NEED a CUP of COFFEE before CLASS.

Try not to pronounce “a” and “of” too strongly. They are weak.

Another useful tip: stress the new information. If someone asks, “Do you want tea?” and you answer, “No, I want coffee,” the word “coffee” is stressed because it is the important new idea.

No, I want COFFEE.

But if someone says, “Maria wants coffee,” and that’s wrong, you might say: No, I want coffee. Here, “I” is stressed to correct the person.

No, I want coffee.

So remember: sentence stress depends on meaning, contrast, and context.

Let’s recap. English rhythm is based on strong and weak words. We usually stress content words like nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and negatives. We usually reduce function words like articles, prepositions, pronouns, and auxiliary verbs. Stress can also change the meaning of a sentence, especially when we want to correct or contrast information.

Your challenge today is simple: choose three English sentences and mark the stressed words. Then read them aloud with a strong rhythm. Make the important words clear, and make the small words softer. With practice, your English will sound more natural, more fluent, and much easier to understand.

506c3089752f96b3.title: Sentence Stress and the Rhythm of English
506c3089752f96b3.transcriptText: Have you ever understood every word in an English sentence, but still felt that the speaker's rhythm was strange or difficult to follow? That's because English is not only about words and grammar, it also has music. And one of the most important parts of that music is sentence stress. Today, we're going to talk about sentence stress and the rhythm of English, especially for Spanish-speaking learners. This topic can make your English sound much more natural, and it can also help you understand native speakers more easily. Let's start with a key idea. English is a stress-timed language. Spanish is more syllable-timed. What does that mean? In Spanish, syllables usually have a more regular rhythm. Each syllable tends to receive a similar amount of time. For example, in a Spanish sentence, you often pronounce most syllables clearly and evenly. But English works differently. In English, some words are strong, and other words are weak. The strong words carry the main meaning. The weak words are often shorter, faster, and less clear. This creates the rhythm of English – strong, weak, weak, strong, weak, strong. Let's look at an example. I want to go to the store. If we pronounce every word with the same stress, it sounds unnatural. I want to go to the store. That sounds a bit robotic. In natural English, we usually stress the important words want, go, store. So it sounds more like I want to go to the store. Notice that I to the, and sometimes even to again, are weaker. They are not as important for the main message. In English, we usually stress content words. Content words are words that carry meaning – nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and negative words. For example, coffee, study, beautiful, quickly, never. We usually do not stress function words. Function words help with grammar, articles, prepositions, pronouns, auxiliary verbs, and conjunctions. For example, the to of he, she, can do, and, but. Let's practice with a sentence. She can speak English very well. Which words are important? Speak English well. Can be very too, because it adds emphasis. So the rhythm is, she can speak English very well. The word can is usually weak in positive sentences. It may sound like can a, she can speak. Not she can speak, but she can speak. However, if we want to emphasize ability, we can stress can. For example, you think she can't speak English? She can speak English. So stress can change depending on meaning. That's very important. Let's compare two sentences. I didn't say he stole the money. This sentence can have different meanings depending on which words we stress. I didn't say he stole the money. Someone else said it, not me. I didn't say he stole the money. I did not say it. I didn't say he stole the money. Maybe I suggested it, but I didn't say it directly. I didn't say he stole the money. Maybe someone else stole it. I didn't say he stole the money. Maybe he borrowed it or found it. I didn't say he stole the money. Maybe he stole something else. This is why sentence stress is powerful. It doesn't just make your pronunciation better. It changes the message. Now let's talk about rhythm. In English, the time between stressed words tends to be more regular. This means weak words often get compressed or reduced to fit the rhythm. For example, what are you going to do? In careful pronunciation, you can hear every word clearly. But in natural speech, it often sounds like, what are you going to do? The most important word is do because it asks about the action. Going to often becomes gonna in casual speech. Another example. I have to leave at five. The stressed words are have, leave, five. In natural speech, have to may sound like hafta. I hafta leave at five. For Spanish speakers, one common challenge is giving too much stress to every word. This can make English sound flat or two-syllable by syllable. To sound more natural, try to make the important words longer, louder, and clearer. Make the small grammar words shorter and softer. Let's practice with a few sentences. Listen to the stressed words. I'm meeting my friends after work. We need to finish the project by Friday. She doesn't like spicy food. Can you help me with this email? In each sentence, the stressed words carry the main information. If you only heard those words, you could understand the basic message. Friends, work, finish, project, Friday, like, spicy food, help, email. Here's a simple exercise you can do. Take any English sentence and underline the words that carry the main meaning. Then read only those words. After that, add the small words back in, but say them quickly and softly. For example, I need a cup of coffee before class. Main words, need, cup, coffee, class. Now say the full sentence. I need a cup of coffee before class. Try not to pronounce a and of too strongly. They are weak. Another useful tip, stress the new information. If someone asks, do you want tea? And you answer, no, I want coffee. The word coffee is stressed because it is the important new idea. No, I want coffee. But if someone says, Maria wants coffee, and that's wrong, you might say, no, I want coffee. Here, I is stressed to correct the person, no, I want coffee. So remember, sentence stress depends on meaning, contrast, and context. Let's recap, English rhythm is based on strong and weak words. We usually stress content words like nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and negatives. We usually reduce function words like articles, prepositions, pronouns, and auxiliary verbs. Stress can also change the meaning of a sentence, especially when we want to correct or contrast information. Your challenge today is simple. Choose three English sentences and mark the stressed words. Then read them aloud with a strong rhythm. Make the important words clear and make the small words softer. With practice, your English will sound more natural, more fluent, and much easier to understand.

c672b4280a230f92.topic: Sonidos difíciles para hispanohablantes: /ɪ/ vs /iː/, /æ/ vs /ʌ/

lesson.title: Tricky English Vowels: /ɪ/ vs /iː/ and /æ/ vs /ʌ/
lesson.prompt: Sonidos difíciles para hispanohablantes: /ɪ/ vs /iː/, /æ/ vs /ʌ/
lesson.script:
Can one tiny vowel sound change the whole meaning of your sentence? Absolutely. If you say “ship” like “sheep,” or “cat” like “cut,” people may understand you from context, but your English will sound less clear. Today, we’re going to train four difficult sounds for Spanish speakers: /ɪ/ and /iː/, like in “ship” and “sheep,” and /æ/ and /ʌ/, like in “cat” and “cut.”

Let’s start with /ɪ/ versus /iː/. Spanish has a sound similar to the English /iː/, as in “see,” “green,” and “teacher.” It is a long, tense sound. Your mouth is smiling a little, your tongue is high, and the sound is longer: /iː/. Listen: “sheep,” “leave,” “feel,” “beat.”

Now, /ɪ/ is different. It is shorter and more relaxed. Your mouth is not smiling as much, and the tongue is a little lower. Listen: /ɪ/. “ship,” “live,” “fill,” “bit.”

Compare these pairs: “ship” and “sheep.” “I saw a ship.” “I saw a sheep.” “live” and “leave.” “I live here.” “Please leave now.” “fill” and “feel.” “Fill the glass.” “I feel happy.”

A common mistake for Spanish speakers is using /iː/ for both sounds. So “ship” becomes “sheep,” and “live” becomes “leave.” To practice, make /iː/ long and tense: “sheeeep.” Then make /ɪ/ short and relaxed: “ship.” Try this pattern: “ship, sheep, ship, sheep.” Now in a sentence: “The ship is near the sheep.”

Here is a useful trick. For /iː/, imagine you are smiling for a photo: “cheese.” For /ɪ/, relax your face and keep the sound short, like a quick sound in the middle of your mouth: “sit.” Practice: “sit,” “seat.” “This,” “these.” “bit,” “beat.”

Now let’s move to /æ/ versus /ʌ/. These two sounds can be especially difficult because they don’t exist in exactly the same way in Spanish.

First, /æ/, like in “cat,” “man,” “bad,” and “happy.” This sound is open and wide. Your mouth opens more than for Spanish “e,” and your tongue is low and forward. It can feel a little exaggerated at first. Listen: /æ/. “cat,” “black,” “sand,” “family.”

Now, /ʌ/, like in “cut,” “sun,” “love,” and “money.” This sound is short and relaxed. Your mouth is more neutral, not wide, and your tongue is more central. Listen: /ʌ/. “cut,” “bus,” “luck,” “mother.”

Compare these pairs: “cat” and “cut.” “The cat is small.” “Cut the paper.” “cap” and “cup.” “I need a cap.” “I need a cup.” “ankle” and “uncle.” “My ankle hurts.” “My uncle is funny.”

Many Spanish speakers make /æ/ sound too much like Spanish “a.” But English /æ/ is not exactly “a.” It is wider and more forward. Try saying “a” in Spanish, then open your mouth a little wider and smile slightly: /æ/. “cat.” “man.” “bad.”

For /ʌ/, avoid making it too open like Spanish “a.” Keep it short and central: “cup,” not “cap.” “luck,” not “lack.” Try this contrast: “lack, luck.” “I lack time.” “Good luck!”

Let’s do a short practice with all four sounds. Repeat these pairs slowly: “ship, sheep.” “sit, seat.” “fill, feel.” “cat, cut.” “cap, cup.” “lack, luck.”

Now repeat these sentences: “I live near the beach.” Notice: “live” has /ɪ/, and “beach” has /iː/. “This sheep is on a ship.” “The man has a cup.” “My uncle has a black cat.” “I feel lucky today.”

Here’s one final tip: don’t only practice single words. Practice minimal pairs, then short sentences, then real conversation. Your brain needs to hear and produce the difference many times. Record yourself saying “ship” and “sheep,” or “cap” and “cup,” and compare your pronunciation with a native speaker.

Quick recap: /iː/ is long and tense, like “sheep.” /ɪ/ is short and relaxed, like “ship.” /æ/ is open and wide, like “cat.” /ʌ/ is short and central, like “cut.” Practice these sounds a little every day, and your English pronunciation will become much clearer and more natural.

lesson.title: Master the Two TH Sounds in English
lesson.prompt: La 'TH' — voiced y voiceless
lesson.script:
Think about these two words: think and this. They both have the letters T H, but they do not have the same sound. And for Spanish speakers, this can feel strange at first, because Spanish does not use these exact sounds in the same way. But don’t worry. Today you’ll learn the two TH sounds in English: the voiceless TH, as in think, and the voiced TH, as in this.

Let’s start with the most important idea: there are two TH sounds.

The first one is voiceless TH: /θ/. You hear it in words like think, three, thank you, mouth, and both. It is called voiceless because your vocal cords do not vibrate. It is just air.

The second one is voiced TH: /ð/. You hear it in words like this, that, these, those, mother, and brother. It is called voiced because your vocal cords vibrate. You use your voice.

Now, how do you make these sounds?

For both TH sounds, place the tip of your tongue gently between your teeth, or just behind your top teeth. The key word is gently. You do not need to bite your tongue. Then let the air pass.

For the voiceless TH, /θ/, use only air. Try this: think. Three. Thank you. Both. Mouth. You should feel air coming out, but no vibration in your throat.

Put your fingers on your throat and say: sssss. No vibration. Now say: think. Also no vibration. That is voiceless.

Now let’s try the voiced TH, /ð/. Put your tongue in the same position, but add your voice. Try: this. That. These. Those. Mother. Brother. You should feel vibration in your throat.

Put your fingers on your throat and say: zzzzz. You feel vibration. Now say: this. That. You should feel vibration too. That is voiced.

A common mistake for Spanish speakers is replacing TH with T, D, S, or F. For example, think may sound like tink or sink. This may sound like dis. Three may sound like tree. In many situations, people will still understand you, but if you want clearer pronunciation, practicing TH will help a lot.

Let’s compare some minimal pairs. Listen to the difference.

Think and sink. Think: tongue between the teeth, air only. Sink: tongue stays inside, like Spanish S.

Three and tree. Three has TH. Tree has T R.

Thin and tin. Thin starts with voiceless TH. Tin starts with T.

Then and den. Then starts with voiced TH. Den starts with D.

They and day. They has voiced TH. Day has D.

Now repeat these short phrases:

I think so.

Three things.

Thank you for everything.

Both of them.

This is my brother.

These are better than those.

My mother is there.

They live together.

Notice something useful: many common grammar words use the voiced TH, /ð/. Words like the, this, that, these, those, they, them, their, there, then, and than. Because these words are very frequent, practicing the voiced TH can make your English sound much more natural.

For example, say: the book. Not de book. Try to make a soft voiced TH: the book. The teacher. The other day. This and that. These and those.

Now, not every word with TH follows a perfect rule, but here is a helpful pattern. Many content words, like nouns, verbs, and adjectives, often use the voiceless TH: think, thought, thing, three, thirsty, healthy, truth, bath. Many small grammar words often use the voiced TH: the, this, that, they, them, their, there, then. And family words like mother, father, brother also use voiced TH.

Let’s practice with a simple sentence that has both sounds:

I think this is the third thing.

Listen again: I think this is the third thing.

Think is voiceless: /θ/. This and the are voiced: /ð/. Third and thing are voiceless.

Try another one:

These three brothers live together.

These is voiced. Three is voiceless. Brothers is voiced. Together is voiced.

Here’s a quick trick. If you are not sure whether you are making the sound correctly, use the throat test. Put two fingers on your throat. For think, three, and thank, you should not feel vibration. For this, they, and mother, you should feel vibration.

And remember: the tongue position is similar for both sounds. The big difference is voice. No voice for think. Voice for this.

Let’s finish with a mini practice. Repeat after me:

Think. This.

Three. They.

Thank. That.

Thin. Then.

Both. Brother.

Mouth. Mother.

Great. Today you learned that English has two TH sounds: voiceless TH, /θ/, as in think, three, and thank you; and voiced TH, /ð/, as in this, they, and mother. Keep practicing slowly, use the throat test, and focus on a gentle tongue position. With a little daily practice, your TH will become much clearer and more natural.

d6e2d10f0cdcd238.topic: Contracciones que debes usar al hablar. Vocab: I'd've, shouldn't've, there're

lesson.title: Three Contractions That Make Your English Sound More Natural
lesson.prompt: Contracciones que debes usar al hablar. Vocab: I'd've, shouldn't've, there're
lesson.script:
Have you ever heard a native speaker say something like, “I’d’ve called you,” and thought, “Wait… what did they just say?” Don’t worry. You’re not alone. English speakers often reduce words when they talk, and these reductions can sound confusing at first. But once you understand them, your listening improves a lot, and your speaking sounds much more natural.

Today, we’re going to look at three useful spoken contractions: “I’d’ve,” “shouldn’t’ve,” and “there’re.” These are especially common in casual conversation, TV shows, podcasts, and real-life English.

Let’s start with “I’d’ve.” This is the contraction of “I would have.” In fast speech, “I would have” becomes “I’d have,” and then even shorter: “I’d’ve.” It sounds like “I-duv” or “I’d-uv.”

For example: “I’d’ve gone to the party, but I was too tired.” That means: “I would have gone to the party, but I was too tired.”

Here are a few more examples. “I’d’ve helped you if you’d asked me.” “I’d’ve bought that jacket, but it was too expensive.” “I’d’ve called earlier, but my phone died.”

Notice that we use “I’d’ve” when we are talking about an imaginary past situation. Something didn’t happen, but we are imagining a different result. In Spanish, this is similar to “habría…” For example, “I’d’ve gone” means “habría ido.”

Now, very important: “I’d’ve” is common in speech, but in formal writing, it’s better to write “I would have.” In a text message to a friend, it’s okay. In an academic essay or business report, use the full form.

Next, let’s talk about “shouldn’t’ve.” This is the contraction of “should not have.” First, “should not” becomes “shouldn’t.” Then “shouldn’t have” becomes “shouldn’t’ve.” It sounds like “shouldn’t-uv.”

We use “shouldn’t’ve” when we regret something in the past, or when we think something was a bad idea. For example: “I shouldn’t’ve eaten so much.” That means: “I should not have eaten so much.” Maybe now I feel sick, so I regret it.

More examples: “You shouldn’t’ve told him the secret.” “She shouldn’t’ve driven so fast.” “We shouldn’t’ve spent all our money on the first day of the trip.”

This structure is very useful because people often talk about regrets, mistakes, or criticism of past actions. You can also use it to sound softer or more reflective. For example: “I shouldn’t’ve said that. I was angry.” That sounds natural and honest.

Be careful with pronunciation. Don’t pronounce every word separately if you want to sound conversational. Instead of “I should not have done that,” in casual speech you’ll usually hear: “I shouldn’t’ve done that.”

Now, our third contraction: “there’re.” This is the contraction of “there are.” It sounds like “there-er,” but many speakers pronounce it very quickly, almost like one word.

For example: “There’re two restaurants near my house.” That means: “There are two restaurants near my house.”

More examples: “There’re a lot of people outside.” “There’re some things we need to discuss.” “There’re three messages for you.”

This contraction is useful, but here’s something interesting: in very careful speech, some people avoid saying “there’re” because it can feel a little awkward to pronounce. Instead, many native speakers say the full form, “there are,” or they reduce it naturally without thinking too much.

For example, you might hear: “There are a lot of options.” Or in fast speech: “There’re a lot of options.” Both are possible. The key is to recognize it when you hear it.

Let’s compare these contractions with full forms.

“I would have called you” becomes “I’d’ve called you.” “I should not have said that” becomes “I shouldn’t’ve said that.” “There are many reasons” becomes “There’re many reasons.”

Now let’s put them in a short conversation.

Imagine your friend says: “Why didn’t you come to dinner last night?” You answer: “I’d’ve come, but I had to work late.” Then your friend says: “That’s too bad. I shouldn’t’ve ordered so much food.” And you say: “Well, there’re always leftovers!”

That sounds natural, relaxed, and very conversational.

Before we finish, here’s a quick tip: you don’t need to use these contractions all the time. The most important thing is to understand them when you hear them. Then, when you feel comfortable, start using them in casual speaking. Try repeating sentences like: “I’d’ve gone,” “I shouldn’t’ve done that,” and “There’re a lot of people.” Say them slowly first, then a little faster.

So, quick recap. “I’d’ve” means “I would have,” and we use it for imaginary past situations. “Shouldn’t’ve” means “should not have,” and we use it for regrets or past mistakes. “There’re” means “there are,” and we use it to talk about the existence of plural things.

Practice these contractions out loud today. They may look strange on paper, but they’re very common in real spoken English. The more you notice them, the easier native speakers will be to understand.

lesson.title: Intonation: Questions, Sarcasm, and Emotion
lesson.prompt: Entonación: preguntas, sarcasmo y emoción
lesson.script:
Have you ever said a sentence in English and people understood the words, but not your real meaning? Maybe you wanted to sound interested, but you sounded bored. Or you wanted to make a joke, but it sounded serious. Very often, the problem is not grammar or vocabulary. The problem is intonation.

Intonation is the music of English. It is the way your voice goes up and down when you speak. In Spanish, intonation is also important, of course, but English has some patterns that can change the meaning of a sentence completely. Today, we’ll focus on three key areas: questions, sarcasm, and emotion.

Let’s start with questions.

In English, yes-or-no questions often have rising intonation. That means your voice goes up at the end. For example: “Are you ready?” Your voice rises on “ready.” “Do you like coffee?” Your voice rises on “coffee.” This rising tone shows that you are asking for confirmation: yes or no.

Now compare that with information questions, the questions that begin with words like what, where, when, why, who, or how. These usually have falling intonation. For example: “Where do you live?” Your voice goes down at the end. “What did you say?” Your voice goes down on “say.” This falling tone sounds more complete and natural.

So we have: “Are you coming?” rising intonation. But: “When are you coming?” falling intonation.

Be careful, because if you use rising intonation all the time, you may sound unsure. For example, if you say, “I work in marketing?” with your voice rising, it can sound like you are not confident. But if you say, “I work in marketing.” with falling intonation, it sounds clear and confident.

However, English is flexible. Sometimes information questions can rise if you want to show surprise or ask someone to repeat. For example, imagine your friend says, “I paid 500 dollars for this T-shirt.” You answer: “How much?” with rising intonation. That means: “I can’t believe it. Please repeat that.”

Now let’s talk about sarcasm.

Sarcasm is when you say one thing, but you really mean the opposite. Intonation is essential here. Without the correct tone, sarcasm can be confusing or even rude.

For example, imagine it is raining heavily, and someone says: “What a beautiful day.” If they say it with a flat or exaggerated tone, “What a beautiful day,” they probably mean the opposite: the weather is terrible.

Another example: Your friend arrives one hour late, and you say: “Oh, great timing.” If you say it with a normal happy tone, it sounds sincere. But if your voice is slower, flatter, or exaggerated, “Oh, great timing,” it sounds sarcastic. You mean: “Your timing is not great at all.”

A useful sarcasm pattern in English is to stretch the key word a little. For example: “That was so helpful.” If someone did not help you at all, you might say it slowly: “That was sooo helpful.” The length and tone tell the listener that you mean the opposite.

But be careful with sarcasm. In English-speaking cultures, sarcasm can be funny between friends, but it can sound aggressive in professional situations or with people you don’t know well. If you are not sure, use it lightly.

Now let’s look at emotion.

Intonation helps you show how you feel: excited, bored, angry, surprised, interested, or disappointed.

If you want to sound excited, your voice usually has more movement. It goes up and down more. For example: “That’s amazing!” You don’t want to say it like a robot: “That’s amazing.” Instead, give it energy: “That’s amazing!”

If you want to sound interested, use a warm rising tone in short responses. For example: “Really?” “That’s interesting.” “And then what happened?” These small phrases are important in conversation. They show the other person that you are listening.

Compare these two versions. First: “Really.” with a flat tone. This can sound bored or even rude. Now: “Really?” with a rising tone. This sounds curious and interested.

For disappointment, English often uses a lower, softer tone. For example: “Oh, that’s a shame.” Or: “I was really hoping to go.” Your voice falls and sounds less energetic.

For anger, the voice may become sharper, stronger, and more direct. For example: “I told you not to do that.” The stress is strong, especially on important words like “told” and “not.” But remember, anger in English is not only about volume. You can sound angry even when speaking quietly if your intonation is firm and tense.

Here’s an important tip: intonation works together with word stress. In English, the meaning can change depending on which word you emphasize.

Listen to this sentence: “I didn’t say he stole the money.”

If you stress “I” — “I didn’t say he stole the money” — it means someone else said it.

If you stress “say” — “I didn’t say he stole the money” — maybe you suggested it, but didn’t say it directly.

If you stress “he” — “I didn’t say he stole the money” — maybe someone else stole it.

If you stress “money” — “I didn’t say he stole the money” — maybe he stole something else.

Same words, different meaning. That is the power of intonation and stress.

So, quick recap. Yes-or-no questions usually rise: “Are you ready?” Information questions usually fall: “Where are you going?” Sarcasm often uses a flat, slow, or exaggerated tone: “Oh, great.” And emotion depends on the movement, energy, and stress in your voice.

Your challenge today is simple: choose one sentence, like “That’s great,” and say it in three different ways: sincerely, sarcastically, and with surprise. Record yourself if you can. Remember, in English, it’s not only what you say. It’s how you say it.

281a18b1de5cc8ab.topic: Filler words naturales (sin abusar). Vocab: you know, I mean, like, sort of, kind of, well

lesson.title: Natural Filler Words in English: Sound Fluent Without Overusing Them
lesson.prompt: Filler words naturales (sin abusar). Vocab: you know, I mean, like, sort of, kind of, well
lesson.script:
Do you ever feel that your English sounds too perfect, too rigid, or maybe a little robotic? Here’s a secret: native speakers don’t usually speak in perfect sentences. They pause, restart, soften ideas, and use little expressions to give themselves time to think. These expressions are called filler words, and today you’ll learn how to use common ones naturally, without sounding unclear or overusing them.

Filler words are words or short phrases that help us organize our thoughts while we speak. They don’t always add strong meaning, but they make speech sound more natural. In Spanish, you might use words like “pues,” “o sea,” “como,” or “bueno.” In English, we often use words like “well,” “you know,” “I mean,” “like,” “sort of,” and “kind of.”

Let’s start with “well.” We use “well” at the beginning of an answer when we need a second to think, or when the answer is not completely simple. For example: “Do you like living in the city?” “Well, yes, but it can be very noisy.” Notice that “well” gives you a natural pause. It sounds much better than staying silent for too long or saying “ehhh.” Another example: “Well, I’m not sure that’s the best option.” It can also make disagreement sound softer.

Next, “you know.” This phrase is very common in conversation. We use it when we think the other person understands the feeling or situation. For example: “The meeting was really long, you know, the kind where everyone talks but nothing gets decided.” Here, “you know” creates connection. It’s like saying, “You understand what I mean, right?” But be careful. If you use “you know” in every sentence, it can become annoying. Use it sometimes, especially when you are explaining a shared experience.

Now let’s look at “I mean.” We use “I mean” when we want to clarify, correct, or explain our idea. For example: “The movie was good. I mean, it wasn’t amazing, but I enjoyed it.” You can also use it when you want to be more precise: “She’s very direct. I mean, she tells you exactly what she thinks.” This is similar to “o sea” in Spanish, but again, don’t use it too much. It’s useful when you want to explain your real meaning.

Next is “like.” This one is extremely common, especially in informal speech. One use of “like” is to give an example or approximate idea. For example: “There were like twenty people at the party.” This means maybe around twenty, not exactly twenty. Another example: “It was like impossible to find a taxi.” Here, “like” adds emphasis, but it’s informal. You can use it with friends, but in a formal presentation or job interview, use it less.

“Like” is also used before reported thoughts or reactions in casual conversation. For example: “I was like, ‘No way!’” This means “I thought or said, ‘No way!’” It’s very natural in storytelling, but it’s not formal. So, if you’re telling a funny story to friends, it works. If you’re writing a business email, don’t use it this way.

Now let’s talk about “sort of” and “kind of.” These two expressions are very similar. They mean “a little,” “in some way,” or “not completely.” They are great for softening your opinion. For example: “The instructions were kind of confusing.” That sounds softer than “The instructions were confusing.” Another example: “I’m sort of tired, but I can continue.” This means you’re a little tired, not completely exhausted.

You can also use “kind of” and “sort of” when you don’t want to sound too direct. For example: “That idea is kind of risky.” This is softer and more polite than “That idea is bad.” In English, softening language is very important, especially in professional situations. It helps you sound respectful and diplomatic.

So, how can you use filler words naturally without abusing them? Here are three simple tips.

First, use filler words to gain time, not to fill every space. If you need a moment, say, “Well…” or “I mean…” and then continue. But don’t put five fillers in one sentence.

Second, choose the right level of formality. “Well,” “I mean,” “sort of,” and “kind of” can be used in many everyday situations. “Like” is more informal, especially when you use it many times. “You know” is conversational and friendly, but not ideal in formal writing.

Third, practice replacing long silent pauses. Instead of stopping completely, try saying: “Well, let me think.” Or: “I mean, it depends.” Or: “It’s kind of difficult to explain.” These phrases sound natural and give your brain time to organize the next idea.

Let’s compare two versions. First, a very robotic answer: “I did not like the restaurant. The food was expensive. The service was slow.” Now a more natural version: “Well, I didn’t really love the restaurant. I mean, the food was kind of expensive, and the service was sort of slow, you know?” The second version sounds more conversational and less aggressive.

But here’s the key: filler words are like salt in food. A little makes your English sound natural. Too much makes it hard to listen to. You don’t need to sound like a native speaker by using fillers constantly. The goal is to communicate clearly and naturally.

Quick recap: use “well” to start an answer or soften disagreement. Use “you know” to connect with the listener. Use “I mean” to clarify. Use “like” for informal examples or storytelling. Use “sort of” and “kind of” to soften ideas or say “a little.” Now, choose two of these expressions and try using them today in a short conversation. Keep it natural, keep it clear, and don’t overdo it.

lesson.title: How to Start Thinking in English: Practical Techniques That Work
lesson.prompt: Cómo pensar en inglés (técnicas prácticas)
lesson.script:
Have you ever tried to speak English and felt like your brain was doing a slow translation from Spanish to English? You know the idea, you know the words, but the sentence arrives late. This is very common, and the good news is: you can train your brain to think more directly in English.

Thinking in English does not mean you need to become perfectly fluent overnight. It means you start creating small mental habits in English, so your brain stops depending on Spanish for every sentence. Let’s look at some practical techniques you can use every day.

First, start with simple labeling. Look around you and name things in English: door, window, phone, keys, water, shoes. If you are making breakfast, think: coffee, bread, eggs, plate, spoon. Don’t translate from “cuchara” to “spoon.” Just connect the object directly with the English word. This is simple, but powerful. Your brain learns: object, English word. Not object, Spanish word, English word.

Next, use short English thoughts during your daily routine. You don’t need complex sentences. Start with things like: “I’m tired.” “I need coffee.” “It’s cold today.” “Where are my keys?” “I have a meeting at nine.” These little thoughts are the building blocks of real fluency. If you wait until you can think like a native speaker, you will never start. Start small, and repeat often.

A very useful technique is self-narration. This means describing what you are doing in English, in your mind or quietly out loud. For example: “I’m opening my laptop. I’m checking my email. I’m writing a message. I’m going to call my friend.” It may feel strange at first, but it trains you to produce English automatically. You are not studying English; you are living part of your day in English.

Another great technique is to ask yourself questions in English. Questions make your brain respond. Try simple questions: “What do I need to do today?” “What should I eat?” “How do I feel?” “What did I do yesterday?” Then answer with easy sentences. “I need to finish a report.” “I should eat something healthy.” “I feel a bit stressed.” “Yesterday I watched a movie.” This helps you practice real communication, even when you are alone.

Now, here is an important point: don’t translate full sentences. If you think in Spanish, “Tengo ganas de salir,” and then you try to translate it word by word, you might get stuck. Instead, learn useful English chunks. A chunk is a group of words that native speakers use naturally. For example: “I feel like going out.” “I’m not in the mood.” “That makes sense.” “Let me think about it.” “I’m looking forward to it.”

Chunks are magic because they help you speak faster. You don’t build every sentence word by word. You use ready-made pieces. So, when you learn a new expression, don’t just learn one word. Learn the whole phrase.

Another practical method is to create an English environment. Change your phone language to English if you can. Follow English accounts on social media. Watch short videos in English. Listen to podcasts while walking or cooking. The goal is not to understand every word. The goal is to make English feel normal, not foreign. Your brain needs contact with the language every day.

You can also keep a mini English diary. Every night, write three to five simple sentences about your day. For example: “Today I went to work. I had lunch with my sister. I was very busy. In the evening, I watched a series. Tomorrow I want to wake up early.” This helps you think about your real life in English. And your real life is the best material for learning.

If you are at an intermediate or advanced level, try mental debates. Choose a topic and give your opinion in English. For example: “Should people work from home?” Then think: “In my opinion, working from home is convenient because you save time. However, it can also feel lonely.” This is excellent practice for interviews, meetings, exams, and real conversations.

One more tip: accept simple English. Many learners want to express a complex idea exactly as they would in Spanish. But sometimes the best strategy is to simplify. If you can’t say, “Me da pena llegar tarde,” you can say, “I feel bad about being late.” It’s clear. It’s natural. It works. Fluency is not about saying everything perfectly. It’s about communicating smoothly.

Finally, be patient with your brain. At first, you will translate a lot. That’s normal. But if you practice labeling, short thoughts, self-narration, questions, chunks, and daily exposure, you will slowly start to think more directly in English.

So, here’s your challenge for today: choose one routine, like making coffee, walking to work, or getting ready in the morning, and narrate it in English for two minutes. Keep it simple. Repeat it tomorrow. Little by little, English will become not just something you study, but something you use inside your mind.

This means describing what you're doing in English in your mind or quietly out loud. For example, I'm opening my laptop, I'm checking my email, I'm writing a message. I'm going to call my friend. It may feel strange at first, but it trains you to produce English automatically. You're not studying English, you're living part of your day in English. Another great technique is to ask yourself questions in English. Questions make your brain respond. Try simple questions. What do I need to do today? What should I eat? How do I feel? What did I do yesterday? Then answer with easy sentences. I need to finish a report. I should eat something healthy. I feel a bit stressed. Yesterday, I watched a movie. This helps you practice real communication, even when you're alone. Now, here is an important point. Don't translate full sentences. If you think in Spanish, tengo ganas de salir, and then you try to translate it word by word, you might get stuck. Instead, learn useful English chunks. A chunk is a group of words that native speakers use naturally. For example, I feel like going out. I'm not in the mood. That makes sense. Let me think about it. I'm looking forward to it. Chucks are magic because they help you speak faster. You don't build every sentence word by word. You use ready-made pieces. So, when you learn a new expression, don't just learn one word. Learn the whole phrase. Another practical method is to create an English environment. Change your phone language to English, if you can. Follow English accounts on social media. Watch short videos in English. Listen to podcasts while walking or cooking. The goal is not to understand every word. The goal is to make English feel normal, not foreign. Your brain needs contact with the language every day. You can also keep a mini English diary. Every night, write three to five simple sentences about your day. For example, Today, I went to work. I had lunch with my sister. I was very busy. In the evening, I watched a series. Tomorrow, I want to wake up early. This helps you think about your real life in English, and your real life is the best material for learning. If you are at an intermediate or advanced level, try mental debates. Choose a topic and give your opinion in English. For example, should people work from home? Then think, in my opinion, working from home is convenient because you save time. However, it can also feel lonely. This is excellent practice for interviews, meetings, exams, and real conversations. One more tip. Accept simple English. Many learners want to express a complex idea exactly as they would in Spanish. But sometimes the best strategy is to simplify. If you can't say, me da pena llegar tarde, you can say, I feel bad about being late. It's clear. It's natural. It works. Fluency is not about saying everything perfectly. It's about communicating smoothly. Finally, be patient with your brain. At first, you will translate a lot. That's normal. But if you practice labeling, short thoughts, self-narration, questions, chunks, and daily exposure, you will slowly start to think more directly in English. So here's your challenge for today. Choose one routine, like making coffee, walking to work, or getting ready in the morning, and narrate it in English for two minutes. Keep it simple. Repeat it tomorrow. Little by little, English will become not just something you study, but something you use inside your mind.
