0ebc6a4cca6dcbc9.topic: Small talk: arrancar y mantener conversaciones. Vocab: How's it going?, What have you been up to?, By the way…

lesson.title: Small Talk: Start and Keep Conversations Going
lesson.prompt: Small talk: arrancar y mantener conversaciones. Vocab: How's it going?, What have you been up to?, By the way…
lesson.script:
Have you ever wanted to start a conversation in English, but your mind suddenly went blank? Maybe you know the person, maybe you don’t, and you just need one simple phrase to break the ice. Good news: small talk does not need to be deep, perfect, or complicated. It just needs to be friendly.

Today, we’re going to learn how to start and maintain small talk in English using three very useful expressions: “How’s it going?”, “What have you been up to?”, and “By the way…” These phrases are common, natural, and perfect for real conversations at work, at school, while traveling, or when meeting friends of friends.

Let’s start with the first one: “How’s it going?” This is a casual way to say, “How are you?” It sounds friendly and natural. You can use it with colleagues, classmates, neighbors, or people you already know a little.

For example: “Hey, how’s it going?”

The answer can be short: “Good, thanks. How about you?” Or: “Pretty good. How’s it going with you?” If things are not perfect, you can say: “Not bad,” or “I’m doing okay.” In English small talk, people often give a short answer first, and then continue with a small detail.

For example: “Pretty good, thanks. I’ve been busy with work.” Or: “Not bad. I’m just trying to survive this week!” That last one is informal and a little funny.

Now, a small pronunciation tip. “How’s it going?” often sounds like “Howzit going?” The words connect. You don’t need to pronounce every word separately. Try saying it smoothly: “How’s it going?”

The second expression is: “What have you been up to?” This means, “What have you been doing recently?” It is great when you haven’t seen someone for a while, or when you want to invite the other person to talk about their life.

For example: “Hey, long time no see! What have you been up to?”

Possible answers include: “Not much, just working a lot.” “I’ve been studying for an exam.” “I’ve been traveling a bit.” “I started a new job recently.”

Notice the grammar: “What have you been up to?” uses the present perfect, because we are talking about recent life, from the past until now. But don’t worry too much about the grammar while speaking. Learn the phrase as one complete expression.

If someone asks you, “What have you been up to?”, you can answer and then ask back: “I’ve been pretty busy with work. What about you?” That little question, “What about you?”, is very important. It helps keep the conversation going.

Small talk is like a tennis match. You don’t want to keep the ball forever, and you don’t want to let it drop. You answer, add a small detail, and ask a question back.

For example:

“How’s it going?”

“Pretty good, thanks. I’ve been working on a new project. What about you?”

“Same here, actually. Work has been busy.”

“Oh really? What kind of project are you working on?”

See? The conversation continues naturally because each person gives a little information and asks a follow-up question.

Now let’s look at the third expression: “By the way…” This phrase is extremely useful when you want to change the topic or add something new. In Spanish, it is similar to “por cierto.”

For example: “By the way, did you see the email from Ana?” Or: “By the way, are you coming to the meeting tomorrow?” Or: “By the way, I love your jacket. Where did you get it?”

“By the way” helps you move smoothly from one topic to another. Without it, the change can feel sudden. With it, you sound more natural.

Imagine this conversation:

“How’s it going?”

“Good, thanks. I’ve been busy, but everything’s fine. What have you been up to?”

“Not much. I’ve been trying to exercise more.”

“That’s great. By the way, are you still going to the gym near the office?”

Here, “By the way” connects the conversation to a new but related topic.

Let’s practice a simple small talk formula. Step one: greet the person. Step two: ask a friendly question. Step three: react to their answer. Step four: add a detail or ask a follow-up question.

For example:

“Hey, how’s it going?”

“Good, thanks. What have you been up to?”

“I’ve been studying English a lot.”

“Nice! Are you taking a course?”

This is simple, but it works.

You can also use small reactions to sound more natural. Try phrases like: “Oh, nice!” “That sounds interesting.” “Really?” “No way!” “That’s great.” “I know what you mean.” These small phrases show that you are listening.

For example:

“What have you been up to?”

“I started a new job.”

“Oh, nice! How’s it going so far?”

Or:

“I’ve been really busy lately.”

“I know what you mean. This month has been crazy for me too.”

One important tip: don’t give one-word answers if you want to maintain the conversation. If someone asks, “How’s it going?” and you say only “Good,” the conversation may stop. Instead, say: “Good, thanks. I had a relaxing weekend. How about you?” That gives the other person something to respond to.

Let’s recap. “How’s it going?” is a natural, casual way to ask how someone is. “What have you been up to?” asks about recent activities or life updates. “By the way…” helps you introduce a new topic smoothly. To keep small talk going, answer, add a small detail, and ask a question back.

Your challenge today is simple: practice one mini conversation out loud. Start with “How’s it going?”, use “What have you been up to?”, and then change the topic with “By the way…” The more you practice, the more natural it will feel.

8374e2349ad54795.topic: Inglés para el trabajo: emails profesionales. Vocab: I'm reaching out to…, Please find attached, Looking forward to hearing from you

lesson.title: Professional Emails in English: Three Phrases You Need at Work
lesson.prompt: Inglés para el trabajo: emails profesionales. Vocab: I'm reaching out to…, Please find attached, Looking forward to hearing from you
lesson.script:
Have you ever written a work email in English and thought, “Is this too direct? Too informal? Too Spanish?” Don’t worry. Today you’ll learn three very common phrases that will make your professional emails sound clear, polite, and natural: “I’m reaching out to…”, “Please find attached…”, and “Looking forward to hearing from you.”

These phrases are useful for many situations: contacting a client, sending a document, applying for a job, asking for information, or following up with a colleague. Let’s look at each one with examples you can use immediately.

First: “I’m reaching out to…”

This phrase means “I’m contacting you to…” It sounds professional and friendly. In Spanish, you might think of “Me pongo en contacto con usted para…” But in English, “I’m reaching out to…” feels natural, especially in business contexts.

For example: “I’m reaching out to ask about the status of the project.”

Or: “I’m reaching out to schedule a meeting for next week.”

Or: “I’m reaching out to see if you’re available for a quick call tomorrow.”

Notice the structure: “I’m reaching out to” plus a verb in the base form. “I’m reaching out to ask…” “I’m reaching out to confirm…” “I’m reaching out to follow up…”

A very useful expression is: “I’m reaching out to follow up on…” This means you are contacting someone again about something you discussed before.

For example: “I’m reaching out to follow up on my previous email.”

This is polite and professional, especially when someone hasn’t replied.

Now, the second phrase: “Please find attached…”

This phrase is used when you send a file with your email. For example, a report, an invoice, a CV, a presentation, or a contract.

You can write: “Please find attached the report for this month.”

Or: “Please find attached my CV and cover letter.”

Or: “Please find attached the invoice for your review.”

This phrase is common in formal and professional emails. However, in modern business English, some people prefer a slightly more natural version: “I’ve attached…”

For example: “I’ve attached the presentation for tomorrow’s meeting.”

Both are correct. “Please find attached…” is more formal. “I’ve attached…” is more direct and natural. If you are writing to a client, a manager, or someone you don’t know well, “Please find attached…” is a safe option. If you are writing to a colleague, “I’ve attached…” is perfectly fine.

Be careful with one common mistake: don’t say “Please find attached here.” Just say “Please find attached the document.” Or “I’ve attached the document.”

Now, the third phrase: “Looking forward to hearing from you.”

This is a polite way to end an email when you expect a reply. It means you are waiting for the person’s response, but in a friendly and professional way.

For example: “Looking forward to hearing from you.”

You can also make it more specific: “I look forward to hearing from you soon.” This version is a little more formal.

Or: “I look forward to your feedback.”

Or: “Looking forward to your response.”

A quick grammar note: after “look forward to,” we use a noun or a verb with -ing. So we say: “I look forward to hearing from you,” not “I look forward to hear from you.” This is a very common mistake for Spanish speakers.

Let’s put everything together in a complete email.

Subject: Meeting Follow-Up

Hello Ms. Johnson,

I hope you’re doing well.

I’m reaching out to follow up on our meeting from Monday. Please find attached the updated proposal for your review.

If you have any questions, please let me know.

Looking forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,

Carlos García

Simple, clear, and professional.

Let’s look at another example, this time for a job application.

Subject: Application for Marketing Assistant Position

Dear Hiring Manager,

I’m reaching out to apply for the Marketing Assistant position advertised on your website. Please find attached my CV and cover letter for your consideration.

Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,

Ana López

Now let’s make these phrases more flexible. Instead of always saying “I’m reaching out to…,” you can also say “I’m writing to…” This is another excellent professional phrase.

For example: “I’m writing to confirm our appointment.”

Or: “I’m writing to request more information about your services.”

“I’m writing to…” is a little more traditional. “I’m reaching out to…” is friendly and modern. Both are useful.

For attachments, remember these options: “Please find attached the document.” More formal. “I’ve attached the document.” More natural and direct.

For closing, you can use: “Looking forward to hearing from you,” “I look forward to your reply,” or “I look forward to your feedback.”

Before we finish, here’s a mini template you can adapt for many professional emails:

Hello, I hope you’re doing well.

I’m reaching out to ask about…

Please find attached…

Let me know if you have any questions.

Looking forward to hearing from you.

Best regards.

Quick recap: use “I’m reaching out to…” when you want to explain why you are contacting someone. Use “Please find attached…” when you send a file. And use “Looking forward to hearing from you” when you want to end politely and invite a response.

Try writing one short professional email today using all three phrases. The more you practice, the more natural your English emails will sound.

0032c0431c4c3c79.topic: Inglés para reuniones y videollamadas. Vocab: Let's circle back, touch base, on the same page, action items

lesson.title: English for Meetings: Sound Natural in Video Calls
lesson.prompt: Inglés para reuniones y videollamadas. Vocab: Let's circle back, touch base, on the same page, action items
lesson.script:
Have you ever been in a meeting in English and understood every word, but still felt lost when someone said, “Let’s circle back” or “Are we on the same page?” Don’t worry. These are very common business expressions, and once you learn them, you’ll sound much more natural and confident in meetings and video calls.

Today, we’ll learn four essential phrases: “let’s circle back,” “touch base,” “on the same page,” and “action items.” These expressions are used all the time in professional English, especially in team meetings, project updates, and online calls.

Let’s start with “let’s circle back.” This means “let’s return to this topic later.” We use it when a topic is important, but maybe it’s not the right moment to discuss it in detail.

For example, imagine you are in a meeting about a marketing campaign. Someone asks a question about the budget, but the meeting is focused on the timeline. You can say, “That’s a good question. Let’s circle back to the budget at the end of the meeting.”

This sounds polite and organized. You are not ignoring the question. You are simply saying, “We’ll talk about it later.” Another example: “We don’t have all the information right now, so let’s circle back next week.”

Now, let’s look at “touch base.” To “touch base” means to contact someone briefly to check in, share updates, or coordinate. It’s very common in emails and meetings.

For example, “Let’s touch base tomorrow morning to review the numbers.” This means, “Let’s have a quick conversation tomorrow morning.” You can also say, “I wanted to touch base with you about the client presentation.” That means you want to talk briefly about the presentation.

Be careful: “touch base” usually suggests a short conversation, not a long meeting. If you say, “Let’s touch base for two hours,” that sounds a little strange. It’s better for quick updates.

The third expression is “on the same page.” If people are “on the same page,” they understand and agree about the situation, the plan, or the next steps.

For example, at the beginning of a meeting, you might say, “Before we start, I want to make sure we’re all on the same page.” This means, “I want to make sure everyone has the same understanding.”

You can also use it when there has been confusion. For example, “Let’s review the timeline so we’re all on the same page.” Or, “I think we’re not on the same page about the deadline.” This is a polite way to say, “I think there is a misunderstanding.”

This phrase is very useful because it helps you manage communication without sounding aggressive. Instead of saying, “You didn’t understand,” you can say, “Maybe we’re not on the same page.” Much softer, much more professional.

Finally, let’s talk about “action items.” An “action item” is a specific task that someone needs to do after a meeting. In Spanish, you might think of it as “tareas pendientes” or “acciones a realizar.”

At the end of a meeting, someone might say, “Let’s review the action items.” This means, “Let’s confirm who is going to do what.” For example: “The first action item is for Maria to send the updated report by Friday. The second action item is for David to contact the supplier.”

In English-speaking work environments, action items are very important because meetings should lead to clear next steps. A good phrase to use is, “What are the action items from today’s meeting?” Or, “Can we confirm the action items before we finish?”

Now let’s put these expressions together in a realistic meeting example.

Imagine you’re on a video call. You can say, “Before we get into the details, I want to make sure we’re all on the same page about the project goals. Today, we’ll review the timeline, discuss any risks, and confirm the action items. If we don’t have time to discuss the budget, let’s circle back to that topic next week. Also, I’ll touch base with Ana tomorrow to check the latest numbers.”

That sounds natural, professional, and clear.

Here are a few more useful meeting sentences you can practice:

“Let’s circle back to that after we finish the main agenda.”

“I’ll touch base with the design team and get back to you.”

“Just to make sure we’re on the same page, the deadline is next Thursday, right?”

“Before we end the call, let’s go over the action items.”

A quick pronunciation tip: In natural spoken English, “let’s” often sounds like “lets,” very short and connected. “Let’s circle back.” “Let’s touch base.” Try not to separate every word too much. Smooth, connected speech will help you sound more fluent.

Let’s recap. “Let’s circle back” means let’s return to this topic later. “Touch base” means have a quick check-in or conversation. “On the same page” means everyone has the same understanding. And “action items” are the specific tasks people need to complete after a meeting.

cf2fa9b79fd561c7.topic: Negociar y dar tu opinión sin sonar grosero. Vocab: I see your point, but…, I'd push back on that, fair enough

lesson.title: How to Disagree Politely in English
lesson.prompt: Negociar y dar tu opinión sin sonar grosero. Vocab: I see your point, but…, I'd push back on that, fair enough
lesson.script:
Have you ever wanted to say “I don’t agree” in English, but you were afraid of sounding rude? This is a very common problem, especially in meetings, negotiations, or even casual conversations. The good news is: in English, you can disagree clearly and still sound respectful. Today, you’ll learn three very useful phrases: “I see your point, but…”, “I’d push back on that”, and “fair enough.”

Let’s start with the first phrase: “I see your point, but…” This is one of the most useful ways to disagree politely. It means: “I understand what you’re saying, but I have a different opinion.” It shows that you are listening before you give your own idea.

For example, imagine your colleague says, “We should reduce the budget for marketing.” You can answer, “I see your point, but I think marketing is essential right now if we want to attract new customers.”

Notice the structure: first, you recognize the other person’s idea. Then, you introduce your different opinion. This sounds much softer than saying, “No, that’s wrong.” In English, directly saying “you’re wrong” can sound too aggressive in many professional situations.

Here’s another example: “I see your point, but I’m not sure that plan will work with our current timeline.” This is polite, clear, and professional.

Now let’s look at the second phrase: “I’d push back on that.” This is a little stronger. It means: “I disagree with that idea, and I want to challenge it.” You often hear this in business conversations, debates, and negotiations. It is not rude if you say it with a calm tone, but it is more direct than “I see your point, but…”

For example, someone says, “The client will definitely accept a higher price.” You could say, “I’d push back on that. The client has already mentioned that their budget is limited.”

This phrase is useful when you need to defend your position. It shows confidence. But be careful: because it is stronger, it’s good to explain your reason immediately after.

Another example: “I’d push back on that. I don’t think we have enough data to make that decision yet.”

You can also make it softer by saying, “I’d gently push back on that.” This sounds more diplomatic. For example: “I’d gently push back on that. From my experience, customers usually need more time before making a decision.”

Now, let’s talk about “fair enough.” This phrase is very common in spoken English. It means something like: “Okay, I understand,” or “That’s a reasonable point.” It doesn’t always mean you completely agree. Sometimes it means you accept the other person’s argument, even if your opinion is still different.

For example, you say, “I think we should launch the product this month.” Your colleague says, “I’m worried we haven’t tested it enough.” You can answer, “Fair enough. Let’s do one more round of testing before we decide.”

Here, “fair enough” shows that you are flexible and reasonable. It helps reduce tension in a negotiation.

Another example: “Fair enough. I hadn’t considered that.” This is a great phrase when someone gives you new information and you want to show openness.

But pronunciation and tone matter. If you say “fair enough” with a friendly tone, it sounds respectful. If you say it with a cold or sarcastic tone, it can sound dismissive. So keep your voice calm and natural.

Let’s compare these three phrases in a mini negotiation.

Person A says, “I think we should ask for a 20 percent discount.”

You say, “I see your point, but 20 percent might be too much for the supplier. Maybe we could start with 15 percent.”

Person A says, “But we need to reduce costs quickly.”

You say, “Fair enough. Cost reduction is important. Still, I’d push back on asking for too much too soon. We don’t want to damage the relationship.”

This sounds polite, strategic, and professional. You are not simply saying yes to everything, but you are also not attacking the other person.

Here’s a simple formula you can use when giving your opinion in English: acknowledge, disagree politely, and give a reason.

For example: “I see your point, but I’d look at it differently. The numbers show that customer retention is improving.”

Or: “Fair enough, but I still think we should wait until we have more information.”

Or stronger: “I’d push back on that because the deadline is not realistic for the team.”

The key is to avoid sounding personal. Don’t say, “You don’t understand,” or “That’s a bad idea.” Instead, focus on the idea, the data, the timeline, the budget, or the risk.

So, quick recap: use “I see your point, but…” when you want to disagree softly. Use “I’d push back on that” when you want to challenge an idea more confidently. And use “fair enough” when you want to show that you understand or accept part of the other person’s argument.

Practice these phrases out loud today. Try creating three examples from your own work or daily life. The more you use them, the more natural and confident you’ll sound in English negotiations and conversations.

1625ac7e7967b3d6.topic: Storytelling: cómo contar una anécdota en inglés. Tiempos narrativos y conectores

lesson.title: How to Tell a Great Anecdote in English
lesson.prompt: Storytelling: cómo contar una anécdota en inglés. Tiempos narrativos y conectores
lesson.script:
Have you ever started telling a story in English and suddenly thought, “Wait… should I use the past simple, past continuous, or past perfect?” Don’t worry. Today you’ll learn how to tell a clear, natural anecdote in English using narrative tenses and connectors, so your stories sound more fluent and more engaging.

Let’s begin with the basic structure of an anecdote. A good short story usually has three parts: the setting, the main events, and the ending or reaction.

First, the setting. This is where you explain when and where the story happened, and what was happening at that moment. For this, we often use the past continuous.

For example: “Last Saturday, I was walking home from the gym when something really strange happened.”

“I was walking” gives the background. It sets the scene. Then “something happened” introduces the main action.

Now, for the main events, we usually use the past simple. The past simple is for completed actions, one after another.

For example: “I heard a noise, turned around, and saw a dog running towards me.”

These are the key actions in the story: heard, turned, saw. Simple, clear, and direct.

Next, we use the past perfect when we want to talk about something that happened before another past action.

For example: “I realized I had left my sandwich in my bag.”

The leaving happened before the realizing, so we use “had left.” This helps your listener understand the order of events.

Let’s compare two examples. “When I arrived, the meeting started.” This means I arrived, and then the meeting started. But “When I arrived, the meeting had started” means the meeting started before I arrived. Very different meaning.

Now let’s talk about connectors. Connectors are essential because they help your story flow. Without connectors, your story can sound like a list: “I arrived. I saw my friend. We talked. We left.” It’s understandable, but not very engaging.

To start your anecdote, you can use expressions like: “A few years ago,” “Last weekend,” “One day,” “When I was at university,” or “This happened when I was on holiday.”

For example: “A few years ago, I was travelling around Italy with a friend.”

To move the story forward, use connectors like “then,” “after that,” “a few minutes later,” “suddenly,” and “while.”

For example: “We were looking for our hotel when suddenly it started to rain.”

“Suddenly” is great for surprises. “While” is useful for background actions: “While we were waiting for a taxi, a man came up to us.”

To show contrast, use “but,” “however,” or “although.”

For example: “We were exhausted, but we decided to keep walking.” Or: “Although I was nervous, I tried to stay calm.”

To show cause and result, use “because,” “so,” and “that’s why.”

For example: “I didn’t have any battery on my phone, so I couldn’t check the address.”

And to finish your anecdote, you can use phrases like: “In the end,” “Eventually,” “Finally,” or “The funny thing is…”

For example: “In the end, we discovered that our hotel was only two streets away.”

Now let’s put everything together in a complete anecdote.

“Last year, I was visiting London for the first time. I had planned everything carefully: the museums, the restaurants, and even the exact train routes. On the second day, I was walking to the underground station when I realized I had left my wallet at the hotel. I felt really stressed because I didn’t have any cash or cards with me. While I was checking my bag for the third time, a woman asked me if I needed help. I explained the situation, and she kindly paid for my ticket. Then she said, ‘Don’t worry, this happened to me last week!’ In the end, I got back to the hotel, found my wallet on the bed, and learned an important lesson: always check your bag before leaving.”

Notice the tenses. “I was visiting” and “I was walking” give background. “I realized,” “I felt,” “she asked,” and “I explained” are main events in the past simple. “I had left” and “I had planned” show actions that happened earlier.

Here’s a simple formula you can use: start with the time and place, set the scene with the past continuous, describe the main events with the past simple, use the past perfect for earlier actions, and connect everything with words like “suddenly,” “then,” “while,” “so,” and “in the end.”

So, quick recap: past continuous for background, past simple for main events, past perfect for the earlier past, and connectors to make your story flow naturally. Now try telling a short anecdote from your own life in English. Start with: “A few years ago, I was…” and build from there. The more you practise, the more natural your storytelling will sound.

b9410707eef7f50e.topic: Inglés para viajar: aeropuerto, hotel, restaurante (nivel avanzado). Más allá del básico

lesson.title: Advanced Travel English: Sound Confident at Airports, Hotels, and Restaurants
lesson.prompt: Inglés para viajar: aeropuerto, hotel, restaurante (nivel avanzado). Más allá del básico
lesson.script:
Have you ever known the basic travel phrases, but still felt lost when someone at the airport, hotel, or restaurant spoke naturally? Today we’re going beyond “Where is the gate?” and “I have a reservation.” We’ll learn polished, practical English that helps you sound confident, flexible, and clear when things don’t go perfectly.

Let’s start at the airport. At an advanced level, you need to handle changes, delays, and special requests. For example, instead of saying, “My flight is late,” you can say, “Do you have any updated information on the delay?” Or, “Has the boarding time been pushed back?” This phrase, “pushed back,” means delayed or moved to a later time.

If you have a connection, you might say, “I have a tight connection. Is there any chance you could check whether I’ll still make it?” A “tight connection” means very little time between flights. If you need help, try, “Would it be possible to put me on an earlier flight?” or “Could you check if there are any alternative routes?” These sound polite and natural.

At security or immigration, you may hear questions like, “What’s the purpose of your visit?” Instead of just saying, “Tourism,” you can answer more naturally: “I’m here on holiday for about ten days,” or “I’m attending a conference, but I’ll also be doing some sightseeing.” If they ask, “Where will you be staying?” you can say, “I’ll be staying at the Riverside Hotel for the first few nights, then with friends.” Notice the future structure “I’ll be staying,” which sounds natural when talking about travel plans.

Now let’s move to the hotel. Basic English gets you checked in, but advanced English helps you solve problems politely. Imagine your room is noisy. You could say, “I’m afraid the room is a bit noisier than expected. Would it be possible to move to a quieter one?” “I’m afraid” here does not mean you are scared. It’s a polite way to introduce a complaint.

If the air conditioning doesn’t work, say, “The air conditioning doesn’t seem to be working properly. Could someone take a look at it?” This is softer than “It doesn’t work.” Another useful phrase is, “Is there any flexibility with check-out time?” This is a natural way to ask if you can leave later. You can also say, “Would it be possible to store my luggage after check-out?”

If you want to ask about services, try these: “Is breakfast included in the rate?” “Do you offer airport transfers?” “Could you recommend somewhere nearby that isn’t too touristy?” That last phrase is excellent. “Too touristy” means a place feels made only for tourists, not very authentic.

Now, the restaurant. At an advanced level, it’s not only about ordering food. It’s about preferences, allergies, recommendations, and tone. Instead of “I want this,” say, “I’ll have the grilled salmon, please,” or “I think I’ll go for the risotto.” “Go for” is a very natural way to say “choose.”

If you need a recommendation, ask, “What would you recommend if I’m in the mood for something light?” or “What’s your most popular dish?” If you have dietary restrictions, be clear: “I’m allergic to peanuts. If something is wrong, stay polite but direct. “I’m sorry, but I think this may not be what I ordered.” Or, “Would you mind checking on our order? We’ve been waiting for quite a while.” “Quite a while” means a long time, but it sounds more polite than complaining aggressively.

You can say, “Sorry, could you say that again a bit more slowly?” or “Just to make sure I understood, the gate has changed to B12, right?” This phrase, “Just to make sure I understood,” sounds advanced and prevents mistakes.

Another useful strategy is confirming details. For example: “So check-out is at eleven, and breakfast is served until ten, correct?” Or, “So the kitchen closes in about fifteen minutes, is that right?” These small confirmations make you sound fluent and organized.

The goal is not just to speak English, but to manage real situations with confidence.

6b97b699eeaeb758.topic: Quejarse educadamente (complaints). Vocab: I'm afraid there's been a mix-up, I'd appreciate it if…

lesson.title: Polite Complaints in English
lesson.prompt: Quejarse educadamente (complaints). Vocab: I'm afraid there's been a mix-up, I'd appreciate it if…
lesson.script:
Have you ever needed to complain in English, but you didn’t want to sound rude or aggressive? Maybe your hotel room wasn’t ready, your order was wrong, or someone made a mistake with your booking. In these situations, the words you choose are very important. A polite complaint can solve the problem faster and help you sound calm, professional, and confident.

Today, you’ll learn how to complain politely in English using natural phrases like “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up” and “I’d appreciate it if…” These expressions are very useful in restaurants, hotels, shops, airports, workplaces, and customer service situations.

Let’s start with the phrase “I’m afraid…” In English, “I’m afraid” does not always mean “I’m scared.” It is often used to introduce bad news or a problem politely. For example, instead of saying, “You made a mistake,” which can sound too direct, you can say, “I’m afraid there’s been a mistake.” This sounds much softer.

Now let’s look at this key phrase: “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up.” A “mix-up” means confusion or a mistake, especially when information, orders, reservations, or details are incorrect. For example, imagine you arrive at a hotel and they say you booked a single room, but you booked a double room. You could say, “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up. I booked a double room, not a single room.”

Notice the tone. You are not attacking the person. You are explaining the problem clearly. This is much better than saying, “This is wrong” or “You made a mistake with my room.”

Here are more examples. At a restaurant, if the waiter brings the wrong dish, you can say, “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up. I ordered the chicken salad, not the pasta.” At the airport, if your seat number is different from the one you selected, you might say, “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with my seat reservation.” At work, if a meeting was scheduled at the wrong time, you could say, “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up about the meeting time. I had it in my calendar for three o’clock.”

Another very useful phrase is “I’d appreciate it if…” This means “I would be grateful if…” or “I would like you to…” but it sounds more polite and professional. It is a great way to ask someone to fix a problem.

For example: “I’d appreciate it if you could check the booking again.” Or, “I’d appreciate it if you could send me the correct invoice.” Or, “I’d appreciate it if this could be resolved as soon as possible.”

Be careful with the grammar. After “I’d appreciate it if,” we often use a subject plus a past form or “could.” For example, “I’d appreciate it if you could call me back.” “I’d appreciate it if you sent the documents today.” In everyday speech, “could” is very common because it sounds polite and natural.

Let’s compare direct and polite complaints. Direct: “You charged me too much.” Polite: “I’m afraid there’s been a mistake with the bill. I’d appreciate it if you could check it for me.” Direct: “This product doesn’t work.” Polite: “I’m afraid this product isn’t working properly. I’d appreciate it if you could help me with a replacement.” Direct: “Nobody answered my email.” Polite: “I’m afraid I haven’t received a reply to my email yet. I’d appreciate it if someone could get back to me soon.”

A good polite complaint usually has three parts. First, introduce the problem politely. Second, explain the facts clearly. Third, ask for a solution.

For example: “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with my order. I ordered a medium coffee and a cheese sandwich, but I received a large tea and a ham sandwich. I’d appreciate it if you could correct the order, please.”

Here’s another example in a hotel: “Excuse me, I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with my reservation. I booked a room with a sea view, but the room I was given faces the car park. I’d appreciate it if you could look into this for me.”

And one more in a workplace situation: “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with the report. I received last month’s version instead of the updated one. I’d appreciate it if you could send me the latest file when you have a moment.”

To sound even more polite, you can add softeners like “Excuse me,” “Sorry to bother you,” “when you have a moment,” and “please.” For example, “Excuse me, I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with the bill. I’d appreciate it if you could check it when you have a moment, please.”

But remember: polite does not mean weak. You can be polite and still be clear. Avoid angry language, but don’t be so indirect that the other person doesn’t understand the problem. Say what happened, give the correct information, and explain what you need.

Let’s recap. Use “I’m afraid…” to introduce a problem politely. Use “There’s been a mix-up” when there has been confusion or an error. Use “I’d appreciate it if…” to ask for a solution in a respectful way. A simple formula is: “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up with… I’d appreciate it if you could…”

Now try making your own polite complaint. Think of a real situation: a wrong order, a late delivery, or an incorrect bill. Start with “I’m afraid there’s been a mix-up,” then ask for help with “I’d appreciate it if you could…” The more you practice, the more natural and confident you’ll sound in English.

01acc2ef155ea28f.topic: Disculparse y aceptar disculpas con matices. Vocab: My bad, I owe you an apology, no worries, don't sweat it

lesson.title: Apologizing Naturally: From “My Bad” to “I Owe You an Apology”
lesson.prompt: Disculparse y aceptar disculpas con matices. Vocab: My bad, I owe you an apology, no worries, don't sweat it
lesson.script:
Have you ever said “sorry” in English and felt like it was too much, too little, or just not natural? In real conversations, apologizing is not only about the word “sorry.” It is also about tone, context, and how serious the situation is. Today, you’ll learn how to apologize and accept apologies with more nuance, using useful expressions like “My bad,” “I owe you an apology,” “No worries,” and “Don’t sweat it.”

Let’s start with a very casual apology: “My bad.” This means “That was my mistake.” It is informal, friendly, and common in everyday situations. For example, imagine you send your friend the wrong address for a café. When you realize, you can say, “Oh, my bad. I sent you the old address.” Or if you interrupt someone by accident, you might say, “Sorry, my bad. Go ahead.”

“My bad” is useful when the mistake is not very serious. It shows that you accept responsibility, but in a relaxed way. However, be careful: don’t use “my bad” for serious problems. If you forgot an important meeting with your boss, “My bad” may sound too casual or even disrespectful.

For more serious or sincere situations, use “I owe you an apology.” This phrase is stronger and more thoughtful. It means, “I need to apologize to you because I did something wrong.” For example: “I owe you an apology. I was impatient yesterday, and that wasn’t fair to you.” Or, “I owe you an apology for not replying sooner. I know you were waiting for my answer.”

This expression is excellent when you want to sound mature, responsible, and sincere. It is common in professional and personal contexts. You can follow it with a clear explanation: “I owe you an apology. I misunderstood what you said, and I reacted too quickly.” Notice the structure: first, you recognize the mistake; then, you explain briefly; and finally, if needed, you say what you’ll do differently.

A complete apology often has three parts. First: acknowledge the problem. “I’m sorry I was late.” Second: take responsibility. “I should have left earlier.” Third: repair or improve the situation. “Next time, I’ll send you a message if I’m delayed.” This sounds much better than only saying “Sorry” and moving on.

Now let’s talk about accepting apologies. In English, people often respond in a calm, friendly way, especially when the problem is small. One of the most common expressions is “No worries.” It means “It’s okay” or “Don’t worry about it.” For example, if someone says, “Sorry I’m five minutes late,” you can answer, “No worries. I just got here too.” If a coworker says, “Sorry, I forgot to attach the file,” you might reply, “No worries. Just send it when you can.”

“No worries” is warm and relaxed. It tells the other person that you are not angry. It is common in many English-speaking countries, especially in casual and semi-formal situations.

Another useful phrase is “Don’t sweat it.” This is very informal and means “Don’t stress about it.” For example, if your friend spills a little coffee on the table and says, “Oh no, I’m so sorry,” you can say, “Don’t sweat it. I’ll grab some napkins.” Or if someone makes a small mistake during a game, you can say, “Don’t sweat it. It happens.”

Like “my bad,” “don’t sweat it” is casual. It’s great with friends, classmates, or close coworkers. But in a formal situation, it may sound too relaxed. If your manager apologizes for changing your schedule, “Don’t sweat it” might be okay if you have a friendly relationship, but “No worries” or “That’s okay” may sound more neutral.

Now, let’s compare tones. If you make a small mistake, you can say, “Oops, my bad.” If the mistake affects someone more, say, “I’m really sorry about that.” If you need to be more serious, say, “I owe you an apology.”

And when someone apologizes to you, choose your response depending on how you feel. If it is truly fine, say, “No worries.” If it is very small, say, “Don’t sweat it.” If you appreciate the apology but the situation was serious, you can say, “Thank you for apologizing. I appreciate it.” This is important because you don’t always have to say “It’s okay” immediately. Sometimes, you may need to acknowledge the apology without pretending everything is perfect.

For example, imagine someone says, “I owe you an apology. I shouldn’t have spoken to you like that.” You could answer, “Thank you for saying that. I appreciate your apology.” This sounds honest and respectful. You are accepting the apology, but not minimizing what happened.

Let’s practice with a few mini-dialogues. “Sorry, I took your pen by mistake.” “No worries.” “My bad, I forgot to call you back.” “Don’t sweat it. I know you were busy.” “I owe you an apology. I gave you the wrong information in the meeting.” “Thank you for letting me know. I appreciate your honesty.”

So, quick recap: use “My bad” for small, casual mistakes. Use “I owe you an apology” when you want to sound sincere and take responsibility. Use “No worries” to accept an apology in a friendly, calm way. And use “Don’t sweat it” when the problem is small and you want the other person to relax.

This week, try noticing how people apologize in English in movies, series, or real conversations. Don’t just listen for “sorry.” Listen for the tone, the situation, and the response. That’s how your English becomes not only correct, but natural.

759ae3ab2797bdeb.topic: Discusiones y desacuerdos civilizados. Vocab: I beg to differ, with all due respect, I'm not so sure about that

lesson.title: How to Disagree Politely in English
lesson.prompt: Discusiones y desacuerdos civilizados. Vocab: I beg to differ, with all due respect, I'm not so sure about that
lesson.script:
Have you ever wanted to disagree in English, but you were afraid of sounding rude, aggressive, or too direct? This is a very common problem, especially for Spanish speakers, because the way we express disagreement changes a lot from culture to culture. The good news is that English gives you many polite and elegant ways to say, “I don’t agree,” without creating tension.

Today, we’re going to learn three useful expressions for civilized discussions and disagreements: “I beg to differ,” “with all due respect,” and “I’m not so sure about that.” These phrases are especially useful in meetings, debates, conversations with colleagues, or any situation where you want to give a different opinion respectfully.

Let’s start with “I beg to differ.” This expression means “I disagree,” but in a more formal and polite way. It sounds confident, and sometimes a little old-fashioned or elegant. You can use it when someone says something and you want to challenge the idea clearly, but without being rude.

For example, imagine someone says, “Learning English after the age of thirty is almost impossible.” You could answer, “I beg to differ. Many adults become fluent in English with consistent practice.”

Notice that after “I beg to differ,” we usually explain why. We don’t just say the phrase and stop. We give a reason. Another example: “I beg to differ. In my experience, remote work can actually improve productivity.”

Now, be careful. “I beg to differ” is polite, but it is also quite direct. It clearly says, “I disagree.” So it’s better for situations where a clear opinion is appropriate, like a discussion, a meeting, or a debate.

The second expression is “with all due respect.” This phrase is used before a disagreement, especially when you are speaking to someone who has authority, more experience, or a strong opinion. It means something like, “I respect you, but I disagree.”

For example: “With all due respect, I don’t think that solution will work in the long term.”

Or: “With all due respect, we need to consider the cost before making a final decision.”

This phrase can be very useful, but you need to use the right tone. If your tone is calm and respectful, it sounds professional. But if your tone is sarcastic or angry, it can sound rude. In fact, native speakers sometimes use “with all due respect” when they are annoyed, so context and voice are very important.

Here’s a good structure: “With all due respect, I understand your point, but I see it differently.” This softens the disagreement. You are showing that you listened before presenting your opinion.

For example: “With all due respect, I understand your point, but I see it differently. I think the team needs more time to finish the project properly.”

The third expression is “I’m not so sure about that.” This is softer and more conversational. It means you have doubts or you don’t fully agree. It’s less direct than “I beg to differ,” and it’s perfect when you don’t want to sound too strong.

For example, someone says, “This marketing campaign will definitely be a success.” You could say, “I’m not so sure about that. We haven’t tested it with younger customers yet.”

Or someone says, “We should cancel the meeting.” You might respond, “I’m not so sure about that. Maybe we should make it shorter instead.”

This phrase is excellent because it opens the door to discussion. You are not attacking the other person’s idea. You are simply saying, “Let’s think about this more carefully.”

Now let’s compare the three expressions.

“I beg to differ” is clear and confident. Use it when you strongly disagree, but still want to sound polite. For example: “I beg to differ. The data actually shows the opposite.”

“With all due respect” is formal and careful. Use it when you disagree with someone respectfully, especially in professional or serious situations. For example: “With all due respect, I think we should review the proposal again.”

“I’m not so sure about that” is softer and more natural in everyday conversation. Use it when you have doubts or want to disagree gently. For example: “I’m not so sure about that. It might be more complicated than it seems.”

A very important tip: in English, polite disagreement often includes three parts. First, acknowledge the other person’s idea. Second, introduce your disagreement politely. Third, give a reason.

For example: “I see what you mean, but I’m not so sure about that. The timeline seems too short.”

Another example: “That’s an interesting point. With all due respect, I think we should look at the numbers before deciding.”

And one more: “I understand why you think that, but I beg to differ. The situation has changed since last year.”

This structure helps you sound respectful, mature, and professional. You are not saying, “You’re wrong.” You are saying, “I see your point, but here is another perspective.”

Let’s practice with a few mini-dialogues. Someone says, “Online classes are never as effective as face-to-face classes.” You can answer, “I beg to differ. Online classes can be very effective when they are interactive and well organized.”

Someone says, “We don’t need to prepare for the presentation.” You can say, “I’m not so sure about that. We should at least review the main points.”

Someone says, “This is the only possible solution.” You can respond, “With all due respect, I think there may be other options we haven’t considered.”

So, quick recap. Use “I beg to differ” when you want to disagree clearly but politely. Use “with all due respect” when you want to show respect before giving a different opinion. Use “I’m not so sure about that” when you want to disagree gently or express doubt.

Your challenge today is to use one of these phrases in your own sentence. Think of an opinion you disagree with, and respond politely in English. Remember: civilized disagreement is not about winning an argument. It’s about expressing your ideas clearly, respectfully, and confidently.

44c46e5263f07ea4.topic: Humor en inglés: sarcasmo, ironía y juegos de palabras

lesson.title: Humor in English: Sarcasm, Irony, and Puns
lesson.prompt: Humor en inglés: sarcasmo, ironía y juegos de palabras
lesson.script:
Have you ever heard a joke in English, understood every word, and still thought, “Wait… why is that funny?” Don’t worry. English humor can be tricky, especially because a lot of it depends on tone, double meanings, and saying the opposite of what you really mean.

Today, we’ll look at three important types of humor in English: sarcasm, irony, and puns. These are very common in movies, series, social media, and everyday conversations. By the end, you’ll recognize them more easily and understand why people laugh.

Let’s start with sarcasm.

Sarcasm is when someone says the opposite of what they really mean, usually to be funny, critical, or a little dramatic. The key is tone of voice. For example, imagine it’s raining heavily, your shoes are completely wet, and your friend says, “What a beautiful day.” They don’t really mean the weather is beautiful. They mean the opposite.

Another example: your computer freezes right before an important meeting, and you say, “Great. Perfect timing.” Again, you don’t mean it’s great. You mean it’s terrible timing.

Sarcasm in English often uses positive words in negative situations. Words like “great,” “wonderful,” “fantastic,” and “perfect” can become sarcastic depending on the tone. For example: “Oh, fantastic. More homework.” Or: “Lovely. The bus is late again.”

Be careful, though. Sarcasm can sound rude if used with people you don’t know well. With close friends, it can be funny. In professional situations, use it carefully. A safe way to recognize sarcasm is to ask yourself: Does the sentence match the situation? If someone says “Amazing!” after dropping their coffee, it is probably sarcasm.

Now, let’s talk about irony.

Irony is when there is a contrast between what you expect and what actually happens. It is similar to sarcasm, but not exactly the same. Sarcasm is usually something a person says. Irony can be a situation.

For example, imagine a fire station burns down. That’s ironic because a fire station is supposed to stop fires. Or imagine a traffic police officer gets a parking ticket. That’s ironic because they enforce traffic rules, but they broke one.

Here’s another everyday example: You spend an hour cleaning your car, and five minutes later, a bird makes it dirty again. That’s not just unlucky. It can feel ironic because the result is the opposite of what you wanted.

In English, people often say, “That’s ironic,” when something surprising happens in an opposite or unexpected way. But many learners, and even native speakers, confuse irony with simple coincidence. If you meet your friend at the supermarket by chance, that’s a coincidence. But if you go to the supermarket to avoid your friend and then you meet them there, that could be ironic.

A useful phrase is: “The irony is…” For example: “The irony is, I bought a book about saving money, and it was really expensive.”

Now let’s move to puns.

A pun is a joke based on words with double meanings or similar sounds. Puns are very common in English because English has many words that sound the same but have different meanings.

For example: “I used to be a baker, but I couldn’t make enough dough.” This is a pun because “dough” means the mixture used to make bread, but it also means money in informal English. So the joke is: the baker couldn’t make enough bread dough, and also couldn’t make enough money.

Here’s another one: “I’m reading a book about anti-gravity. It’s impossible to put down.” “Put down” can mean to place something on a table, but it also means to stop reading a book. So the joke has two meanings.

One more: “Time flies like an arrow. Fruit flies like a banana.” This is a classic pun. In the first sentence, “flies” is a verb: time moves fast. In the second sentence, “fruit flies” are small insects, and “like” means enjoy. So the sentence changes meaning completely.

Puns can be clever, silly, or very bad. In fact, English speakers often use the expression “dad joke” for a simple, predictable pun. For example: “I’m afraid for the calendar. Its days are numbered.” It’s funny because “days are numbered” means something will end soon, but a calendar literally has numbered days.

For Spanish speakers, puns can be especially challenging because they usually don’t translate well. If you translate them word by word, the joke disappears. The best strategy is to identify the two meanings of the key word. Ask yourself: Does one word have another meaning? Does it sound like a different word?

Let’s compare the three quickly.

Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean, often with a special tone. “Great, another meeting.”

Irony is when reality is the opposite of what you expect. A dentist with terrible teeth, for example.

A pun is wordplay, using double meanings or similar sounds. “I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.” Here, “interest” means both curiosity and money earned in a bank.

So, how can you improve your understanding of humor in English? Watch short comedy clips with subtitles. Pay attention to tone. Notice when people laugh. Write down jokes that confuse you and look for double meanings. And remember: if you don’t understand a joke immediately, it doesn’t mean your English is bad. Humor is one of the hardest parts of any language.

Quick recap: sarcasm depends on saying the opposite, irony depends on unexpected contrast, and puns depend on wordplay. The next time you hear a joke in English, don’t panic. Listen for the tone, check the situation, and look for double meanings. Little by little, English humor will start to make much more sense.

d84cdc068296622a.topic: Inversion avanzada para énfasis. Vocab: Not only… but also, Under no circumstances, Only then did I realize

lesson.title: Advanced Inversion for Emphasis: Sound More Powerful in English
lesson.prompt: Inversion avanzada para énfasis. Vocab: Not only… but also, Under no circumstances, Only then did I realize
lesson.script:
Have you ever heard a sentence like, “Under no circumstances should you open that door,” and thought, “Wait… why is the verb before the subject?” That unusual word order is called inversion, and advanced English speakers use it to add emphasis, drama, and formality. Today, you’ll learn how to use inversion with three powerful structures: “Not only… but also,” “Under no circumstances,” and “Only then did I realize.”

Let’s start with the basic idea. In normal English, we usually say: subject plus verb. For example: “I realized the truth.” But with inversion, we change the order, often putting an auxiliary verb before the subject: “Only then did I realize the truth.” This sounds more dramatic and emphatic.

This structure is common in formal writing, speeches, exams, storytelling, and professional communication. You don’t need to use it in every conversation, but when you use it well, your English sounds more sophisticated.

First: “Not only… but also.” We use this to add strong emphasis when we want to say that two things are true, and the second thing is often surprising or impressive.

A normal sentence would be: “She speaks English fluently, and she also writes beautifully.”

With inversion, we can say: “Not only does she speak English fluently, but she also writes beautifully.”

Notice the pattern: “Not only” plus auxiliary verb plus subject plus main verb. “Not only does she speak…” Not “Not only she speaks.” This is a common mistake for Spanish speakers, because in Spanish the word order can feel more flexible. In English, after “Not only” at the beginning, we need inversion.

Here are more examples. “Not only did we miss the train, but we also lost our tickets.” “Not only is this course practical, but it is also enjoyable.” “Not only has he improved his pronunciation, but he has also gained confidence.”

Pay attention to the auxiliary. In the present simple, use “do” or “does”: “Not only does he work hard…” In the past simple, use “did”: “Not only did they arrive late…” With the verb “be,” just invert the verb and subject: “Not only is she talented…” With perfect tenses, invert “have” or “has”: “Not only has the company grown…”

Now let’s look at “Under no circumstances.” This expression means “absolutely never” or “in no situation.” It is strong, formal, and very clear. You might see it in rules, warnings, contracts, or serious advice.

Normal sentence: “You should not share your password under any circumstances.”

With inversion: “Under no circumstances should you share your password.”

Again, notice the word order: “should you share,” not “you should share.” The negative expression comes first, so we invert the auxiliary and the subject.

More examples: “Under no circumstances should employees enter this area without permission.” “Under no circumstances can the data be copied.” “Under no circumstances are visitors allowed to feed the animals.”

This structure sounds very firm. If you say, “You shouldn’t do that,” it sounds like advice. But if you say, “Under no circumstances should you do that,” it sounds like a serious rule or warning.

Now for our third phrase: “Only then did I realize.” This is excellent for storytelling. We use it when something becomes clear after a specific moment or event.

Normal sentence: “I realized the mistake only then.”

With inversion: “Only then did I realize the mistake.”

This sounds more dramatic. It creates suspense. Imagine a story: “I checked my bag, looked at my phone, and searched every pocket. Only then did I realize my passport was still at home.” Much stronger, right?

Here are more examples. “Only then did we understand the real problem.” “Only after the meeting did she tell us the truth.” “Only when I moved abroad did I understand how important culture is.”

Be careful: when “only” introduces a time expression at the beginning, we often use inversion. For example: “Only after three months did he find a job.” “Only when the lights went out did we notice the storm.” “Only then did they decide to apologize.”

Let’s compare the emotional effect. Normal: “I understood the situation only when I spoke to her.” Emphatic: “Only when I spoke to her did I understand the situation.” The second version highlights the moment of realization.

Here is a useful formula for these structures. With negative or limiting expressions at the beginning, use auxiliary verb plus subject plus main verb. For example: “Not only did I learn new vocabulary…” “Under no circumstances should you ignore the instructions.” “Only then did I realize what had happened.”

One important tip: don’t overuse inversion. If every sentence sounds dramatic, the effect disappears. Use it when you want to emphasize contrast, seriousness, surprise, or an important discovery.

Let’s finish with a mini practice. Transform this normal sentence: “She not only passed the exam, but she also got the highest score.” The advanced version is: “Not only did she pass the exam, but she also got the highest score.”

Another one: “You should never sign a contract without reading it.” More formal and emphatic: “Under no circumstances should you sign a contract without reading it.”

Last one: “I realized how much I had changed only then.” More dramatic: “Only then did I realize how much I had changed.”

So, quick recap: use “Not only… but also” to emphasize two impressive facts. Use “Under no circumstances” for strong rules or warnings. Use “Only then did I realize” to make a moment of discovery more dramatic. Try writing three sentences today using these structures, and you’ll immediately add more power and sophistication to your English.

A normal sentence would be, she speaks English fluently, and she also writes beautifully. With inversion, we can say, not only does she speak English fluently, but she also writes beautifully. This is a common mistake for Spanish speakers, because in Spanish, the word order can feel more flexible. In English, after not only at the beginning, we need inversion. Here are more examples. Not only did we miss the train, but we also lost our tickets. Not only is this course practical, but it is also enjoyable. Not only has he improved his pronunciation, but he has also gained confidence. Pay attention to the auxiliary. d260cac1dca79013.topic: Cleft sentences: 'It was John who…', 'What I need is…'

lesson.title: Cleft Sentences: How to Emphasize What Really Matters
lesson.prompt: Cleft sentences: 'It was John who…', 'What I need is…'
lesson.script:
Have you ever wanted to make one part of your sentence sound more important, more dramatic, or more precise? Instead of saying, “John broke the window,” you can say, “It was John who broke the window.” Suddenly, the focus is clear: not Peter, not Maria, not the dog. John. This is the power of cleft sentences.

Today we’re going to look at cleft sentences like “It was John who…” and “What I need is…” These structures are very common in English, especially when we want to emphasize information, correct someone, or sound more natural and expressive.

Let’s start with the first type: “It was… who” or “It was… that.”

A normal sentence could be: “John called me yesterday.”

If I want to emphasize the person, I can say: “It was John who called me yesterday.”

This means John was the important or surprising information. Maybe I expected someone else to call. Maybe someone asked, “Was it Mark?” and I answer, “No, it was John who called me.”

We can emphasize different parts of the sentence. Listen to these examples.

“John called me yesterday.”

If we emphasize the person: “It was John who called me yesterday.”

If we emphasize the time: “It was yesterday that John called me.”

If we emphasize the action or event, we usually use a different structure, which we’ll see in a moment.

Here are more examples.

“It was my sister who told me the news.” This emphasizes my sister.

“It was in Madrid that we met for the first time.” This emphasizes the place.

“It was after the meeting that she explained the problem.” This emphasizes the time.

A useful detail: when we talk about people, we often use “who.” For things, places, or times, we often use “that.” For example: “It was the noise that woke me up.” “It was in June that they got married.”

Now, be careful. Spanish speakers sometimes translate directly and produce sentences that sound unnatural. In English, the structure is usually: “It was” plus the emphasized information plus “who” or “that” plus the rest of the sentence.

For example, don’t say: “Was John who called me.” Say: “It was John who called me.” The word “it” is necessary.

Now let’s look at the second common type: “What I need is…”

This is called a wh-cleft sentence. It begins with a “what” clause, and then we give the important information after the verb “be.”

For example: “I need a break.” That’s a normal sentence.

If I want to emphasize “a break,” I can say: “What I need is a break.”

This sounds stronger and more focused. It’s like saying, “The thing I really need is a break.”

Here are more examples.

“I want more time.” becomes “What I want is more time.”

“She needs support.” becomes “What she needs is support.”

“We need a clear plan.” becomes “What we need is a clear plan.”

This structure is very useful in conversations, meetings, presentations, and even arguments, because it helps you sound clear and confident.

For example, imagine your team is discussing a problem. You can say: “What we need is better communication.” That sounds more powerful than just “We need better communication.”

Or imagine someone is giving you too many explanations, but you want action. You can say: “What I need is a solution, not an excuse.”

Notice the contrast: “a solution, not an excuse.” Cleft sentences are excellent for contrasts.

Let’s compare normal sentences and cleft sentences.

Normal: “You forgot to send the email.”

Cleft: “What you forgot to do was send the email.”

Normal: “I like the ending of the movie.”

Cleft: “What I like about the movie is the ending.”

Normal: “He bought a new laptop.”

Cleft: “What he bought was a new laptop.”

In wh-cleft sentences, we often use expressions like: “What I like is…,” “What I hate is…,” “What I don’t understand is…,” “What happened was…,” and “What you need to do is…”

Let’s look at these in context.

“What I don’t understand is why he left so early.” This emphasizes the thing I don’t understand.

“What happened was that we missed the train.” This is very common when explaining a situation.

“What you need to do is call the office.” This emphasizes the action someone should take.

One important grammar point: after “What you need to do is,” the next verb can be in the base form: “call,” “send,” “check,” “wait.” For example: “What you need to do is check your email.”

You may also hear: “What you need to do is to check your email.” Both are possible, but without “to” is very common in spoken English.

Now let’s think about pronunciation and rhythm. In cleft sentences, the emphasized information usually receives stronger stress.

“It was John who called me.” Stress “John.”

“What I need is a break.” Stress “break.”

“What we need is a clear plan.” Stress “clear plan.”

This stress helps listeners understand your message immediately.

So, when should you use cleft sentences? Use them when you want to emphasize, clarify, correct, or contrast.

For example, to correct: “It wasn’t John who called me. It was his brother.”

To emphasize: “What I really need is some rest.”

To contrast: “What I wanted was advice, not criticism.”

To explain: “What happened was that I lost my keys.”

Let’s do a quick practice. Change this sentence: “Maria organized the event.” If we emphasize Maria, we say: “It was Maria who organized the event.”

Now change: “I need more information.” We say: “What I need is more information.”

Great. To recap, use “It was… who” or “It was… that” to emphasize a person, thing, place, or time. Use “What I need is…” and similar structures to emphasize the most important idea, need, action, or explanation.

Try creating three sentences today: one with “It was… who,” one with “It was… that,” and one with “What I need is…” The more you use cleft sentences, the more natural and expressive your English will sound.

b1253018706f159b.topic: Subjunctive en inglés (sí existe). Vocab: I suggest that he be…, If I were you…

lesson.title: The Subjunctive in English: Yes, It Exists!
lesson.prompt: Subjunctive en inglés (sí existe). Vocab: I suggest that he be…, If I were you…
lesson.script:
Did you know English has a subjunctive? Many learners think the subjunctive is only important in Spanish, with forms like fuera, tenga, or sea. But English has it too. It is just more hidden, and often much simpler. Today, you will learn two very useful structures: I suggest that he be, and If I were you.

Let’s start with the big idea. The subjunctive is used to talk about things that are not simply facts. We use it for recommendations, demands, important wishes, imaginary situations, and advice. In Spanish, the subjunctive changes a lot depending on the verb and the person. In English, the form is usually easier, but you need to recognize it.

First, let’s look at the present subjunctive after verbs like suggest, recommend, demand, insist, request, and propose.

For example: I suggest that he be more careful.

Notice something interesting. We do not say he is. We say he be. That sounds strange if you are thinking about normal grammar, because normally we say he is, she is, it is. But in the subjunctive, we use the base form of the verb: be, go, study, arrive, speak, not the third-person form.

Here are more examples: She recommended that he study more. The teacher insisted that everyone arrive on time. They requested that the report be finished by Friday. I propose that we start earlier.

In all these examples, the verb after that is in the base form: study, arrive, be, start. Not studies, arrives, is, or starts.

Let’s compare normal English and subjunctive English.

Normal fact: He is careful. Subjunctive recommendation: I suggest that he be careful.

Normal fact: She studies every day. Subjunctive recommendation: I recommend that she study every day.

Normal fact: The meeting starts at nine. Subjunctive proposal: I propose that the meeting start at nine.

This form is common in formal English, business English, academic English, and American English in particular. In British English, people often use should instead. For example, I suggest that he should be more careful. Or, I recommend that she should study more. Both are understandable, but the subjunctive without should sounds very natural in formal American English.

Now, important detail: after suggest, we do not normally say suggest someone to do something. Spanish speakers often want to say, I suggest him to study. But that is not natural. Say: I suggest that he study. Or more informally: I suggest studying more. Another option is: I think he should study more.

So remember these patterns: I suggest that he study. I recommend that she go. I insist that they be honest. The company requires that all employees wear ID badges.

Now let’s move to the second key expression: If I were you.

This is also subjunctive. Why? Because I am not you. It is an imaginary situation. In normal past grammar, we say I was, he was, she was. But in the subjunctive for hypothetical situations, we often use were for all subjects.

If I were you, I would apologize. If she were here, she would know what to do. If he were more patient, he would be a better manager.

Again, this is not about the real past. It is about an unreal or imaginary situation. If I were you means imagining that I am in your position. It is one of the most common ways to give advice in English.

Let’s compare: I was tired yesterday. That is a real past fact. If I were rich, I would travel around the world. That is imaginary, not a real past event.

You may also hear people say If I was you, especially in informal conversation. Many native speakers say it. However, If I were you is the standard and more correct form, especially in exams, writing, interviews, and professional situations. If you learn one version, learn this one: If I were you.

Now let’s practice with useful examples.

If I were you, I would talk to your boss. If I were you, I would not send that email. If I were you, I would take the opportunity. If I were you, I would ask for more information.

Notice the structure: If I were you, I would plus base verb. I would talk. I would not send. I would take. I would ask.

You can also use were with other subjects: If he were more organized, he would finish faster. If we were in Madrid right now, we would visit the Prado Museum. If this were easier, everyone would do it.

Let’s connect this to Spanish. If I were you is similar to Si yo fuera tú. And I suggest that he be more careful is similar in meaning to Sugiero que él sea más cuidadoso. But be careful: do not translate word by word. English uses a very simple base verb form in many subjunctive sentences.

Let’s do a quick correction practice. Which sentence sounds better?

I suggest that he is on time. Or: I suggest that he be on time. The second one is the subjunctive and sounds more formal and correct.

I recommend that she goes to the doctor. Or: I recommend that she go to the doctor. The correct subjunctive form is: she go.

If I was you, I would wait. Or: If I were you, I would wait. The standard form is: If I were you.

So, quick recap. Yes, English has a subjunctive. Use the base verb after expressions like I suggest that, I recommend that, I insist that, and it is important that. For example: I suggest that he be honest. I recommend that she study tonight. And use were for imaginary situations and advice: If I were you, I would practice this structure.

Your challenge today: create three sentences. One with I suggest that, one with I recommend that, and one with If I were you. Say them out loud, because grammar becomes real when you use it.

1160bc5c3e8c4d5b.topic: Phrasal verbs avanzados (parte 4). Vocab: put up with, come down to, boil down to, run by, weigh in on

lesson.title: Advanced Phrasal Verbs: From Tolerating Problems to Giving Opinions
lesson.prompt: Phrasal verbs avanzados (parte 4). Vocab: put up with, come down to, boil down to, run by, weigh in on
lesson.script:
Have you ever understood every word in a sentence, but still felt lost because of the phrasal verb? For example: “I can’t put up with this anymore,” or “Let me run that by my boss.” These expressions are extremely common in natural English, especially in work conversations, discussions, and everyday problems. Today, we’ll learn five advanced phrasal verbs that will make your English sound much more fluent: put up with, come down to, boil down to, run by, and weigh in on.

Let’s start with put up with. To put up with something means to tolerate it, especially when it is annoying, difficult, or unpleasant. In Spanish, it’s similar to “soportar” or “aguantar.” For example: “I can’t put up with the noise from my neighbors anymore.” That means the noise is bothering me, and I don’t want to tolerate it. Another example: “She puts up with a lot of stress at work.” Notice the structure: put up with plus a noun or situation. “I put up with the traffic.” “He puts up with rude customers.” And in a question: “How do you put up with that?” Very useful.

Now, come down to. This means that the final result depends on one main factor. It’s often used when you reduce a situation to the most important point. For example: “The decision comes down to money.” This means money is the key factor. Maybe there are many details, but in the end, money decides. Another example: “The match came down to the last five minutes.” That means the final five minutes were decisive. You can also say: “It all comes down to trust.” Beautiful phrase. It means trust is the essential thing.

Next, boil down to. This is very similar to come down to, but it often means “when you simplify everything, the real issue is…” Imagine you have a long, complicated problem, and you want to explain the basic idea. You can say: “It boils down to communication.” In other words, after analyzing everything, the real problem is communication. Another example: “Their argument boils down to a lack of respect.” Or: “Success often boils down to consistency.” For Spanish speakers, think of “se reduce a” or “en el fondo es.” The difference between come down to and boil down to is subtle.
